items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.summary: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . Tags: c , research , sqlite , rust , claude
items.summary_html:
Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust

I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted.

I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted:

I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse

Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting.so(or whatever) file

This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster!

Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted:

Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation

And it did, using "Clinger's fast path":

Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better:

first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns

Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this:

Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder

Here's the resulting report.

Tags: c, research, sqlite, rust, claude

items.title: Your Chatbot Is Not a Vault: 13 Things to Keep Out of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini Before a Judge…
items.summary: Your Chatbot Is Not a Vault: 13 Things to Keep Out of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini Before a Judge Reads Them A federal judge, a 20-million-log court order and OpenAI’s own CEO agree: what you type into a chatbot has no legal shield. Your Chatbot Is Not a Vault: Why AI Chats Are Fragile? Photo by Google DeepMind on Unsplash When FBI agents searched Bradley Heppner’s home, they walked out with about 31 documents that recorded his conversations with an AI chatbot. Not contracts. Not bank statements. Chat transcripts. Heppner was a defendant in a criminal fraud case, and he had been using the public version of Claude to think through his legal exposure. Some of what he typed came from his own lawyers. His defense team said the pages were privileged. In February 2026, a federal judge in Manhattan disagreed . Judge Jed Rakoff’s reasoning began with a point so basic it sounds like a punchline: the chatbot is not a lawyer. One case is a story. A few of them together are a pattern. OpenAI’s CEO has said on the record that ChatGPT conversations carry no legal confidentiality the way a therapist’s or lawyer’s office does. A federal judge in New York has ordered OpenAI to produce 20 million de-identified chat logs in the New York Times copyright fight. None of this is rumor. All of it is documented. Nobody needs to quit chatbots over this. They are useful, and they aren’t going anywhere. The point is narrower. What you type into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini is closer to a message passed through a company than a thought kept in a locked notebook. The law hasn’t caught up with how personal we’ve all become with these tools. Below are 13 things I’d keep out of the chat box, ordered roughly from “could hurt you in court” to “could hurt you in your inbox.” The heavy ones come first. General information, not legal advice. The rules here are changing fast. 1. Your legal trouble, in any amount of detail Heppner’s real mistake wasn’t asking a chatbot questions. It was feeding it what his lawyers had told him. The government argued, and the judge agreed, that sharing privileged material with a third-party AI platform may waive protection over the original attorney-client conversations too. The court also saw no reasonable expectation of confidentiality on a consumer platform. Read that twice. The damage didn’t stop at his chatbot chats. It reached back to the real ones. The ruling did leave a narrow door open. The judge noted that if counsel had directed Heppner to use the tool, the picture might have looked different. White & Case’s reading of the decision draws the same line between lawyer-directed use and a client freelancing at midnight. If you’re in a dispute, a divorce, an investigation or a lawsuit, treat a chatbot like a stranger sitting at the next table. Ask your lawyer whether you should use AI at all, and never paste in their emails or their advice. 2. A confession, even a joking or half-true one Chat logs get read the way search histories get read, as a window into your state of mind. A CNN wire story carried by CTV News describes investigators increasingly using AI chat histories as evidence. Legal experts in it compare them to Google searches, which can reveal motive and intent. One cybersecurity lawyer called them a “treasure trove” for law enforcement. In the Palisades fire case, prosecutors say Jonathan Rinderknecht used ChatGPT to generate fire imagery months earlier. They also say that after calling 911 to report the blaze, he asked whether a cigarette makes you at fault for a fire. CNN’s story adds that he has pleaded not guilty and that his lawyer is seeking to exclude some of the ChatGPT evidence. You don’t have to be guilty of anything for this to matter. A dark joke, a hypothetical about a coworker, a “how would someone even do that” typed out of pure curiosity: it all sits in a log with a timestamp and no context. Someone else gets to supply the context. 3. The 2 a.m. emotional dump Plenty of people use these tools as a therapist now. Altman said so himself on a podcast. Young people especially treat ChatGPT like a life coach. He also said that if you bring it your most sensitive stuff and a lawsuit follows, OpenAI “could be required to produce that.” He called the situation a problem, and he’s right. A therapist works under confidentiality rules. A chatbot works under a privacy policy. A privacy policy can be rewritten, and a judge’s order can override it. The warm tone of a reply doesn’t change which of those you’re dealing with. If you need to vent, vent into a notes app. If you want a chatbot’s help thinking something through, strip out the names, places and anything else that points to a real person, including you. And if things feel heavy, a friend, a counselor or a helpline is a better first call than a chat window. 4. Medical records, lab results and diagnoses Uploading a blood test to a chatbot feels like a clever second opinion. Legally, it’s a different animal from handing the same sheet to your doctor. HIPAA, the US health privacy law, binds hospitals, insurers and their partners. Becker’s Hospital Review summarized a New York Times report in which privacy experts said it doesn’t cover popular chatbots, and that uploaded records could be used for training. OpenAI has since launched ChatGPT Health, which lets people connect medical records and apps like Apple Health. The company says those conversations are encrypted, stored separately and not used to train its models. Privacy advocates still point out that the data isn’t protected by HIPAA, and one said OpenAI hasn’t explained how it decides when to share health data with law enforcement. That’s a company promise, not a statute. Ask about symptoms in general terms. Leave out your name, date of birth, insurance ID and the scan itself. If you want an AI to read your records, use a tool your provider has formally approved. 5. Your employer’s source code and trade secrets Samsung’s engineers weren’t trying to leak anything. They were trying to debug. After the company let them use ChatGPT, TechRadar reported three separate leaks of sensitive data, source code among them, and Samsung responded with a ban on company devices. It wasn’t only Samsung. Amazon had reportedly warned its own staff months earlier not to share code or confidential information with ChatGPT, after the company noticed answers that resembled internal Amazon data. The lesson is simple. If your company hasn’t handed you an approved AI tool and a written rule about it, assume the answer is no. Ask before you paste. “I was only fixing a bug” is a weak thing to say in a disciplinary meeting. 6. Client data and anything under NDA Freelancers and consultants make this mistake more than anyone, because nobody is watching. A client’s contract, a customer spreadsheet, a pitch deck marked confidential: dropping any of it into a personal chatbot account hands it to a third party you promised to keep it from. The account terms matter here. A Stanford team that compared the privacy policies of Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI found that all six appear to use chat data for training by default. Opt-outs exist, but you have to go find them. Read your contract before you paste anything. Many NDAs treat any outside disclosure as a breach, whether or not a human ever reads the chat. Redact names, figures and anything identifying. Work plans can come with different data terms from personal accounts, so read those before you assume. 7. Passwords, API keys and recovery codes This one sounds too obvious to list, and it still happens constantly, usually by accident. You paste a config file to fix an error, or a script with a token sitting on line 12, and the secret rides along without you noticing. In January 2025, researchers at Wiz found a publicly exposed DeepSeek database holding over a million lines of logs, including chat history and secret keys. DeepSeek secured it quickly after being told. The point isn’t about one company. Chat logs and credentials end up in the same pile, and piles leak. Swap real tokens for placeholders before you paste. If a secret has already gone into a chat, treat it as burned. Rotate it, because deleting the chat won’t undo anything. The same goes for passwords, two-factor backup codes and wallet recovery phrases. No useful answer ever needs the real one. 8. ID numbers, bank logins and card details Social Security number, Aadhaar, passport number, card number, net banking password. A chatbot doesn’t need any of them to help you with a form or a statement. Black them out first. The platform’s own plumbing can fail too. In March 2023, a bug in an open-source library meant OpenAI said payment-related information of 1.2% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers may have been visible to another user during a nine-hour window. It listed name, email, payment address, card type, the last four digits and the expiry date. OpenAI also said full card numbers were not exposed and that the number of people who actually saw anything was extremely low. That leak came from subscription pages, not from anything users typed into chats. That’s exactly why it matters. If a bug can surface billing details, assume a pasted scan of your passport is a bigger prize. Type “XXXX” where the number would go. The answer will be just as good. 9. Other people’s private business Your sister’s diagnosis. A friend’s affair. A coworker’s HR complaint. You’re typing it out to get advice, and your intentions are good, but the person you’re describing never agreed to be part of the conversation. The policies behind these tools are thin on what happens next. The same Stanford researchers, in their peer-reviewed analysis of those privacy policies , found that some developers retain chat data indefinitely. A secret about someone else can outlive the friendship it came from. And as item 1 showed, a chat about a named person can be read by a lawyer or an investigator as easily as one about you. Change the names. Make it “a friend” and “a coworker.” Cut anything that would let a stranger work out who is who. If you couldn’t say it to the person’s face, think twice before typing it behind their back. 10. Threats, even when you’re only venting Anger types fast. A rant about a boss, an ex or a neighbor can feel harmless at 1 a.m., and a chatbot will happily keep talking while you type it. OpenAI has said its systems flag conversations where users seem to be planning harm to others. Those chats go to human reviewers , and if a reviewer decides there is an imminent threat, the company can report it to law enforcement. To an automated filter, a furious rant and a real plan can look alike. A person then has to decide which one it was. You don’t need to be dangerous for this to go badly. You only need to be misread. Put the anger into a notes app, a voice memo or a text to a friend who knows you. A chat window is a bad place to say something you’d be nervous to see quoted in a report. 11. Your address, your routine and photos that give both away Typing “we’re out of town from the 12th to the 20th” next to a home address is the kind of detail that should never share a sentence, in any app. Photos can say it for you. In 2025, a viral reverse-location trend showed OpenAI’s newer models working out where a picture was taken from visual clues alone, and it raised doxxing concerns. Your balcony view, a street corner or the front of your building can be enough. If you want help with a photo, crop out street signs, house numbers and landmarks. Ask about neighborhoods in general terms instead of giving your exact block. Keep dates away from places. Your routine is part of your safety, and it’s very easy to give away one sentence at a time. 12. Your children’s photos, names and school Parents ask chatbots about homework, tantrums, health worries and birthday parties, and the details creep in. A full name, a school, a photo for “what’s wrong with this rash.” Each one is small. Together they build a profile of a person who never agreed to be profiled. The American Psychological Association’s June 2026 piece on sharenting notes that children’s faces count as sensitive biometric data . It says they can be scraped from posts and used to create deepfakes. Uploading a picture to a chatbot isn’t the same as posting it publicly. The principle still holds, though: once a child’s likeness leaves your hands, you can’t call it back. Use first names or none. Describe the situation instead of uploading the face. If you’re asking about your child’s health, type the symptom and the age range, not the whole story. They’ll have their own digital footprint soon enough, and it shouldn’t start with yours. 13. Anything you’d hate to see behind a Share button The most embarrassing leaks in this story weren’t hacks. They were buttons. In 2025, Fast Company found more than 4,500 shared ChatGPT links indexed by Google , some with names, resumes and confidential work content. People had made them discoverable with a checkbox. OpenAI pulled the option after the backlash. Meta’s AI app has a public Discover feed. After users unwittingly posted chats there, Engadget reported that Meta added a warning telling people to avoid sharing personal or sensitive information. Meta says posting takes several deliberate steps. Plenty of people still ended up on the feed. Before you share a chat, read it as a stranger would, from the top. Look for names, numbers and anything that points to you. If you ever shared one in the past, go back through your shared links and delete the ones you don’t need. The one test worth keeping Thirteen items is a lot to remember. Here’s a shorter version. Before you hit enter, picture the conversation printed out and sitting on a table between you and a stranger. Imagine a lawyer, a coworker, a journalist or a hacker holding the pages. If your stomach drops, rewrite it or don’t send it. None of this means giving up chatbots. They’re useful, and nobody needs to feel guilty for using them. The law just hasn’t caught up with how we use them. Even OpenAI’s CEO has said he wants privacy protections for AI chats closer to what a doctor or lawyer gets. Until that exists, the only protection you can count on is the one you apply yourself. Bradley Heppner learned the lesson the hard way, in front of a federal judge. You can learn it for free, by deciding what never goes in the box. Your Chatbot Is Not a Vault: 13 Things to Keep Out of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini Before a Judge… was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

If you want help with a photo, crop out street signs, house numbers and landmarks. Ask about neighborhoods in general terms instead of giving your exact block. Keep dates away from places. Your routine is part of your safety, and it’s very easy to give away one sentence at a time.

12. Your children’s photos, names and school

Parents ask chatbots about homework, tantrums, health worries and birthday parties, and the details creep in. A full name, a school, a photo for “what’s wrong with this rash.” Each one is small. Together they build a profile of a person who never agreed to be profiled.

The American Psychological Association’s June 2026 piece on sharenting notes that children’s faces count as sensitive biometric data. It says they can be scraped from posts and used to create deepfakes. Uploading a picture to a chatbot isn’t the same as posting it publicly. The principle still holds, though: once a child’s likeness leaves your hands, you can’t call it back.

Use first names or none. Describe the situation instead of uploading the face. If you’re asking about your child’s health, type the symptom and the age range, not the whole story. They’ll have their own digital footprint soon enough, and it shouldn’t start with yours.

13. Anything you’d hate to see behind a Share button

The most embarrassing leaks in this story weren’t hacks. They were buttons.

In 2025, Fast Company found more than 4,500 shared ChatGPT links indexed by Google, some with names, resumes and confidential work content. People had made them discoverable with a checkbox. OpenAI pulled the option after the backlash.

Meta’s AI app has a public Discover feed. After users unwittingly posted chats there, Engadget reported that Meta added a warning telling people to avoid sharing personal or sensitive information. Meta says posting takes several deliberate steps. Plenty of people still ended up on the feed.

Before you share a chat, read it as a stranger would, from the top. Look for names, numbers and anything that points to you. If you ever shared one in the past, go back through your shared links and delete the ones you don’t need.

The one test worth keeping

Thirteen items is a lot to remember. Here’s a shorter version.

Before you hit enter, picture the conversation printed out and sitting on a table between you and a stranger. Imagine a lawyer, a coworker, a journalist or a hacker holding the pages. If your stomach drops, rewrite it or don’t send it.

None of this means giving up chatbots. They’re useful, and nobody needs to feel guilty for using them. The law just hasn’t caught up with how we use them. Even OpenAI’s CEO has said he wants privacy protections for AI chats closer to what a doctor or lawyer gets. Until that exists, the only protection you can count on is the one you apply yourself.

Bradley Heppner learned the lesson the hard way, in front of a federal judge. You can learn it for free, by deciding what never goes in the box.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he was 'unfaithful' to his wife: Read his note to staff
items.summary: Nvidia said it's investigating whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang said he had an affair in a note to staff on Sunday. US officials believe the woman with whom Huang had the affair was recruited as a spy by the Chinese government, the NYT reported. Nvidia said Sunday it was investigating whether Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang apologized for being "unfaithful" to his wife in a note to staff on Sunday. Earlier in the day, Nvidia said its board of directors opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The New York Times reported last month that US officials believe Alice Huang, a former executive at a data center company in Singapore, was a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing. The outlet reported that surveillance of Huang showed that she had developed a relationship with the Nvidia founder. Read Huang's note to staffers here: To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. Jensen Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Nvidia Inquiry, Anthropic, CoreWeave and Unity News Promise Big Week
items.summary: If you were hoping for a quiet week after the turmoil of the past few days, take a vacation. This week is promising to be nearly as busy as the last one was. Nvidia's announcement this afternoon that its board is “initiating an independent investigation” about reports that CEO Jensen Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” casts a shadow over the future of one of the most important people in AI. Nvidia added that the “board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Still, once an inquiry like this starts, who knows where it will lead? It will coincide with a congressional inquiry into the same subject. Buckle up. Meanwhile, Anthropic is next week expected to start its institutional road show to market its IPO, my colleague Valida reported on Friday. The volatility of the market lately has prompted questions about whether the AI firm might delay the offering, but so far it appears to be on track. What valuation Anthropic will get is a whole other question , however. OpenAI won’t be left out: The AI firm is expected to host a call with investors next week to discuss its third-quarter results, we reported on Friday. Maybe it should include reporters on the call to make life easier for everyone (especially us). While all this is underway, neocloud investors need to brace for another volatile week. CoreWeave, arguably the best known of that bunch of companies, is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. This will give CEO Michael Intrator an opportunity to try to reassure investors about the company’s ability to weather the tightening AI financing market.

items.title: Nvidia says it's investigating whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a 'foreign intelligence effort'
items.summary: Jensen Huang. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia said its board of directors is opening an investigation into CEO and founder Jensen Huang. On Sunday, Huang said in a note to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. Read his note to staffers below. Nvidia's board of directors says it is opening an investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." The announcement came after Huang sent a note to Nvidia staff admitting he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang wrote. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully." The New York Times reported that US officials believed Alice Huang, an executive at one of Nvidia's customers, Megaspeed — with whom the Nvidia CEO had reportedly had a relationship — had been recruited as a spy to gather information about Nvidia for the Chinese government. That raised national security concerns, given Nvidia's relationship with China — a major market where US export controls limit its chip sales. Last week, a group of lawmakers sent a letter to Huang requesting he participate in a closed-door briefing on security protocols against "foreign adversary espionage" and Huang's relationship with Alice Huang. The meeting was proposed for November 18. In a statement on Sunday, Nvidia said the board of directors prioritizes US national and economic security, which it considers "paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders." The board added that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," a spokesperson for the company told Business Insider. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." A former Nvidia employee told Business Insider they were "very sad and disappointed," adding that "it really was not something you might expect from Jensen." Another former employee said many of their colleagues still at the company were shocked and saddened, and had expressed concern for Huang's wife and family. Bill Ackman, the billionaire founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, said in an X post on Sunday that the Nvidia CEO is an "incredible human" and that "even incredible humans make mistakes." "He takes full responsibility as he should," Ackman wrote. "We should all support him and his family." items.title: [One Million AI Engineer Special] How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.summary: What do you assign when a coding agent can finish last year’s homework in one prompt? In the second run of Stanford’s CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and explain the patch to the person who might merge it. We invited Mihail, who teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, to celebrate one million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. He opens up the course syllabus and shows us which lessons survived contact with his own engineering team. Monaco built its agent workspaces, bought its code review tools, and gave an on-call agent access to Datadog and GitHub. We ask how he decides which tools his team needs to own. Watch the full interview and screenshares on YouTube . Show notes Stanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus and assignments. The Emperor Has No Clothes — Mihail builds a coding agent from scratch. Demystifying Claude Code — Mihail traces a real agent harness. Monaco’s agent workspaces — How the team sets up a workspace for each agent. How to Kill the Code Review — Our essay on what happens when code generation outruns review. Basis’s Authority Map — How agents distinguish current behavior from earlier design decisions. items.title: How AI Agents Remember: A Simple Guide to Memory, Vector Search, and RAG
items.summary:
Why Do AI Agents Need Memory Management? An AI chatbot may seem to remember earlier messages, but the language model (LLM) does not remember them on its own. It uses the information sent to it with each request. The agent — the system around the model — keeps track of useful information. It sends the model the details it needs for each task. Here’s why this matters: 1. The model has limited space. It can read only a certain amount of text at once. This limit is called the context window. Long conversations, files, and search results can fill it up. Older information may then be left out, even if it is important. 2. More text can cost more and take longer. Sending the whole conversation each time adds extra work. Sending only useful details can save time and money. 3. Too much unrelated information can hurt answers. Important details can get lost in the clutter. Clear, focused input helps the model answer better. 4. Long tasks need progress tracking. The agent needs to know what is finished, what is next, and what has been decided. Otherwise, it may repeat work or ignore earlier decisions. 5. The model may lack needed information. Private data and recent information may not be part of its training. Search tools can find these details when needed. 6. Users need control over memory. Memory management helps decide what to save, forget, or avoid storing. It can also let users view and delete saved information. Core Memory Strategies for AI Agents Two simple ways to manage memory are a rolling context window and keyword search. A rolling window keeps recent messages. Keyword search finds saved information by matching words. Context Windows, Explained Simply What is a context window? It is the space available for the information sent to the model in one request. Think of it as short-term memory for that request. What is context length? It is the maximum amount of text the model can handle at once, measured in tokens. What is a token? A token is a small piece of text. In English, it is roughly three-quarters of a word, or about four characters. · 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words How big are context windows? · Older models: about 4,000 tokens (~3,000 words, ~12 pages) or 8,000 tokens (~6,000 words, ~24 pages) · GPT-5 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet: up to 272,000 tokens · Gemini 2.5: up to 1 million tokens Why it matters The context window has limited space. Include what the model needs and leave out unrelated details. The simplest approach Send the current question and the conversation so far. When there is not enough space, keep the newest messages. Rolling context window · Send the conversation history that fits in the window with each request. · When the window fills up, remove the oldest messages to make room for new ones. Pros · Easy to build · Simple · Works for many use cases Cons · Older information is removed even when it is important. · Long questions and answers can fill the window quickly. import argparse import os import re from langchain_core.messages import ( AIMessage, AnyMessage, HumanMessage, RemoveMessage, SystemMessage, ) from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver from langgraph.graph import END, START, MessagesState, StateGraph MAX_MESSAGES = 6 # summarize once state holds more than this many messages KEEP_LAST = 2 # how many recent messages survive a summarization pass OLLAMA_MODEL = "llama3.2" # also try gpt-oss:20b, qwen:4b, deepseek-r1:1.5b OLLAMA_URL = os.environ.get("OLLAMA_HOST", "http://localhost:11434") class State(MessagesState): summary: str def _strip_thinking(msg: AIMessage) -> AIMessage: """Reasoning models (deepseek-r1, ...) may inline blocks; keep them out of state.""" if isinstance(msg.content, str): msg.content = re.sub(r" .*? ", "", msg.content, flags=re.DOTALL).strip() return msg def make_llm(model: str | None): from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama model = model or OLLAMA_MODEL print(f"Using Ollama model '{model}' at {OLLAMA_URL}
") return ChatOllama(model=model, base_url=OLLAMA_URL, temperature=0) | RunnableLambda(_strip_thinking) def build_graph(llm): def chat(state: State): prompt: list[AnyMessage] = [SystemMessage("You are a helpful, concise assistant.")] if state.get("summary"): prompt.append( SystemMessage( "Earlier messages in this conversation were condensed into this summary. " f"Treat it as things you remember about the user:
{state['summary']}" ) ) prompt += state["messages"] print(f" -> sending {len(prompt)} messages to the model") return {"messages": [llm.invoke(prompt)]} def should_summarize(state: State): return "summarize" if len(state["messages"]) > MAX_MESSAGES else END def summarize(state: State): old, summary = state["messages"][:-KEEP_LAST], state.get("summary", "") rules = ( "Write it as short bullet points. Always keep every personal fact about the user " "(name, location, preferences) and the topics discussed. Output only the bullets." ) if summary: instruction = ( f"This is the summary so far:
{summary}

" f"Rewrite the summary so it also covers the new messages above. {rules}" ) else: instruction = f"Summarize the conversation above. {rules}" new_summary = llm.invoke(old + [HumanMessage(instruction)]).content print(f" ** rolled {len(old)} old messages into the summary") # RemoveMessage tells the add_messages reducer to drop these ids from state. return {"summary": new_summary, "messages": [RemoveMessage(id=m.id) for m in old]} builder = StateGraph(State) builder.add_node("chat", chat) builder.add_node("summarize", summarize) builder.add_edge(START, "chat") builder.add_conditional_edges("chat", should_summarize, ["summarize", END]) builder.add_edge("summarize", END) # The checkpointer persists state per thread_id across invocations. return builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) DEMO_TURNS = [ "Hi! My name is Deepak and I live in Noida.", "I'm learning LangGraph. What is a StateGraph in one sentence?", "What is a checkpointer for?", "My favourite language is Python.", "Give me one tip for writing good prompts.", "What's a reducer in LangGraph?", "Do you still remember my name and city?", ] def show_state(graph, config): state = graph.get_state(config).values print(f" state: {len(state['messages'])} messages kept, summary={'yes' if state.get('summary') else 'no'}") def main() -> None: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="LangGraph rolling-context demo") parser.add_argument("-i", "--interactive", action="store_true", help="chat yourself instead of the scripted demo") parser.add_argument("-m", "--model", help=f"Ollama model name (default: {OLLAMA_MODEL})") args = parser.parse_args() graph = build_graph(make_llm(args.model)) config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "demo"}} def turn(text: str): print(f"USER: {text}") result = graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(text)]}, config) reply = next(m for m in reversed(result["messages"]) if isinstance(m, AIMessage)) print(f"AI: {reply.content}") show_state(graph, config) print() if args.interactive: print("Type 'quit' to exit, 'summary' to print the rolling summary.
") while (text := input("> ").strip()).lower() not in {"quit", "exit"}: if text == "summary": print(graph.get_state(config).values.get("summary") or "(no summary yet)", "
") elif text: turn(text) else: for text in DEMO_TURNS: turn(text) print("Final rolling summary:
" + (graph.get_state(config).values.get("summary") or "(none)")) Keyword Search, Explained Simply What it is: Full-text search finds information by matching words. An agent can use it to find useful past messages or documents and add them to the model’s input. How it works 1. Build an index First, the system prepares the text for searching: · Split the text into words. This is called tokenization. · Make words easier to match. For example, change them to lowercase and shorten “running” and “runs” to “run.” These steps are called normalization and stemming. · Remove common words such as “the,” “is,” and “and.” This is called stop-word removal. The system then lists which messages or documents contain each word. This list is called an inverted index . It works like the index at the back of a book. Why it is fast: The system looks up a word in the index instead of reading every document again. 2. Put the best matches first A scoring method called BM25 helps rank matching passages. It considers: · How often a search word appears in a passage. · How rare the word is across the saved documents. Less common words carry more weight. · The length of the passage. The score is adjusted so length does not unfairly affect the result. 3. Search and use the results When a user asks something: 1. Prepare the search question in the same way as the saved text. 2. Use BM25 to score the matching passages. 3. Choose the best few results. This is called selecting the “top K.” 4. Add those results to the model’s input, shortening or summarizing them if needed. This gives the model useful background without sending the full history. In practice You can build a simple version in Python. Larger systems usually keep the index in a database. Useful memory is about more than finding old messages. An agent can also remember a user’s preferences and past requests to give more helpful answers. Example: Imagine a food-ordering assistant. · Without memory: When the user says “Order my usual lunch,” the assistant must ask what food they want, whether they have dietary preferences, and where to deliver it. · With memory: The assistant has saved that the user is vegetarian, usually orders paneer tikka, and wants weekday deliveries to the office. It can reply, “Paneer tikka from your usual place, delivered to your office. Shall I place the order?” To do this, the agent saves conversation history in a database. For each new request, it finds relevant details and adds them to the model’s input. Semantic search and vector stores can help with this. """Full-text search (BM25) memory with LangGraph. Only the last WINDOW messages stay in the prompt. Older messages are moved into an inverted index; on every turn the user's question is searched with BM25 and the top K past messages are added to the prompt. START -> retrieve -> chat -> archive -> END 1. Index: tokenize -> lowercase -> drop stop words -> stem -> inverted index 2. Rank: BM25 (term frequency, rarity of the term, document length) 3. Answer: analyze the question the same way, score, take the top K, add to prompt """ import argparse import heapq import math import re from collections import Counter, defaultdict import snowballstemmer from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, AnyMessage, HumanMessage, RemoveMessage, SystemMessage from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver from langgraph.graph import END, START, MessagesState, StateGraph from rolling_context import OLLAMA_MODEL, make_llm WINDOW = 4 # messages kept verbatim in the prompt (2 user/assistant turns) TOP_K = 3 # past messages pulled back in by search SNIPPET_CHARS = 300 # long hits are shortened before going into the prompt STOP_WORDS = set( "a an and are as at be but by can do does for from had has have how i i'm in is it its " "me my of on or so that the their them then there these they this to was we what when " "where which who why will with you your about could would should did any all just " "he him his she her our us get got hi hello s m t d ll re ve".split() ) _stemmer = snowballstemmer.stemmer("english") def analyze(text: str) -> list[str]: """Tokenize, lowercase, remove stop words and stem: 'running', 'runs' -> 'run'.""" tokens = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower()) return _stemmer.stemWords([t for t in tokens if t not in STOP_WORDS]) class BM25Index: """An in-memory inverted index ranked with BM25. Real systems keep this in a database.""" def __init__(self, k1: float = 1.5, b: float = 0.75): self.k1, self.b = k1, b self.docs: list[str] = [] self.doc_len: list[int] = [] self.postings: dict[str, dict[int, int]] = defaultdict(dict) # term -> {doc_id: term freq} def add(self, text: str) -> int: doc_id = len(self.docs) terms = analyze(text) self.docs.append(text) self.doc_len.append(len(terms)) for term, tf in Counter(terms).items(): self.postings[term][doc_id] = tf return doc_id def search(self, query: str, k: int = TOP_K) -> list[tuple[float, str]]: if not self.docs: return [] n_docs, avg_len = len(self.docs), sum(self.doc_len) / len(self.docs) scores: dict[int, float] = defaultdict(float) for term in set(analyze(query)): posting = self.postings.get(term) if not posting: continue # the index lookup skips every document without this term # Rare terms (few documents contain them) get a higher weight. idf = math.log(1 + (n_docs - len(posting) + 0.5) / (len(posting) + 0.5)) for doc_id, tf in posting.items(): # More occurrences help, with diminishing returns; long documents are penalized. length_norm = 1 - self.b + self.b * self.doc_len[doc_id] / avg_len scores[doc_id] += idf * tf * (self.k1 + 1) / (tf + self.k1 * length_norm) top = heapq.nlargest(k, scores.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]) return [(score, self.docs[doc_id]) for doc_id, score in top] class State(MessagesState): retrieved: list[str] def build_graph(llm, index: BM25Index, top_k: int = TOP_K): def retrieve(state: State): query = state["messages"][-1].content hits = index.search(query, top_k) print(f" search terms: {analyze(query)}") for score, text in hits: print(f" hit {score:5.2f} {text[:90]!r}") if not hits: print(" (no hits)") return {"retrieved": [text[:SNIPPET_CHARS] for _, text in hits]} def chat(state: State): prompt: list[AnyMessage] = [SystemMessage("You are a helpful, concise assistant.")] if state["retrieved"]: memories = "
".join(f"- {m}" for m in state["retrieved"]) prompt.append( SystemMessage( "These earlier messages from this conversation were found by search. " f"Use them if they help answer the user:
{memories}" ) ) prompt += state["messages"] print(f" -> sending {len(prompt)} messages to the model") return {"messages": [llm.invoke(prompt)]} def archive(state: State): old = state["messages"][:-WINDOW] for m in old: index.add(f"{'user' if isinstance(m, HumanMessage) else 'assistant'}: {m.content}") if old: print(f" ** archived {len(old)} messages into the index ({len(index.docs)} docs, {len(index.postings)} terms)") return {"messages": [RemoveMessage(id=m.id) for m in old]} builder = StateGraph(State) builder.add_node("retrieve", retrieve) builder.add_node("chat", chat) builder.add_node("archive", archive) builder.add_edge(START, "retrieve") builder.add_edge("retrieve", "chat") builder.add_edge("chat", "archive") builder.add_edge("archive", END) return builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) DEMO_TURNS = [ "Hi, I'm Deepak. I'm planning a trip to Japan in April.", "My laptop is a ThinkPad X1 running Fedora Linux.", "Invoice #4512 from Acme Corp is overdue by 30 days, I need to chase them.", "My son's birthday is on 14 March and she loves painting.", "Explain BM25 in one sentence.", "Suggest a name for a cat.", # Everything above has left the prompt window by now; only search can bring it back. "When is my son's birthday, and what gift could I get her?", "Which invoice was overdue, and from which company?", "What operating system runs on my laptop?", ] def main() -> None: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="LangGraph full-text search (BM25) memory demo") parser.add_argument("-i", "--interactive", action="store_true", help="chat yourself instead of the scripted demo") parser.add_argument("-m", "--model", help=f"Ollama model name (default: {OLLAMA_MODEL})") parser.add_argument("-k", "--top-k", type=int, default=TOP_K, help="past messages to retrieve per turn") args = parser.parse_args() index = BM25Index() graph = build_graph(make_llm(args.model), index, args.top_k) config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "demo"}} def turn(text: str): print(f"USER: {text}") result = graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(text)]}, config) reply = next(m for m in reversed(result["messages"]) if isinstance(m, AIMessage)) print(f"AI: {reply.content}
") if args.interactive: print("Type 'quit' to exit, 'index' to list the indexed messages.
") while (text := input("> ").strip()).lower() not in {"quit", "exit"}: if text == "index": print("
".join(f"[{i}] {d}" for i, d in enumerate(index.docs)) or "(empty)", "
") elif text: turn(text) else: for text in DEMO_TURNS: turn(text) Semantic Memory and Vector Stores What is semantic memory? It is long-term memory for facts, concepts, and knowledge. An agent retrieves this information when it needs it. “Semantic” means “related to meaning.” Semantic search looks for similar meanings, not just matching words. Example: A user has saved this message: “I’m vegetarian, please don’t suggest chicken or fish.” Later, the user asks: “What food should I avoid recommending?” · Keyword search: It looks for words such as “food,” “avoid,” and “recommending.” These words are not in the saved message, so the search can miss it. · Semantic search: It looks for a similar meaning. It can connect “food to avoid” with “don’t suggest chicken or fish” and find the message. How semantic search works 1. Turn each message into a list of numbers called an embedding . Think of it as a point on a map of meanings. 2. Messages with similar meanings are close on this map. For example, “car” and “automobile” are close, while “car” and “banana” are far apart. 3. Turn the question into an embedding too. Then find the saved messages with the closest embeddings. How are results saved and retrieved? There are two stages: saving information first, then finding it when a question comes in. Phase 1: Saving (before any question is asked) 1. Create an embedding for each message. For example, the vegetarian message becomes a list of numbers like [0.9, 0.1, …]. These numbers are only an illustration. 2. Save the embedding and the original text in a vector database. This database searches lists of numbers. 3. Here are some example entries. The numbers are for illustration only: Text Embedding “I’m vegetarian, please don’t suggest chicken or fish.” [0.9, 0.1, …] “My office address is on MG Road.” [0.1, 0.9, …] “I usually order lunch around 1 pm.” [0.4, 0.7, …] Phase 2: Retrieving (when the user asks something) 1. Create an embedding for the question. Use the same embedding model as before. For example, “What food should I avoid recommending?” becomes a list like [0.85, 0.15, …]. 2. Compare the embeddings. A measure called cosine similarity compares the directions of the number lists. Higher scores mean a closer match. Here are example scores, not results from a real search: Vegetarian message: 0.98 Lunch time message: 0.62 Office address message: 0.28 3. Choose the best few matches. Sort the results by score and keep the top K, such as the top two. A minimum score can help leave out weak matches. 4. Add useful results to the model’s input. For example: Past messages: I’m vegetarian, please don’t suggest chicken or fish. Question: What food should I avoid recommending? 5. The model answers using the saved details: “Avoid recommending meat or fish, since you’re vegetarian.” """Semantic memory with a vector store, using LangGraph and Ollama. Each thing the user tells the assistant is embedded (turned into a vector of numbers that captures its meaning) and saved in LangGraph's long-term Store. On every turn the question is embedded too, and the memories whose vectors are closest in meaning (cosine similarity) are added to the prompt. Unlike the BM25 example, no shared keywords are needed: "a gift for my kid's special day" finds "my daughter's birthday is on 14 March". And unlike a checkpointer, the Store is shared across threads, so a brand-new conversation can still recall facts from an old one. START -> recall -> chat -> remember -> END """ import argparse import uuid from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, AnyMessage, HumanMessage, SystemMessage from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig from langchain_ollama import OllamaEmbeddings from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver from langgraph.graph import END, START, MessagesState, StateGraph from langgraph.store.base import BaseStore from langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore from rolling_context import OLLAMA_MODEL, OLLAMA_URL, make_llm EMBED_MODEL = "nomic-embed-text" # install with: ollama pull nomic-embed-text EMBED_DIMS = 768 # vector size produced by nomic-embed-text WINDOW = 4 # recent messages sent verbatim TOP_K = 3 # memories retrieved per turn MIN_SCORE = 0.45 # cosine similarity below this is treated as "not related" class State(MessagesState): memories: list[str] def make_store(embed_model: str = EMBED_MODEL) -> InMemoryStore: """A key-value store with a vector index on the 'text' field. Swap for PostgresStore in production.""" embeddings = OllamaEmbeddings(model=embed_model, base_url=OLLAMA_URL) return InMemoryStore(index={"embed": embeddings, "dims": EMBED_DIMS, "fields": ["text"]}) def build_graph(llm, store: BaseStore, top_k: int = TOP_K): def namespace(config: RunnableConfig): # Memories belong to a user, not to a thread, so every thread of that user can see them. return ("memories", config["configurable"]["user_id"]) def recall(state: State, config: RunnableConfig, *, store: BaseStore): query = state["messages"][-1].content hits = store.search(namespace(config), query=query, limit=top_k) for h in hits: mark = "use " if h.score >= MIN_SCORE else "skip" print(f" {mark} {h.score:.3f} {h.value['text']!r}") if not hits: print(" (memory is empty)") return {"memories": [h.value["text"] for h in hits if h.score >= MIN_SCORE]} def chat(state: State): prompt: list[AnyMessage] = [SystemMessage("You are a helpful, concise assistant.")] if state["memories"]: facts = "
".join(f"- {m}" for m in state["memories"]) prompt.append( SystemMessage( "Things the user told you in earlier conversations (retrieved by meaning). " f"Use them when relevant:
{facts}" ) ) prompt += state["messages"][-WINDOW:] print(f" -> sending {len(prompt)} messages to the model") return {"messages": [llm.invoke(prompt)]} def remember(state: State, config: RunnableConfig, *, store: BaseStore): text = state["messages"][-2].content # the user message of this turn # Simple heuristic: statements are worth remembering, questions usually aren't. if not text.rstrip().endswith("?"): store.put(namespace(config), str(uuid.uuid4()), {"text": text}) # embedded on put print(" ** saved to semantic memory") return {} builder = StateGraph(State) builder.add_node("recall", recall) builder.add_node("chat", chat) builder.add_node("remember", remember) builder.add_edge(START, "recall") builder.add_edge("recall", "chat") builder.add_edge("chat", "remember") builder.add_edge("remember", END) # Checkpointer = short-term memory per thread; store = long-term memory per user. return builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver(), store=store) # Two separate conversations (threads). The second starts with an empty history and # its questions share almost no words with the facts, so only semantic search can help. DEMO_SESSIONS = { "monday": [ "Hi, I'm Deepak and I live in Noida.", "I'm allergic to peanuts.", "My daughter turns eight on 14 March and she adores painting.", "I drive a red Tata Nexon electric car.", "At work I'm building an AI agent with LangGraph.", ], "friday": [ "What should I get my kid for her special day?", "Suggest a quick snack recipe that is safe for me to eat.", "Any tips for a long road trip in my vehicle?", "What framework am I using for my project at the office?", ], } def main() -> None: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="LangGraph semantic memory (vector store) demo") parser.add_argument("-i", "--interactive", action="store_true", help="chat yourself instead of the scripted demo") parser.add_argument("-m", "--model", help=f"Ollama chat model (default: {OLLAMA_MODEL})") parser.add_argument("-e", "--embed-model", default=EMBED_MODEL, help=f"Ollama embedding model (default: {EMBED_MODEL})") parser.add_argument("-k", "--top-k", type=int, default=TOP_K, help="memories to retrieve per turn") args = parser.parse_args() store = make_store(args.embed_model) graph = build_graph(make_llm(args.model), store, args.top_k) user_id = "deepak" def turn(text: str, thread_id: str): print(f"USER: {text}") config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id, "user_id": user_id}} result = graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(text)]}, config) reply = next(m for m in reversed(result["messages"]) if isinstance(m, AIMessage)) print(f"AI: {reply.content}
") if args.interactive: thread = 1 print("Type 'quit' to exit, 'new' to start a new thread (memory is kept), 'memories' to list them.
") while (text := input(f"[thread {thread}]> ").strip()).lower() not in {"quit", "exit"}: if text == "new": thread += 1 print(f"--- new thread {thread}: chat history is empty, semantic memory is not ---
") elif text == "memories": items = store.search(("memories", user_id), limit=100) print("
".join(f"- {i.value['text']}" for i in items) or "(empty)", "
") elif text: turn(text, f"thread-{thread}") else: for thread_id, turns in DEMO_SESSIONS.items(): print(f"=============== thread '{thread_id}' (new conversation) ===============
") for text in turns: turn(text, thread_id) RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation Most organizations have large internal knowledge bases: past tickets, policies, product docs, troubleshooting guides. This is a gold mine of knowledge, but it’s hard to use in the moment. A customer service representative handling a live request often can’t find the relevant article or similar past case quickly enough to act on it. The idea What if an LLM could draw on that same knowledge base? A customer asks a question. The customer service rep passes the query to an AI agent. The agent asks the LLM to retrieve the most relevant information from the internal knowledge base. The LLM answers using that retrieved content, grounded in the organization’s own knowledge rather than general training data. The rep reviews the answer and takes the right action. The solution This is exactly what RAG makes possible. The knowledge base is indexed ahead of time (chunked, embedded, and stored in a vector database). At query time, the most relevant pieces are retrieved and handed to the LLM as context, so its answers are accurate, current, and specific to your organization. RAG 1 Think of the diagram as a library getting ready before anyone walks in to ask a question. Reading left to right: 1. Source document This is your raw knowledge: a help article, a policy, an old support ticket. It’s usually too long to use all at once. 2. Chunks The dashed lines are scissors. The document gets cut into small, bite-sized pieces, each about a paragraph or two. Small pieces make it easier to find the exact part that answers a question, instead of handing over a whole 50-page manual. 3. Encoder Each chunk goes through an encoder, a model that reads the text and captures what it means. 4. Dense vectors The encoder turns each chunk into a list of numbers. Each little square in the strip stands for one number, and its shade shows how big the number is. You can think of this list as the chunk’s meaning fingerprint: chunks that say similar things get similar fingerprints, even if they use different words. “How do I reset my password” and “I forgot my login” end up close together. 5. Vector database These fingerprints are stored as points in a big map. The gray dots are chunks that were already stored. The teal dots are the new ones just added. Chunks with similar meanings sit near each other on this map. Why it matters All of this happens once, ahead of time. Later, when a customer service rep asks something like “customer can’t log in after an update,” that question gets its own fingerprint. The system looks for the nearest points on the map and grabs those chunks. The LLM then uses them to write an answer based on your company’s actual knowledge. Retrieval and generation So far win RAG we have seen how a document is divided into chunks and saved in to vector database. Now lets looks at the retrieval and response generation part. The figure below shows once customer service use case. RAG 2 Retrieval (steps 1–4): finding the right information The rep asks: “Customer updated the app and can’t log in. What should I do?” Step 1, Question: The question goes to the controller, the AI agent the rep is using. Step 2, Encode: The controller sends the question to the embedding model, the same one used to index the knowledge base. It turns the question into a meaning fingerprint (a vector) on the same map as the stored chunks. Step 3, Vector search: That query vector goes to the knowledge base, which looks for the stored chunks closest to it in meaning, not in exact words. Step 4, Top chunks: The best few matches come back to the controller, such as a known-issue note, a troubleshooting article, and a similar past ticket. Generation (steps 5–6): writing the answer Step 5, Question + chunks: The controller combines the original text question with the retrieved chunks, plus instructions like “Answer using only these notes, and say if you don’t know,” and sends this to the LLM. The LLM gets readable text, not vectors. The vector was only needed for the search. Step 6, Reply: The LLM writes a clear answer, for example: “This is a known issue in the latest version. Clear the app cache and sign in again. If it still fails, escalate to tier 2.” The answer goes back to the rep with links to its sources. How AI Agents Remember: A Simple Guide to Memory, Vector Search, and RAG was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Why Do AI Agents Need Memory Management?

An AI chatbot may seem to remember earlier messages, but the language model (LLM) does not remember them on its own. It uses the information sent to it with each request.

The agent — the system around the model — keeps track of useful information. It sends the model the details it needs for each task.

Here’s why this matters:

1. The model has limited space. It can read only a certain amount of text at once. This limit is called the context window. Long conversations, files, and search results can fill it up. Older information may then be left out, even if it is important.

2. More text can cost more and take longer. Sending the whole conversation each time adds extra work. Sending only useful details can save time and money.

3. Too much unrelated information can hurt answers. Important details can get lost in the clutter. Clear, focused input helps the model answer better.

4. Long tasks need progress tracking. The agent needs to know what is finished, what is next, and what has been decided. Otherwise, it may repeat work or ignore earlier decisions.

5. The model may lack needed information. Private data and recent information may not be part of its training. Search tools can find these details when needed.

6. Users need control over memory. Memory management helps decide what to save, forget, or avoid storing. It can also let users view and delete saved information.

Core Memory Strategies for AI Agents

Two simple ways to manage memory are a rolling context window and keyword search. A rolling window keeps recent messages. Keyword search finds saved information by matching words.

Context Windows, Explained Simply

What is a context window?
It is the space available for the information sent to the model in one request. Think of it as short-term memory for that request.

What is context length?
It is the maximum amount of text the model can handle at once, measured in tokens.

What is a token?
A token is a small piece of text. In English, it is roughly three-quarters of a word, or about four characters.

· 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words

How big are context windows?

· Older models: about 4,000 tokens (~3,000 words, ~12 pages) or 8,000 tokens (~6,000 words, ~24 pages)

· GPT-5 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet: up to 272,000 tokens

· Gemini 2.5: up to 1 million tokens

Why it matters
The context window has limited space. Include what the model needs and leave out unrelated details.

The simplest approach
Send the current question and the conversation so far. When there is not enough space, keep the newest messages.

Rolling context window

· Send the conversation history that fits in the window with each request.

· When the window fills up, remove the oldest messages to make room for new ones.

Pros

· Easy to build

· Simple

· Works for many use cases

Cons

· Older information is removed even when it is important.

· Long questions and answers can fill the window quickly.



import argparse
import os
import re

from langchain_core.messages import (
    AIMessage,
    AnyMessage,
    HumanMessage,
    RemoveMessage,
    SystemMessage,
)
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from langgraph.graph import END, START, MessagesState, StateGraph

MAX_MESSAGES = 6  # summarize once state holds more than this many messages
KEEP_LAST = 2  # how many recent messages survive a summarization pass
OLLAMA_MODEL = "llama3.2"  # also try gpt-oss:20b, qwen:4b, deepseek-r1:1.5b
OLLAMA_URL = os.environ.get("OLLAMA_HOST", "http://localhost:11434")


class State(MessagesState):
    summary: str


def _strip_thinking(msg: AIMessage) -> AIMessage:
    """Reasoning models (deepseek-r1, ...) may inline  blocks; keep them out of state."""
    if isinstance(msg.content, str):
        msg.content = re.sub(r".*?", "", msg.content, flags=re.DOTALL).strip()
    return msg


def make_llm(model: str | None):
    from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama

    model = model or OLLAMA_MODEL
    print(f"Using Ollama model '{model}' at {OLLAMA_URL}
")
    return ChatOllama(model=model, base_url=OLLAMA_URL, temperature=0) | RunnableLambda(_strip_thinking)


def build_graph(llm):
    def chat(state: State):
        prompt: list[AnyMessage] = [SystemMessage("You are a helpful, concise assistant.")]
        if state.get("summary"):
            prompt.append(
                SystemMessage(
                    "Earlier messages in this conversation were condensed into this summary. "
                    f"Treat it as things you remember about the user:
{state['summary']}"
                )
            )
        prompt += state["messages"]
        print(f"   -> sending {len(prompt)} messages to the model")
        return {"messages": [llm.invoke(prompt)]}

    def should_summarize(state: State):
        return "summarize" if len(state["messages"]) > MAX_MESSAGES else END

    def summarize(state: State):
        old, summary = state["messages"][:-KEEP_LAST], state.get("summary", "")
        rules = (
            "Write it as short bullet points. Always keep every personal fact about the user "
            "(name, location, preferences) and the topics discussed. Output only the bullets."
        )
        if summary:
            instruction = (
                f"This is the summary so far:
{summary}

"
                f"Rewrite the summary so it also covers the new messages above. {rules}"
            )
        else:
            instruction = f"Summarize the conversation above. {rules}"
        new_summary = llm.invoke(old + [HumanMessage(instruction)]).content
        print(f"   ** rolled {len(old)} old messages into the summary")
        # RemoveMessage tells the add_messages reducer to drop these ids from state.
        return {"summary": new_summary, "messages": [RemoveMessage(id=m.id) for m in old]}

    builder = StateGraph(State)
    builder.add_node("chat", chat)
    builder.add_node("summarize", summarize)
    builder.add_edge(START, "chat")
    builder.add_conditional_edges("chat", should_summarize, ["summarize", END])
    builder.add_edge("summarize", END)
    # The checkpointer persists state per thread_id across invocations.
    return builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())


DEMO_TURNS = [

def show_state(graph, config):
    state = graph.get_state(config).values
    print(f"   state: {len(state['messages'])} messages kept, summary={'yes' if state.get('summary') else 'no'}")


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="LangGraph rolling-context demo")
    parser.add_argument("-i", "--interactive", action="store_true", help="chat yourself instead of the scripted demo")
    parser.add_argument("-m", "--model", help=f"Ollama model name (default: {OLLAMA_MODEL})")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    graph = build_graph(make_llm(args.model))
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "demo"}}

    def turn(text: str):
        print(f"USER: {text}")
        result = graph.invoke({"messages": [HumanMessage(text)]}, config)
        reply = next(m for m in reversed(result["messages"]) if isinstance(m, AIMessage))
        print(f"AI:   {reply.content}")
        show_state(graph, config)
        print()

")

")
            elif text:
