items.title: Part XXI — Streaming State: Watermarks, State Stores, and the 146GB Checkpoint
items.summary: Every Structured Streaming query is a stateful program wearing a batch costume. The watermark is the only thing standing between your state store and unbounded growth — and when it is misconfigured, the checkpoint doesn’t save you. It becomes the incident. Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV | Part XV | Part XVI | Part XVII | Part XVIII | Part XIX | Part XX | Part XXI The 146GB Checkpoint That Ate the Fraud Pipeline The page came at 2:47 AM, and the symptom made no sense at first: fraud.dedup_orders — a Structured Streaming query whose entire job is deduplicating order events — had fallen 93 minutes behind. Not failed. Not erroring. Just… walking, while 38,000 events per second piled up behind it. The consumer lag graph looked like a ski slope. The query was simple enough to be boring. Kafka in, deduplicate on order_id, Delta Lake out. Someone, at some point, had set the watermark to 7 days — "to be safe," the commit message said, "so we never miss a late retry." The upstream payment service does retry failed webhooks for up to 20 minutes. Seven days of safety margin for a 20-minute retry SLA. Here is what seven days of watermark on a 38k-events-per-second firehose means arithmetically: every unique order_id seen in the last seven days must be kept in state, because a duplicate could theoretically still arrive. That's roughly 1.4 billion live keys. The state store — RocksDB, thankfully, or we'd have died much earlier — had swollen to 146GB across 200 partitions . Each two-minute micro-batch spent 41 seconds just writing state changelog deltas to the checkpoint directory, and that number was climbing every day. Then came the deploy. A routine config change, a routine restart. Restarting a Structured Streaming query means reloading the latest state snapshot and replaying the changelog since that snapshot — and our snapshot-plus-changelog replay took 38 minutes . When the executors finally came back, two of them OOM’d during state restoration, the query restarted again, and the lag went from 93 minutes to “we’ll tell you when it’s over.” Part VIII of this series covered the batch-vs-streaming execution contract — one SQL engine, two very different promises. This is the chapter where the streaming side of that contract sends its bill: in Structured Streaming, state is not a feature of the query. State is the query. Everything else is plumbing. So: where does streaming state actually live, what is supposed to bound it, and what does “exactly-once” really cost when the bound is wrong? The Mechanic Underneath: A Streaming Query Is a Versioned Key-Value Store With a SQL Frontend Strip away the DataFrame API and this is what’s running: for every stateful operator in your query, Spark maintains a versioned key-value store , partitioned the same way as your shuffle partitions, versioned by micro-batch ID. Each micro-batch reads the previous version, applies its updates, and writes a new version. The SQL you wrote — the aggregation, the dedup, the join — is a polite fiction over get, put, and delete on that store. Three components implement it: The StateStoreProvider. The default, HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider, keeps the working set in JVM heap and spills deltas to the checkpoint directory. The alternative, RocksDBStateStoreProvider (via spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass), keeps state in an off-heap LSM tree on local disk. Same API, radically different ceiling: heap versus disk. The watermark. Defined as max event time observed so far minus allowed lateness . It is the query’s statement about the future — “I do not expect data older than this” — and the engine uses it as a license to evict state it believes can never be needed again. The checkpoint. Offsets, state snapshots, state changelog deltas, and the commit log, all in the checkpoint directory. It is what makes restart possible and exactly-once semantics achievable. The operators that keep state: streaming aggregations, dropDuplicates, stream-stream joins, and flatMapGroupsWithState/mapGroupsWithState. If your query has none of these, congratulations — you have no state problem. Our dedup query had exactly one, and one was enough. Watermarks Don’t Filter Data; They License Eviction This is the most misunderstood line in the Structured Streaming documentation, so let’s be blunt: a watermark does not filter your data. It authorizes the engine to forget. Data older than the watermark isn’t “processed late” — for stateful operators, it’s dropped silently (or, more precisely, the state that would have matched it is already gone). The watermark only moves forward, and it’s computed as the minimum across partitions — one straggler partition with old event times pins the watermark for the entire query. And critically: without a watermark, stateful operators never evict anything. A dropDuplicates("order_id") with no watermark is an infinite key set with extra steps. Our 7-day watermark was technically an eviction policy — it evicted keys after seven days — but on a 38k/sec firehose, "evict after seven days" is barely distinguishable from "never." The sizing rule is not complicated, which is what makes getting it wrong so embarrassing: the watermark’s allowed lateness should match the upstream lateness SLA, not your anxiety. Our upstream retried for 20 minutes. The correct watermark was 20 minutes (plus a small buffer), which would have kept roughly 46 million keys instead of 1.4 billion. The 7-day setting wasn’t safety; it was a 500x state multiplier purchased with someone else’s disk. Stream-stream joins deserve a special warning here, because they bite differently: a stream-stream join requires watermarks on both sides, and each side’s state is evicted by its own watermark. Leave one side unwatermarked and that side’s state grows forever while the other side stays trim — the asymmetry makes it look like a “mystery” growth problem when it’s really a missing three-line config. RocksDB vs In-Memory: Where the 146GB Actually Lives Had we been on the default HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider, this incident would have been an OOM at 3 AM instead of a slowdown — the entire 146GB working set would have needed JVM heap, and no executor heap is 146GB. RocksDB moved the ceiling from heap to local disk, which is why the query degraded gracefully instead of dying. Give the LSM tree its due: it bought us months. But “graceful degradation” still degrades. Here’s where the 146GB bit us, component by component: Checkpoint write amplification. Every micro-batch writes changelog deltas for every changed key to the checkpoint directory, plus periodic full snapshots. At 1.4B keys with steady churn, our 2-minute micro-batches spent 41 seconds on state I/O alone — over a third of the batch interval burned before any business logic ran. Restart replay. A restart loads the latest snapshot and replays every changelog delta since it. Thirty-eight minutes of replay before the query processed a single new event — during which lag kept accumulating. Compaction debt. RocksDB’s LSM tree needs periodic compaction, and spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.compactOnCommit exists because without it, read amplification during state lookups grows with every uncompacted level. We had it at the default, on executors whose local disks were already 80% full of state. The state store is not a black box you can ignore once you’ve picked RocksDB. It’s a database you’re now operating — with its own storage engine, its own compaction, and its own failure modes. The fraud query’s state directory had become the largest “database” in our infrastructure, and nobody was monitoring it as one. On restart, the arrow runs backward: the query reloads the checkpoint, replays deltas onto the state store, and only then resumes. That backward arrow is the 38 minutes. Exactly-Once Is an End-to-End Property, and the State Store Sends the Bill Let’s settle what “exactly-once” actually means in Structured Streaming, because the phrase gets thrown around like a guarantee and it’s really a contract with four signatories: A replayable source (Kafka offsets can be re-read; a socket stream cannot). Deterministic transformations (your business logic, Spark’s responsibility once you behave). An idempotent sink (writing to Delta with foreachBatch + MERGE on the batch ID, so a retried batch doesn't double-write). A durable checkpoint (offsets + state + commit log, so a restart resumes from a consistent point). Spark delivers 2 and the machinery for 4. You supply 1 and 3. Miss any one and you have at-least-once with extra steps — which is exactly what most “exactly-once” pipelines quietly are. And here is the cost nobody puts in the design doc: exactly-once is purchased with write amplification and restart latency, both proportional to state size. The changelog deltas, the snapshots, the 38-minute replay — that’s the premium on the exactly-once insurance policy, and it’s denominated in state bytes. Our 7-day watermark didn’t just waste disk; it multiplied the cost of every guarantee the query made. Shrink the state and every downstream cost — checkpoint I/O, restart time, compaction debt — shrinks with it. There is no cheaper exactly-once optimization than needing less state. One more contractual fine print: the checkpoint directory is part of the query’s semantics. Change the state schema — the key columns, the aggregation, the watermark column — and you cannot resume from the old checkpoint; you need a new checkpoint location, which means reprocessing from the source’s earliest retained offset. We learned to treat checkpoint paths as immutable infrastructure, versioned alongside the query code. The Fix, and What It Cost The naive version is the one that paged us. The optimized version starts from the upstream SLA and treats the state store as the database it is: # Naive: "be safe" with a 7-day watermark on the default in-memory state store. # (events # .withWatermark("event_ts", "7 days") # 500x more state than the 20-min retry SLA needs # .dropDuplicates("order_id")) # default HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider: heap is the ceiling # Optimized: watermark sized to the upstream retry SLA, state moved off-heap. spark.conf.set( "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass", "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider", ) # off-heap LSM: the ceiling moves from executor heap to local disk spark.conf.set( "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.compactOnCommit", "true" ) # pay compaction incrementally instead of as read-amplification debt deduped = ( events .withWatermark("event_ts", "20 minutes") # upstream retries for 20 min; anything later is dropped BY DESIGN, not by accident .dropDuplicates("order_id") ) Two operational companions, both non-optional: State parallelism matched to key cardinality. We rebalanced to 400 state partitions so no single RocksDB instance held a disproportionate key range — Part VII’s skew playbook applies to state stores too, because a state store is just a partitioned key space. State monitoring as a first-class metric. We added a StreamingQueryListener scraping stateOperators metrics from each progress event — numRowsTotal, memoryUsedBytes — into our dashboards with an alert at 2x the post-fix baseline. The state store is now the largest database we operate; it gets database-grade observability. items.summary_html:
Every Structured Streaming query is a stateful program wearing a batch costume. The watermark is the only thing standing between your state store and unbounded growth — and when it is misconfigured, the checkpoint doesn’t save you. It becomes the incident.

Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV | Part XV | Part XVI | Part XVII | Part XVIII | Part XIX | Part XX| Part XXI

The 146GB Checkpoint That Ate the Fraud Pipeline

The page came at 2:47 AM, and the symptom made no sense at first: fraud.dedup_orders — a Structured Streaming query whose entire job is deduplicating order events — had fallen 93 minutes behind. Not failed. Not erroring. Just… walking, while 38,000 events per second piled up behind it. The consumer lag graph looked like a ski slope.

The query was simple enough to be boring. Kafka in, deduplicate on order_id, Delta Lake out. Someone, at some point, had set the watermark to 7 days — "to be safe," the commit message said, "so we never miss a late retry." The upstream payment service does retry failed webhooks for up to 20 minutes. Seven days of safety margin for a 20-minute retry SLA.

Here is what seven days of watermark on a 38k-events-per-second firehose means arithmetically: every unique order_id seen in the last seven days must be kept in state, because a duplicate could theoretically still arrive. That's roughly 1.4 billion live keys. The state store — RocksDB, thankfully, or we'd have died much earlier — had swollen to 146GB across 200 partitions. Each two-minute micro-batch spent 41 seconds just writing state changelog deltas to the checkpoint directory, and that number was climbing every day.

Then came the deploy. A routine config change, a routine restart. Restarting a Structured Streaming query means reloading the latest state snapshot and replaying the changelog since that snapshot — and our snapshot-plus-changelog replay took 38 minutes. When the executors finally came back, two of them OOM’d during state restoration, the query restarted again, and the lag went from 93 minutes to “we’ll tell you when it’s over.”

Part VIII of this series covered the batch-vs-streaming execution contract — one SQL engine, two very different promises. This is the chapter where the streaming side of that contract sends its bill: in Structured Streaming, state is not a feature of the query. State is the query. Everything else is plumbing.

So: where does streaming state actually live, what is supposed to bound it, and what does “exactly-once” really cost when the bound is wrong?

The Mechanic Underneath: A Streaming Query Is a Versioned Key-Value Store With a SQL Frontend

Strip away the DataFrame API and this is what’s running: for every stateful operator in your query, Spark maintains a versioned key-value store, partitioned the same way as your shuffle partitions, versioned by micro-batch ID. Each micro-batch reads the previous version, applies its updates, and writes a new version. The SQL you wrote — the aggregation, the dedup, the join — is a polite fiction over get, put, and delete on that store.

Three components implement it:

  • The StateStoreProvider. The default, HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider, keeps the working set in JVM heap and spills deltas to the checkpoint directory. The alternative, RocksDBStateStoreProvider (via spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass), keeps state in an off-heap LSM tree on local disk. Same API, radically different ceiling: heap versus disk.
  • The watermark. Defined as max event time observed so far minus allowed lateness. It is the query’s statement about the future — “I do not expect data older than this” — and the engine uses it as a license to evict state it believes can never be needed again.
  • The checkpoint. Offsets, state snapshots, state changelog deltas, and the commit log, all in the checkpoint directory. It is what makes restart possible and exactly-once semantics achievable.

The operators that keep state: streaming aggregations, dropDuplicates, stream-stream joins, and flatMapGroupsWithState/mapGroupsWithState. If your query has none of these, congratulations — you have no state problem. Our dedup query had exactly one, and one was enough.

Watermarks Don’t Filter Data; They License Eviction

This is the most misunderstood line in the Structured Streaming documentation, so let’s be blunt: a watermark does not filter your data. It authorizes the engine to forget. Data older than the watermark isn’t “processed late” — for stateful operators, it’s dropped silently (or, more precisely, the state that would have matched it is already gone).

The watermark only moves forward, and it’s computed as the minimum across partitions — one straggler partition with old event times pins the watermark for the entire query. And critically: without a watermark, stateful operators never evict anything. A dropDuplicates("order_id") with no watermark is an infinite key set with extra steps. Our 7-day watermark was technically an eviction policy — it evicted keys after seven days — but on a 38k/sec firehose, "evict after seven days" is barely distinguishable from "never."

The sizing rule is not complicated, which is what makes getting it wrong so embarrassing: the watermark’s allowed lateness should match the upstream lateness SLA, not your anxiety. Our upstream retried for 20 minutes. The correct watermark was 20 minutes (plus a small buffer), which would have kept roughly 46 million keys instead of 1.4 billion. The 7-day setting wasn’t safety; it was a 500x state multiplier purchased with someone else’s disk.

Stream-stream joins deserve a special warning here, because they bite differently: a stream-stream join requires watermarks on both sides, and each side’s state is evicted by its own watermark. Leave one side unwatermarked and that side’s state grows forever while the other side stays trim — the asymmetry makes it look like a “mystery” growth problem when it’s really a missing three-line config.

RocksDB vs In-Memory: Where the 146GB Actually Lives

Had we been on the default HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider, this incident would have been an OOM at 3 AM instead of a slowdown — the entire 146GB working set would have needed JVM heap, and no executor heap is 146GB. RocksDB moved the ceiling from heap to local disk, which is why the query degraded gracefully instead of dying. Give the LSM tree its due: it bought us months.

But “graceful degradation” still degrades. Here’s where the 146GB bit us, component by component:

  • Checkpoint write amplification. Every micro-batch writes changelog deltas for every changed key to the checkpoint directory, plus periodic full snapshots. At 1.4B keys with steady churn, our 2-minute micro-batches spent 41 seconds on state I/O alone — over a third of the batch interval burned before any business logic ran.
  • Restart replay. A restart loads the latest snapshot and replays every changelog delta since it. Thirty-eight minutes of replay before the query processed a single new event — during which lag kept accumulating.
  • Compaction debt. RocksDB’s LSM tree needs periodic compaction, and spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.compactOnCommit exists because without it, read amplification during state lookups grows with every uncompacted level. We had it at the default, on executors whose local disks were already 80% full of state.

The state store is not a black box you can ignore once you’ve picked RocksDB. It’s a database you’re now operating — with its own storage engine, its own compaction, and its own failure modes. The fraud query’s state directory had become the largest “database” in our infrastructure, and nobody was monitoring it as one.

On restart, the arrow runs backward: the query reloads the checkpoint, replays deltas onto the state store, and only then resumes. That backward arrow is the 38 minutes.

Exactly-Once Is an End-to-End Property, and the State Store Sends the Bill

Let’s settle what “exactly-once” actually means in Structured Streaming, because the phrase gets thrown around like a guarantee and it’s really a contract with four signatories:

  1. A replayable source (Kafka offsets can be re-read; a socket stream cannot).
  2. Deterministic transformations (your business logic, Spark’s responsibility once you behave).
  3. An idempotent sink (writing to Delta with foreachBatch + MERGE on the batch ID, so a retried batch doesn't double-write).
  4. A durable checkpoint (offsets + state + commit log, so a restart resumes from a consistent point).

Spark delivers 2 and the machinery for 4. You supply 1 and 3. Miss any one and you have at-least-once with extra steps — which is exactly what most “exactly-once” pipelines quietly are.

And here is the cost nobody puts in the design doc: exactly-once is purchased with write amplification and restart latency, both proportional to state size. The changelog deltas, the snapshots, the 38-minute replay — that’s the premium on the exactly-once insurance policy, and it’s denominated in state bytes. Our 7-day watermark didn’t just waste disk; it multiplied the cost of every guarantee the query made. Shrink the state and every downstream cost — checkpoint I/O, restart time, compaction debt — shrinks with it. There is no cheaper exactly-once optimization than needing less state.

One more contractual fine print: the checkpoint directory is part of the query’s semantics. Change the state schema — the key columns, the aggregation, the watermark column — and you cannot resume from the old checkpoint; you need a new checkpoint location, which means reprocessing from the source’s earliest retained offset. We learned to treat checkpoint paths as immutable infrastructure, versioned alongside the query code.

The Fix, and What It Cost

The naive version is the one that paged us. The optimized version starts from the upstream SLA and treats the state store as the database it is:

# Naive: "be safe" with a 7-day watermark on the default in-memory state store.
# (events
#   .withWatermark("event_ts", "7 days")   # 500x more state than the 20-min retry SLA needs
#   .dropDuplicates("order_id"))           # default HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider: heap is the ceiling
# Optimized: watermark sized to the upstream retry SLA, state moved off-heap.
spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
    "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider",
)  # off-heap LSM: the ceiling moves from executor heap to local disk
spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.compactOnCommit", "true"
)  # pay compaction incrementally instead of as read-amplification debt
deduped = (
    events
    .withWatermark("event_ts", "20 minutes")
    # upstream retries for 20 min; anything later is dropped BY DESIGN, not by accident
    .dropDuplicates("order_id")
)

Two operational companions, both non-optional:

  • State parallelism matched to key cardinality. We rebalanced to 400 state partitions so no single RocksDB instance held a disproportionate key range — Part VII’s skew playbook applies to state stores too, because a state store is just a partitioned key space.
  • State monitoring as a first-class metric. We added a StreamingQueryListener scraping stateOperators metrics from each progress event — numRowsTotal, memoryUsedBytes — into our dashboards with an alert at 2x the post-fix baseline. The state store is now the largest database we operate; it gets database-grade observability.

The quantified results, two weeks later:

  • State size: 146GB → 11GB. 1.4B live keys → ~46M, matching the 20-minute watermark window.
  • Processing lag: 93 minutes → 35 seconds at the same 38k events/sec input.
  • Checkpoint write per micro-batch: 41s → 3s. State I/O stopped being the bottleneck.
  • Restart time: 38 minutes → 5 minutes. The backward arrow got short.
The Catch: A Watermark Is a Heuristic, and Heuristics Drop Data

The honest counterweight, because every number above came with a trade:

  • Shrinking the watermark changes dedup semantics. Going from 7 days to 20 minutes means a duplicate arriving 21 minutes late is now processed as a new order. That is a business decision wearing an engineering costume — we got written sign-off from the fraud team before deploying it, and you should too.
  • Late data dies silently. There is no dead-letter queue, no warning, no metric that says “I dropped 12,000 late events this hour” unless you build one. If late data matters to you, add a side-output or a counter on the watermark gap before you tighten anything.
  • State schema changes need a new checkpoint. New key, new aggregation, new watermark column — the old checkpoint is unreadable to the new query plan. Version your checkpoint paths with your query code and plan the reprocessing window.
  • RocksDB is not magic disk. It needs fast local SSDs, headroom for compaction (we keep 40% free on state volumes now), and memory budgets of its own (spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.*). On spinning disks or cramped volumes, it compacts forever and your "fix" becomes a new incident.
  • Exactly-once without an idempotent sink is fiction. If your sink can’t tolerate a retried batch, no watermark tuning in the world gives you exactly-once. The guarantee is end-to-end or it isn’t.
Takeaways
  • Every stateful operator is a key-value store: aggregations, dedup, stream-stream joins, and flatMapGroupsWithState all persist versioned state per partition. If you can't name your query's stateful operators, you can't reason about its failure modes.
  • No watermark, no eviction: state without a watermark grows until something breaks — usually the checkpoint, the restart, or the heap, in that order.
  • Size the watermark to the SLA, not your anxiety: allowed lateness should mirror the upstream lateness contract. Every extra hour is a state multiplier on your highest-cardinality key space.
  • RocksDB moves the ceiling from heap to disk: the default in-memory provider makes executor heap your state limit; RocksDB trades that for local-disk capacity and compaction ops. Pick deliberately.
  • The checkpoint is part of the query’s contract: offsets, state snapshots, and the commit log are load-bearing. Version checkpoint paths with your code and never hand-edit them.
  • Exactly-once is end-to-end and priced in state bytes: replayable source, deterministic logic, idempotent sink, durable checkpoint — and every byte of state multiplies the write amplification and restart cost of all four.
  • Monitor state like production data: numRowsTotal and memoryUsedBytes per state operator, alerted at 2x baseline. The state store is a database you're operating whether you admit it or not.

In streaming, state is the query. Everything else is just the plumbing that feeds it.

items.title: Moving from AI adoption to an AI operating model: How Docusign engineering went beyond tool rollout
items.summary: Docusign rolled out AI coding tools across its engineering teams, expecting them to help developers write code faster and do more. Initial enthusiasm was high, but early gains plateaued. By June 2025, Docusign had reached a sticking point. According to its engineering team’s account , 49% of engineers were actively using AI coding tools, while a reported 18% improvement in developer productivity had leveled off. Engineers still needed time to experiment, guidance tailored to Docusign’s codebase, and help fitting the tools into their day-to-day work. Docusign now reports that all of its more than 1,100 engineers are onboarded to and actively using AI coding tools Docusign CTO Sagnik Nandy CTO Sagnik Nandy believes getting people to use the technology is only the beginning. “There’s a big difference between trying to get a few wins versus doing it consistently and doing it right,” Nandy tells The New Stack . Docusign responded by changing how it introduced and measured AI across engineering, moving beyond coding assistants toward reusable agents and automated workflows. Why Docusign turned to its engineers Instead of making AI adoption mandatory, Docusign established a six-person Eng AI Champions team to develop guardrails, share engineering practices, and run workshops. Docusign reports that adoption reached 65% by October 2025. The company then extended that work through AI Multipliers embedded in individual development teams. Nandy says around 75 Multipliers helped teammates put the shared practices into use and fed problems back to the central team. “They were tasked with two things,” Nandy explains. “The decisions, the solutions we built, they had to deploy it within their team, and also get feedback in terms of what’s working, what’s not working, and what’s missing.” Docusign’s account of the initiative showed that active usage reached 93% within two months of introducing the Multipliers, while lines of code updated per developer increased by approximately 52% from the company’s starting point. That code-volume measure does not, by itself, establish a matching improvement in delivery speed or software quality. Nandy believes the combination of central coordination and feedback from individual teams has helped sustain the program, an approach he has also discussed in an engineering leadership podcast . “When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out.” “When I speak to many of my peers, a lot of AI programs start well, and then fizzle out,” he says. “I think the reason that hasn’t happened for us … is because we already have such a rich body of information and feedback flowing in, and people acting on it and then redeploying things.” Teaching AI to ‘speak Docusign’ Once engineers were comfortable using AI for coding, Docusign began looking at entire development workflows. That required tools with access to its repositories, architecture, telemetry, and internal practices, so assistants could work with the company’s own context. “Our solutions and agents, we joke, they speak Docusign,” Nandy says. “They know which internal tools to go look into, what our internal coding guardrails are, guidelines are, what system choices we make, where information resides for disambiguating between different pieces of information.” Nandy describes several internal tools for different engineering tasks: Kody for Docusign-specific coding work, Chronicle for observability and incident investigation, and DocuWiki for code-aware internal documentation. Docusign’s engineering blog also describes an AI-assisted code review tool for identifying potential architectural and security issues during review. Krew brings these capabilities together , allowing teams to build agents called Krewmates for recurring tasks and more complex workflows. “One of the things that the Eng AI Champions and Multipliers did is they identified end-to-end flows, and we wanted to improve the entire flow,” Nandy says. He describes an internal agent that runs overnight, searches error logs for problems, and prepares proposed fixes. “Come morning, the engineer is greeted with, ‘Hey, here’s a PR. This was an issue we found, and this is the fix.’ It’s magical.” In Nandy’s example, Krew coordinates the workflow, drawing on telemetry from Chronicle and Kody’s coding capabilities. The engineer then reviews the proposed pull request. Docusign gives another example . For a task involving infrastructure configuration files, the agent correctly modified 10 of 12 files on its first pass in about 15 minutes, using a sample commit as guidance. The company says the process previously took roughly a week of engineer time. The first pass still left two files to correct; it was not a finished, approved change in 15 minutes. Making successful workflows reusable An agent built for one team has limited value if everyone else has to recreate it. Docusign’s Krew orchestration platform allows engineers to discover, copy, and extend Krewmates connected to internal systems. These agents can handle recurring tasks, respond to triggers, and involve people when needed. “We’ve taken a very open approach,” Nandy says. “All the Krewmates are visible to everyone. You can see how much they are getting used. It’s extremely easy to copy and extend them.” Frequently used Krewmates become more visible, helping teams find existing solutions rather than building their own from scratch. “If something is good, you can try to teach 1,000 other people to do it, or you can make it easy for 1,000 other people to inherit it.” “If something is good, you can try to teach 1,000 other people to do it, or you can make it easy for 1,000 other people to inherit it. And we went for the latter.” The approach also depends on maintaining those shared tools, documenting changes, and feeding problems back to the teams responsible for improving them. Docusign’s Krew team reports that apparently successful runs sometimes left duplicate posts or partial outputs, prompting improvements to run tracking and observability. For leaders adopting this model, a durable workflow needs a named owner, a way to report failures, and periodic checks on quality and running costs. Measuring what matters Docusign’s adoption figures show how widely AI has spread, but Nandy is wary of treating usage as the ultimate measure of success. “We’ve been very focused on value as opposed to anecdotes or gimmicks,” he says. “The way to do that is you keep moving up the value chain.” Initially, Docusign measured how many engineers were using AI, followed by how much code they were generating. Nandy says the next questions concern whether teams are actually delivering better results. “Adoption, so what? … Are you doing more?” he says. “Then you look at feature velocity. Are you shipping things sooner?” Docusign also considers customer satisfaction and reliability, particularly whether faster development introduces problems elsewhere. For engineering leaders, that means examining delivery times, review latency, testing, rework, and incident investigation rather than relying solely on adoption percentages or lines of AI-generated code. Guardrails before speed Giving agents more responsibility doesn’t mean removing human accountability. “Any PR, it’s the responsibility of the individual signing off on it,” Nandy says. “No code goes unreviewed into the system.” Docusign says its autonomous coding agent runs tests before submitting pull requests, with human review, AI-generated-code labels, and quality gates required before merging. Its AI Innovation Principles emphasize human oversight and safeguards. Krew’s documentation makes the boundary explicit: an agent cannot merge a pull request or take an irreversible action without a person’s approval. Nandy compares AI to a chainsaw: a powerful tool that can accomplish more than traditional alternatives, but requires appropriate safeguards. “You need very different gear when you have a chainsaw, otherwise you can hurt yourself.” “You need very different gear when you have a chainsaw, otherwise you can hurt yourself,” he says. “It’s important to get that right.” He also warns against introducing AI where conventional software would work better. Some of Docusign’s internal solutions were developed using AI but run as deterministic processes without continually invoking a model. “I often see people throwing AI at problems that probably don’t need AI,” Nandy says. Beyond the rollout For Nandy, Docusign’s approach rests on five principles: measure value, make successful solutions reusable, keep costs and governance sustainable, establish guardrails and build in the organization’s own context. Together, these principles support a shift from encouraging engineers to try AI to workflows that teams can maintain, measure, and improve across teams. The practical next step for an engineering leader is to choose a well-defined workflow, agree on the outcome to measure, assign an owner, and specify where human approval is required before expanding it. The lesson for engineering leaders is that adoption alone won’t deliver lasting results. Teams also need shared tools, clear ownership, engineer feedback, and measures that show whether the work is actually getting better. More details are available on Docusign’s Engineering blog , alongside its current engineering opportunities . The company says the process previously took roughly a week of engineer time. The first pass still left two files to correct; it was not a finished, approved change in 15 minutes.

Making successful workflows reusable

An agent built for one team has limited value if everyone else has to recreate it.

Docusign’s Krew orchestration platform allows engineers to discover, copy, and extend Krewmates connected to internal systems. These agents can handle recurring tasks, respond to triggers, and involve people when needed.

“We’ve taken a very open approach,” Nandy says. “All the Krewmates are visible to everyone. You can see how much they are getting used. It’s extremely easy to copy and extend them.”

Frequently used Krewmates become more visible, helping teams find existing solutions rather than building their own from scratch.

“If something is good, you can try to teach 1,000 other people to do it, or you can make it easy for 1,000 other people to inherit it.”

“If something is good, you can try to teach 1,000 other people to do it, or you can make it easy for 1,000 other people to inherit it. And we went for the latter.”

The approach also depends on maintaining those shared tools, documenting changes, and feeding problems back to the teams responsible for improving them. Docusign’s Krew team reports that apparently successful runs sometimes left duplicate posts or partial outputs, prompting improvements to run tracking and observability. For leaders adopting this model, a durable workflow needs a named owner, a way to report failures, and periodic checks on quality and running costs.

Measuring what matters

Docusign’s adoption figures show how widely AI has spread, but Nandy is wary of treating usage as the ultimate measure of success.

“We’ve been very focused on value as opposed to anecdotes or gimmicks,” he says. “The way to do that is you keep moving up the value chain.”

Initially, Docusign measured how many engineers were using AI, followed by how much code they were generating. Nandy says the next questions concern whether teams are actually delivering better results.

“Adoption, so what? … Are you doing more?” he says. “Then you look at feature velocity. Are you shipping things sooner?”

Docusign also considers customer satisfaction and reliability, particularly whether faster development introduces problems elsewhere.

For engineering leaders, that means examining delivery times, review latency, testing, rework, and incident investigation rather than relying solely on adoption percentages or lines of AI-generated code.

Guardrails before speed

Giving agents more responsibility doesn’t mean removing human accountability.

“Any PR, it’s the responsibility of the individual signing off on it,” Nandy says. “No code goes unreviewed into the system.”

Docusign says its autonomous coding agent runs tests before submitting pull requests, with human review, AI-generated-code labels, and quality gates required before merging. Its AI Innovation Principles emphasize human oversight and safeguards. Krew’s documentation makes the boundary explicit: an agent cannot merge a pull request or take an irreversible action without a person’s approval.

Nandy compares AI to a chainsaw: a powerful tool that can accomplish more than traditional alternatives, but requires appropriate safeguards.

“You need very different gear when you have a chainsaw, otherwise you can hurt yourself.”

“You need very different gear when you have a chainsaw, otherwise you can hurt yourself,” he says. “It’s important to get that right.”

He also warns against introducing AI where conventional software would work better. Some of Docusign’s internal solutions were developed using AI but run as deterministic processes without continually invoking a model.

“I often see people throwing AI at problems that probably don’t need AI,” Nandy says.

Beyond the rollout

For Nandy, Docusign’s approach rests on five principles: measure value, make successful solutions reusable, keep costs and governance sustainable, establish guardrails and build in the organization’s own context.

Together, these principles support a shift from encouraging engineers to try AI to workflows that teams can maintain, measure, and improve across teams. The practical next step for an engineering leader is to choose a well-defined workflow, agree on the outcome to measure, assign an owner, and specify where human approval is required before expanding it.

The lesson for engineering leaders is that adoption alone won’t deliver lasting results. Teams also need shared tools, clear ownership, engineer feedback, and measures that show whether the work is actually getting better.

More details are available on Docusign’s Engineering blog, alongside its current engineering opportunities.

items.title: 'Saturday Night Live' roasts Elon Musk after midterm rout: 'My car did a flip!'
items.summary: Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, and anchor Colin Jost during "Saturday Night Live" on November 7. : Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images "Saturday Night Live" roasted Elon Musk, played by Jeremy Culhane, during "Weekend Update." Culhane's Musk tried to distract the audience from his expensive US midterm election fumble. "I'm in the news because my car did a flip," the actor said. Elon Musk had a terrible, horrible, no-good, very bad week following the US midterm elections . And "Saturday Night Live" seized the opportunity. The "SNL" crew didn't hold back during the "Weekend Update" segment, when comedian Jeremy Culhane portrayed the tech billionaire discussing his US midterm election fumble. The real Musk donated at least $446 million ahead of the midterm elections to conservative political action committees, including a large chunk to supporting conservative candidates in Texas. Ultimately, it didn't matter. Texas, alongside several other traditionally red states, turned blue this election cycle. During the segment, host Colin Jost said Musk is in the news for "wasting" money on the midterm elections. "Uh, no, I'm in the news because my car did a flip. My car did a flip, remember? It was like a frickin' Hot Wheel," the impersonator said. "It was like poof! And then bah! But I was like, totally chill. I was like, 'Thug life!' Imagine." Tesla flaunted its next-generation Roadster in October by kick-flipping it in the air during a demonstration. Culhane's Musk had a similar answer when asked about his decision to halt production of Tesla's Cybertruck . Musk made the announcement two days after the midterm election. "Hey, remember when my car did a flip? It was epic. It was like poof, pah! But everyone was like, "Whoa!" But I was just like, 'Hold my beer.' Imagine,'" the comedian said. At the end of the sketch, Culhane's Musk decides to show off a new fictitious Grok feature called "vulgar roast." "Elon Musk, you're the worst thing South Africa has ever done," fake Grok said. "When you're on TV, it feels like an episode of 'Hate on the Spectrum.'" Fake Grok added: "Maybe if you have 100 more kids, one of them will talk to you." The fallout from the blue wave that swept the midterm elections was swift for Musk. His net worth fell by $33 billion in one day, while shares of Tesla and SpaceX tumbled . items.title: Scaling an autonomous agent from one team to fifty: A serverless-to-container decision framework
items.summary: QA teams shipping complex products generate test failures around the clock. Every failure needs a bug ticket with steps, screenshots, repro rates, and regression labels. The manual process takes 10-15 minutes per failure. Multiply that by 30+ failures per week across a team, and you have burned an entire engineering day on documentation that should be automatic. I built a system to eliminate this entirely. Not a dashboard. Not a notification bot. An autonomous agent that observes test results, makes judgment calls – is this a new bug, a duplicate, or a regression? And takes action without human intervention. It files structured bugs, attaches screenshots, calculates repro rates, detects regressions build-over-build, and notifies the right people. The team just marks FAIL and moves on. The system runs on Lambda today. It works perfectly for one team. But what happens when other teams want it? What happens when you need to serve 10, 50, or 100 teams? That’s where the architectural decisions get interesting – not because Lambda fails, but because the workload characteristics shift into territory where a different tool becomes the better fit. What I built (and why it works) The architecture is elegant: an EventBridge rule triggers a Lambda function every 15 minutes. The function polls the test management API, processes failures through a decision engine (dedup check against DynamoDB, regression detection against previous build results), and files bugs via the JIRA API. Total infrastructure cost: under $5/month. Lambda was the correct choice here for three reasons: Zero operational overhead: No servers, no scaling config, no patching. Deploy and forget. Cost proportional to usage: One team generates ~200 invocations/month. At Lambda pricing, this is effectively free. Fast iteration: The decision engine went through 20+ revisions in the first month. Lambda’s deployment model let me ship changes in seconds. Within weeks of deploying, the system filed more complete and consistent bugs than the team had ever produced manually. Zero missed failures. Regressions caught in minutes instead of days. Status interruptions to QA dropped to zero because anyone could query the system directly via Slack. 8-10 hours per week saved. Other teams have noticed. “Can we have that?” is a recurring question. The answer seems simple – deploy another instance per team. But at scale, the workload characteristics change in ways that shift the architectural decision. The scaling decision Lambda handles single-tenant agentic workloads beautifully. The challenge at multi-tenant scale isn’t that Lambda can’t do it; it’s that the workload characteristics shift: From stateless events to long-running context: A single team’s poll cycle finishes in seconds. But cross-project correlation – “is this the same failure pattern we’re seeing across three teams?” requires analyzing hundreds of results and their relationships in a single pass. That’s a fundamentally different compute profile. From isolated invocations to shared resource contention: When 50 functions trigger on the same EventBridge schedule, they all hit TestRail and JIRA APIs simultaneously. You need centralized rate limiting, connection pooling, and backpressure – patterns that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure. From single-team to multi-tenant isolation: Each team needs guaranteed resources, network boundaries, and scoped credentials. The isolation model becomes as important as the compute model. Lambda’s recent launches address many of these individually – Managed Instances solve connection persistence, Durable Functions break the 15-minute ceiling for long-running workflows, and Tenant Isolation provides native tenant boundaries. For many multi-tenant workloads, these capabilities narrow the gap significantly. But for this specific workload – long-running agents that need persistent connections, cross-tenant analysis, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation simultaneously- the decision framework points toward a container-native execution model with serverless-like operations. That’s where EKS Auto Mode fits. The decision framework This led me to build a simple decision rubric – not Lambda vs. containers, but which characteristics does your workload actually exhibit? Workload characteristic Lambda (+ Managed Instances, Durable Functions) Auto Mode Event-driven, short-lived Optimal Overengineered Single-tenant, low complexity Optimal Unnecessary Multi-tenant with isolation needs Possible (Tenant Isolation) Native (namespaces, RBAC, NetworkPolicies) Long-running with persistent state Possible (Durable Functions) Native (pods, persistent connections) Cross-tenant analysis requiring shared memory Complex (custom orchestration) Natural (shared services namespace) GPU-burst inference Possible (Lambda GPU – if available) Native (GPU NodePools, scale-to-zero) Centralized rate limiting + connection pooling Custom build (SQS + Step Functions) Shared platform service “The deciding factor for my workload: I need all of the right-column characteristics simultaneously. Together, they compose more naturally in a container-native environment.” The deciding factor for my workload: I need all of the right-column characteristics simultaneously. Cross-team pattern detection requires a shared analysis context. ML-based bug classification requires burst GPU. Per-team isolation requires namespace-level boundaries. Centralized rate limiting requires a persistent shared service. Each of these is individually solvable in Lambda. Together, they compose more naturally in a container-native environment. What unlocks at scale: cross-team intelligence The most interesting architectural capability that emerges at multi-tenant scale isn’t per-team automation – it’s cross-team pattern detection. This is what makes the scaling exercise worthwhile. Cross-team failure correlation When 50 teams run their test suites independently, failures appear isolated. But patterns emerge across teams that no single team can see: Three teams report navigation failures on the same firmware build → systemic regression, not three independent bugs Test failures correlate with deployment timing across unrelated services → infrastructure issue, not product bugs Identical error signatures across teams with different test suites → shared dependency failure This requires an analysis engine that can hold context from all teams simultaneously – comparing fingerprints, correlating timestamps, and identifying shared root causes. That’s a persistent, long-running workload with access to cross-tenant state. It runs naturally as a shared service in a platform namespace, consuming events from all tenant agents. ML-based bug classification Once you have enough historical data (thousands of bugs filed across teams), patterns become classifiable: Auto-assign bugs to the correct component owner based on failure signature Predict severity based on failure characteristics (crash vs. degraded behavior vs. cosmetic) Suggest related bugs for investigation (“this looks like the same root cause as PROJ-4521”) Detect anomalous failure rates before they become incident-scale This inference workload is bursty – you need GPU when bugs arrive, not 24/7. A GPU NodePool that scales to zero when idle and provisions g5 instances only during inference keeps costs proportional to actual usage. The same pod that files a bug can synchronously call the classification service, get a component assignment, and include it in the ticket – all within the same request path. Queryable knowledge base via Slack The agent isn’t just an automation – it becomes the organization’s queryable QA state. Via Slack, anyone can ask: “What’s the failure rate for navigation this week across all teams?” “Show me regressions introduced in build 2.4.1” “Which teams are seeing the most P0 bugs right now?” This transforms the agent from a task automator into an intelligence layer. The answers require cross-team state aggregation, trend computation, and natural language interpretation – all served from persistent, indexed state that accumulates over time. What EKS Auto Mode brings to this architecture EKS Auto Mode launched at re:Invent 2024 with a specific promise: full Kubernetes without managing nodes. For a multi-tenant agent platform, this means: Nodes appear when pods need them. Deploy a tenant namespace with an auto-filer pod. The Karpenter-based scheduler provisions a node within seconds. When the pod is deleted (tenant offboarded), the node is consolidated or terminated automatically. You never think about EC2 instances. Security is not your configuration burden. Nodes run immutable Bottlerocket AMIs – read-only root filesystem, SELinux enforcing, no SSH access. Nodes rotate every 21 days automatically. For long-running agent pods, this means a graceful drain roughly every three weeks. At most one missed poll cycle. Scaling is reactive to demand. During off-hours when agents are idle between polls, Auto Mode consolidates workloads onto fewer nodes. You pay for what you use. GPU workloads slot in without architectural changes. Define a GPU NodePool for the ML classification service. EKS Auto Mode provisions g5 instances only when inference pods are scheduled and terminates them when done. The multi-tenant architecture At scale, the system would have three layers: Shared platform services: a rate limiter that prevents any single tenant from exhausting external API quotas, a connection pool manager that maintains persistent sessions to TestRail and JIRA, and a Prometheus instance collecting metrics across all tenants. Per-tenant agent namespaces: each team gets an isolated namespace containing their auto-filer pod, reporter pod, and Slack bot pod. ResourceQuotas guarantee resources. NetworkPolicies enforce that Team A’s pods cannot talk to Team B’s pods. Each namespace’s service account assumes a tenant-scoped IAM role via IRSA. Shared ML inference namespace: GPU-enabled pods running classification models that all tenants can call. This namespace has its own NodePool that scales to zero when no inference is happening. The agent code would remain essentially the same Python that runs on Lambda today – the core decision engine (observe, dedup, decide, act) doesn’t change. What changes is the execution model: instead of being invoked per-event and destroyed, the agent runs as a long-lived async loop with persistent connections, graceful shutdown handling, and internal scheduling. The AWS portfolio working together The right framing isn’t “migrate off Lambda onto EKS.” It’s “use each service where it fits”: Lambda remains the entry point. New teams start here. Single-team automation at $5/month with zero ops. Event-driven triggers, rapid iteration, pay-per-invocation economics. Lambda + Durable Functions handles teams that need longer analysis windows or multi-step orchestration without leaving the serverless model. EKS Auto Mode serves the platform layer when you need persistent multi-tenant services, cross-team intelligence, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation working together. DynamoDB persists state across all layers – dedup records, bug history, trend data. EventBridge orchestrates events whether the consumer is a Lambda function or a Kubernetes pod. A team that needs 30-minute analysis windows or multi-step workflows (poll → correlate → file → notify → wait for response → update) benefits from Durable Functions without leaving serverless. You stay here until you need cross-tenant shared state or GPU – that’s the signal to evaluate Auto Mode. “Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors.” The intelligence moves up the stack as the organization’s needs mature. Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors. Key takeaways Start serverless: Lambda lets you validate the agentic pattern at zero operational cost. The $5/month price point removes all friction for proving the concept works. Don’t prematurely optimize for scale you don’t have. Design for portability from day one: Structure your Lambda function as a pure decision engine with external state. Containerizing it means wrapping it in an async loop and adding a health endpoint. If you build Lambda functions as self-contained decision engines rather than tightly coupled to the invocation model, the transition is a one-day exercise whenever you need it. The decision trigger isn’t scale – it’s workload characteristics: Don’t move because you hit 50 teams. Move when you need capabilities that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure: cross-team correlation, centralized rate limiting, GPU inference, streaming connections. Multi-tenancy is an isolation problem, not a compute problem: Both Lambda (Tenant Isolation) and Kubernetes (namespaces) solve this. Choose based on what other characteristics your workload needs alongside isolation. EKS Auto Mode closes the operational gap: Before Auto Mode, choosing EKS meant accepting node management overhead. Auto Mode removes that tradeoff. You get container-native execution with serverless-like operations. The cost math Single team on Lambda today: $3-5/month. 8-10 hours/week saved. 67x ROI. Fifty teams on EKS Auto Mode would cost approximately $200-250/month total – roughly $4-5 per team per month. Same per-team economics as Lambda, but with namespace isolation, persistent connections, GPU-ready infrastructure, centralized observability, and built-in organizational governance. The cost-per-team barely changes. What changes is what you get for it! What comes next? The agentic pattern – ‘observe, decide, act’ is infrastructure-agnostic. The decision logic doesn’t care about its deployment target. What changes is what becomes possible when agents stop operating in isolation. “The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents.” The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents. An auto-filer agent detects a failure pattern and hands context to a root-cause agent, which traces the dependency chain across services, identifies the offending commit, and drafts a fix recommendation – all before a human sees the bug ticket. Agent-to-agent delegation, where one agent’s output becomes another’s input without human routing in between. Beyond that: agents that build their own decision models. Today, I hand-code the dedup logic and regression detection rules. Tomorrow, the agent observes which of its filed bugs humans close as duplicates, learns from those corrections, and tightens its own classification boundaries. The system improves not because I ship better code, but because it accumulates organizational judgment over time. The system started as a weekend project to stop filing bugs manually. It now runs in production, eliminating an entire category of manual work from QA operations. The infrastructure question stays the same – serverless for validation, containers for scale. But the agents running on that infrastructure are about to get significantly more capable. Teams with the platform layer ready will be the ones that can adopt those capabilities without rearchitecting.

NetworkPolicies enforce that Team A’s pods cannot talk to Team B’s pods. Each namespace’s service account assumes a tenant-scoped IAM role via IRSA.
  3. Shared ML inference namespace: GPU-enabled pods running classification models that all tenants can call. This namespace has its own NodePool that scales to zero when no inference is happening.

The agent code would remain essentially the same Python that runs on Lambda today – the core decision engine (observe, dedup, decide, act) doesn’t change. What changes is the execution model: instead of being invoked per-event and destroyed, the agent runs as a long-lived async loop with persistent connections, graceful shutdown handling, and internal scheduling.

The AWS portfolio working together

The right framing isn’t “migrate off Lambda onto EKS.” It’s “use each service where it fits”:

  • Lambda remains the entry point. New teams start here. Single-team automation at $5/month with zero ops. Event-driven triggers, rapid iteration, pay-per-invocation economics.
  • Lambda + Durable Functions handles teams that need longer analysis windows or multi-step orchestration without leaving the serverless model.
  • EKS Auto Mode serves the platform layer when you need persistent multi-tenant services, cross-team intelligence, GPU inference, and namespace-level isolation working together.
  • DynamoDB persists state across all layers – dedup records, bug history, trend data.
  • EventBridge orchestrates events whether the consumer is a Lambda function or a Kubernetes pod.

A team that needs 30-minute analysis windows or multi-step workflows (poll → correlate → file → notify → wait for response → update) benefits from Durable Functions without leaving serverless. You stay here until you need cross-tenant shared state or GPU – that’s the signal to evaluate Auto Mode.

“Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors.”

The intelligence moves up the stack as the organization’s needs mature. Lambda validates the pattern. EKS Auto Mode operationalizes it at scale. They’re stages in a journey, not competitors.

Key takeaways
  • Start serverless: Lambda lets you validate the agentic pattern at zero operational cost. The $5/month price point removes all friction for proving the concept works. Don’t prematurely optimize for scale you don’t have.
  • Design for portability from day one: Structure your Lambda function as a pure decision engine with external state. Containerizing it means wrapping it in an async loop and adding a health endpoint. If you build Lambda functions as self-contained decision engines rather than tightly coupled to the invocation model, the transition is a one-day exercise whenever you need it.
  • The decision trigger isn’t scale – it’s workload characteristics: Don’t move because you hit 50 teams. Move when you need capabilities that benefit from persistent, shared infrastructure: cross-team correlation, centralized rate limiting, GPU inference, streaming connections.
  • Multi-tenancy is an isolation problem, not a compute problem: Both Lambda (Tenant Isolation) and Kubernetes (namespaces) solve this. Choose based on what other characteristics your workload needs alongside isolation.
  • EKS Auto Mode closes the operational gap: Before Auto Mode, choosing EKS meant accepting node management overhead. Auto Mode removes that tradeoff. You get container-native execution with serverless-like operations.
The cost math

Single team on Lambda today: $3-5/month. 8-10 hours/week saved. 67x ROI. Fifty teams on EKS Auto Mode would cost approximately $200-250/month total – roughly $4-5 per team per month. Same per-team economics as Lambda, but with namespace isolation, persistent connections, GPU-ready infrastructure, centralized observability, and built-in organizational governance.

The cost-per-team barely changes. What changes is what you get for it!

What comes next?

The agentic pattern – ‘observe, decide, act’ is infrastructure-agnostic. The decision logic doesn’t care about its deployment target. What changes is what becomes possible when agents stop operating in isolation.

“The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents.”

The next frontier isn’t single agents doing single tasks faster. It’s agents coordinating with other agents. An auto-filer agent detects a failure pattern and hands context to a root-cause agent, which traces the dependency chain across services, identifies the offending commit, and drafts a fix recommendation – all before a human sees the bug ticket. Agent-to-agent delegation, where one agent’s output becomes another’s input without human routing in between.

Beyond that: agents that build their own decision models. Today, I hand-code the dedup logic and regression detection rules. Tomorrow, the agent observes which of its filed bugs humans close as duplicates, learns from those corrections, and tightens its own classification boundaries. The system improves not because I ship better code, but because it accumulates organizational judgment over time.

The system started as a weekend project to stop filing bugs manually. It now runs in production, eliminating an entire category of manual work from QA operations. 

The infrastructure question stays the same – serverless for validation, containers for scale. But the agents running on that infrastructure are about to get significantly more capable. Teams with the platform layer ready will be the ones that can adopt those capabilities without rearchitecting.

items.title: How Much More AI Stock Can the Market Absorb?
items.summary: Volatile trading in AI-related stocks this past week has put a spotlight on investors’ appetite for additional share offerings—and the prices companies could get if they opt to sell. While tech giants, chip companies and AI cloud providers have sold or priced more than $300 billion of new stock and mandatory convertible securities so far this year, another roughly $100 billion in potential share sales remains on tap. Most would come through at-the-market programs, which give companies the option to sell shares gradually into the open market, including a proposed $60 billion ATM from Meta Platforms that could launch in early 2027.

items.title: Employees Who Use AI End Up Working Vastly More Time Per Day
items.summary: The world’s capitalists have been waiting with bated breath for the day AI finally delivers on the tech industry’s longstanding promise to create a tool more efficient than human workers. In the four years since AI first became broadly available as a commercial product, these productivity returns have mostly failed to materialize . Now, there’re signs that the push to automate labor is actually backfiring in ironic fashion, as workers who’ve been forced to adopt AI tools are becoming less efficient as time goes on. A new analysis published by the workplace surveillance company ActivTrak, first covered by Gizmodo , found that white collar workers who use AI put in up to 90 minutes more work each day compared to non-users. To arrive at that blistering number, company analysts looked at anonymized work activity from over 9,100 employees at over 450 companies from the period between April and September. For non-AI users observed over that time, the average active workday was 7.6 hours — compared to between 8.4 and 9.1 hours for heavy AI users. For workers, the findings may add to the body of evidence suggesting that sorting through AI-generated slop takes more time than it would to just do workplace tasks by hand. It could also point to the fact that employers aren’t necessarily using AI to replace jobs wholesale, but as an excuse to demand even more labor per worker regardless of any true efficiency gains. From a management point of view, the findings suggest that heavy AI users are having to spend extra billable time working after hours, while experiencing a higher frequency of interrupted work than light- or non-AI users. As head of ActivTrak’s productivity research division Gabriela Mauch wrote in the company’s press report, AI “may help employees complete tasks faster, but our research shows it contributes to longer workdays, more application switching and shorter focus sessions.” More on AI: There Are Now Growing Signs That AI Is Hurting Employment in the Job Market

items.title: Perplexity’s AI agents keep working after you close the tab
items.summary: Perplexity’s new Teammates can coordinate multiple agents, remember where previous sessions left off, and keep working without another prompt. The challenge is keeping everything in sync, especially when agents are working at the same time, sharing project state, and operating with different permissions. Announced Wednesday , Teammates builds on infrastructure Perplexity has spent much of the year developing. The launch puts that earlier work to use in workflows where agents can delegate tasks and continue operating across sessions. The challenge of keeping agents stateful When Nate Kupp , Perplexity’s vice president of infrastructure, took The New Stack inside the company’s agent sandboxes , he described the difficulty of maintaining reliable systems at that scale. “Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build,” Kupp said, pointing to the durability and uptime requirements of operating millions of sandboxes. “Stateful systems are incredibly hard to build” Teammates relies on Perplexity Computer’s existing infrastructure, which separates persistent project state from individual execution environments. That allows agents to continue working on the same project without depending on a single uninterrupted session. Shared state lives in Git In a technical breakdown of its shared workspaces , the company described how it uses Git-backed repositories to keep project state intact across sessions. Each Computer project has its own repository, while agents work in separate sandboxes and submit their changes back to the shared project. That gets more complicated when agents are working on the same code at once since if one agent commits its changes first, another may have to reapply its work against the latest version. Perplexity says fewer than 2% of submissions are rejected because they’re based on outdated repository state. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds. Median submission latency is under 1.7 seconds, while p99 stays below eight seconds. Memory is handled separately through Perplexity’s Brain system, which keeps what agents have learned in dedicated repositories. That lets background agents update shared knowledge without interfering with changes to the project’s files. Pausing and forking agents Perplexity built SPACE around Firecracker microVMs and Btrfs snapshots, making it possible to pause, resume, or fork agent sessions without losing their saved state. With Teammates, developers can connect tools like Slack and GitHub and set up triggers that tell agents when to act. Perplexity hasn’t said much about what happens when that work gets stuck, particularly when one agent is waiting on another or acting on information that’s already out of date. The open permission questions Each teammate runs in its own isolated environment and browser session, with access managed through Computer’s existing permissions and credentials handled securely through encryption. Users can also monitor progress and take control when needed. It’s unclear how it prevents agents from accessing resources beyond their permissions when tasks are handed off. For enterprises, that uncertainty could influence how much autonomy they’re willing to give agents without requiring human approval. Teammates is initially available on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned. items.title: A Repeatable Method for Measuring APT Infrastructure Exposure
items.summary: A Repeatable Method for Measuring APT Infrastructure Exposure An infrastructure query becomes useful when another analyst can reproduce it. The Cisco Talos research on UAT-6275 provides a concrete test case because it includes a narrative report, a Virus Bulletin paper, an IOC repository, and several kinds of infrastructure. A good measurement method should make each query answer a defined question without collapsing different evidence types into one number. The method below starts with the source report, records exact controls, and adds broader context only when it supports the argument. It does not require a large query set. It requires discipline about what each result means. Define the observation before the query Write the claim the query is meant to support. For example: "The published IOC address is still visible in public scan data." The corresponding query is an exact IP search. If the claim is "FortiWeb has a substantial internet-facing population," the query is a product fingerprint, not an exact IOC address. This step prevents count laundering. A broad product count cannot substitute for an exact IOC result. A domain count cannot prove that every subdomain is malicious. A CVE index count cannot measure installed desktop software. The current run used five distinct observations. app="FortiWeb" returned 1,755 all-scope assets at 2026-11-08T14:41:21Z. The exact controls ip="104.248.17.222" and ip="154.205.145.179" returned 12 and 8 observations at 14:42:06Z and 14:42:09Z. domain="securitytactics.com" returned 56 at 14:42:12Z. vul.cve="CVE-2025-8088" returned 0 at 14:42:15Z. Each result is a successful observation with a different scope and meaning. The FortiWeb count describes product visibility. The exact IP and domain counts describe observations connected to published infrastructure patterns. The CVE zero shows that the index did not return an internet-facing asset for a client-side flaw. None of the counts establishes a victim. Record the minimum evidence set Every query record should include the exact dork, scope, timestamp, status, count, source report, and the claim it supports. It should also include a note about what the result does not establish. This last field is easy to omit and difficult to reconstruct later. Store the raw response outside the article workflow if the platform permits it. At minimum, preserve the query result ID and the returned count. If a query fails, keep the error. Do not replace a failed request with zero, and do not rerun until the result becomes more convenient. The source report needs its own date and coverage. Talos described activity observed from June 2025 through August 2026. The scan observations were made in November 2026. The gap matters. A visible address in November may be the same system, a reassigned address, or a stale record. The report should show the gap rather than imply continuous control. Compare like with like Use the same scope when comparing two counts. An all-scope query can include services that a web-only query excludes. A historical result can use a different index or matching rule. If the scope changes, label the comparison as qualitative rather than presenting a percentage change. Separate exact indicators from product populations in tables and prose. A row for FortiWeb exposure should not sit beside a row for one attacker address as though the two numbers describe the same population. Group them by question: incident infrastructure, product exposure, vulnerable desktop software, and local telemetry. The most defensible finding often combines a public observation with an independent source. A ZoomEye result can show a FortiWeb fingerprint. The CVE record defines the affected versions. The asset owner supplies the installed version. Those three sources answer different parts of the exposure question. Build a review checkpoint Before publishing or briefing the result, ask four reviewers to check different properties. One checks the source facts and dates. One checks the query syntax and scope. One checks the interpretation of counts and uncertainty. One checks the writing for a claim that goes beyond the evidence. For a small team, the same person can perform several checks, but the checks should still be explicit. Record the reviewer identity, the source links, the query evidence, and any correction. A short note about a limitation is more valuable than a polished paragraph that hides it. The final output should let a reader answer three questions. What was measured? When was it measured? What decision can the result support? If the answer to the third question is "nothing until we check our own telemetry," say that plainly. A well-scoped negative result is still a useful result. References Cisco Talos, Break the silence: Kazakhstan-nexus UAT-6275 targets CIS government organizations Virus Bulletin, Break the silence: tracking Silent Lynx through exposed infrastructure Cisco Talos IOC repository for UAT-6275 Fortinet PSIRT advisory FG-IR-25-151 CVE record for CVE-2025-8088 ZoomEye Agent documentation

The method below starts with the source report, records exact controls, and adds broader context only when it supports the argument. It does not require a large query set. It requires discipline about what each result means.

Write the claim the query is meant to support. For example: "The published IOC address is still visible in public scan data." The corresponding query is an exact IP search. This step prevents count laundering. A broad product count cannot substitute for an exact IOC result. A domain count cannot prove that every subdomain is malicious. A CVE index count cannot measure installed desktop software.

The current run used five distinct observations. app="FortiWeb" returned 1,755 all-scope assets at 2026-11-08T14:41:21Z. None of the counts establishes a victim.

Record the minimum evidence set

Every query record should include the exact dork, scope, timestamp, status, count, source report, and the claim it supports. It should also include a note about what the result does not establish. This last field is easy to omit and difficult to reconstruct later.

Store the raw response outside the article workflow if the platform permits it. At minimum, preserve the query result ID and the returned count. If a query fails, keep the error. Do not replace a failed request with zero, and do not rerun until the result becomes more convenient.

The source report needs its own date and coverage. Talos described activity observed from June 2025 through August 2026. The scan observations were made in November 2026. The gap matters. Before publishing or briefing the result, ask four reviewers to check different properties. One checks the source facts and dates. One checks the query syntax and scope. One checks the interpretation of counts and uncertainty. One checks the writing for a claim that goes beyond the evidence.

For a small team, the same person can perform several checks, but the checks should still be explicit. Record the reviewer identity, the source links, the query evidence, and any correction. A short note about a limitation is more valuable than a polished paragraph that hides it.

The final output should let a reader answer three questions. What was measured? When was it measured? What decision can the result support? If the answer to the third question is "nothing until we check our own telemetry," say that plainly. A well-scoped negative result is still a useful result.
