Evidence should distinguish requested, attempted, and executed actions. Collection must remain proportionate: prompts and outputs can contain sensitive information, so access and retention require deliberate decisions.

Malicious instructions embedded in source documents may also be captured in logs. AI-assisted investigation tools must treat this material as untrusted content rather than instructions to execute. If an agent tried to transmit sensitive information externally, could the SOC detect it? Could incident response establish what happened? If not, we have an operational gap.

Connecting Security Responsibilities

No single team can secure enterprise AI independently. Security architecture defines trust boundaries, threat scenarios, reference patterns, and the evidence needed to validate controls. Governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) teams manage standards, assurance, and risk records. Identity teams establish

authentication, delegation, and revocation. Data governance addresses classification, retrieval permissions, and retention.

Platform and engineering teams implement and operate safeguards. The SOC develops detections and monitors events. Incident response investigates and contains harmful activity. Formal acceptance of residual risk belongs to authorized business risk owners, not AI agents or automated scoring systems.

Figure 3. Requirements, operational evidence, and incident findings must flow across enterprise security functions.

Defining responsibilities is relatively easy; making the handoffs work is harder. In IBM’s study of breached organizations, 19% said their governance and security teams coordinated on AI. IBM notes that weak coordination can lead to blind spots, policy conflicts, and slower incident response. Requirements must reach engineering, events must be interpretable by the SOC, and findings must inform architecture and risk decisions. Security architecture helps make those connections without owning every control or adding another approval process.

Vendor-operated agents make those handoffs harder. For an agent embedded in a third-party software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform, we may not control its runtime or have detailed execution logs. Security architecture and vendor risk teams should establish its capabilities, permission limits, available evidence, and revocation options. AI features that materially change data access, permissions, autonomy, or exposure should trigger a fresh review. Platform approval does not automatically cover new autonomous capabilities.

Six Things to Test in Your Enterprise

1. Confirm agent identity and access. Select a production agent. Can you identify its owner, credentials, permissions, delegation path, and a way to revoke access without disabling the user or platform?

2. Prove critical controls operate. Select an important safeguard, such as approved tools, restricted data access, or mandatory gateway routing. Can the team provide recent evidence that it worked, including what happened when it failed?

3. Test gateway failure. In a controlled exercise, does the application fail closed, follow an explicitly approved and securely controlled fallback, or silently bypass enforcement? Would the SOC detect the condition?

4. Trace an agent run. Ask the SOC to reconstruct a representative execution across identity, model, tools, endpoint, and network records. Record missing or inconsistent links.

5. Run a controlled agent incident exercise. Place a malicious instruction in a test ticket or document in an isolated test environment. Bring architecture, GRC, engineering, identity, the SOC, and incident response together to test detection, authorization, containment, and risk follow-up.

6. Test retrieval permissions. Select a document that a test user is explicitly denied access to, and confirm the information is not available through other authorized sources. Ask an AI assistant connected to the repository questions that require that document. If restricted content appears, investigate permission enforcement throughout retrieval and response generation. A single test without disclosure does not establish consistent enforcement; repeat across users, queries, and permission changes.

These are not simply pass-or-fail tests. They reveal where technical controls and organizational responsibilities fail to connect, so teams can assign owners, set dates, and close the gaps.

From Approval to Assurance

Standards are evolving alongside these practices. In 2026, the Model Context Protocol tightened its authorization requirements, and the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) launched its AI Agent Standards Initiative. Teams can strengthen operational controls while those efforts continue.

Questions remain about least privilege for general-purpose agents, human oversight, and visibility into vendor-operated agents. Those uncertainties should not stop progress on the fundamentals.

Think back to the coding agent and the support ticket. Each system recorded an apparently legitimate event. The missing piece was the ability to recognize what those actions meant together. AI changes how we apply familiar controls when software interprets instructions and acts across systems.

The next step is more than approving architectures and documenting requirements. We need controls that operate, evidence that connects, and teams that can act when something goes wrong. The measure of enterprise AI security is not what we have approved. It is what we can prove.

items.summary_html:
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani blasted Google’s decision to block its search engine in schools that restrict its AI features.

“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” he wrote in a social media statement. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”

“Our public schools exist to serve students,” Mamdani added, “not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”

Google announced Tuesday that it would turn off AI features in its software for students unless school administrators specifically chose to activate them — something educators have been asking for.

But with this seeming act of goodwill, Google smuggled in a twist: if schools decide to restict all its AI features, it would also disable their access to Google Search. In a statement to the New York Times, which first reported the decision, Google vice president for education Chris Phillips offered little by way of explanation, stating that “Search and AI are deeply integrated.”

Strictly speaking, this is true, and by being intentionally vague Google is giving the impression that it’s a technical problem, not a deliberate choice to ice out AI-wary schools. Its search engine is now laden with AI features. And even before the post-2022 chatbot boom, it long used AI algorithms to improve its search results.

Search and AI are indeed “deeply integrated,” then, but does it have to be this way? Before chatbots, the way Google Search integrated AI still encouraged you to perform the actual act of searching through information instead of giving you entire answers. Even its old-school “featured snippets” that appeared above search results pulled stuff from a webpage word-for-word, prominently linking to the original source and ensuring that nothing was being lost in AI hallucination.

Since then, Google has added its AI Overviews and a full-blown AI mode, turning the experience into something more like using a chatbot. Now, when you search on Google, the top of the page features an AI summary and chat window that will automatically synthesize lengthy answers to even the most specific queries, presenting them authoritatively despite the AI being notoriously prone to hallucinating. A casual user, or the average student, has almost no reason to chase down actual sources of information. 

That’s worrying to parents and educators, who want their children to develop critical thinking skills and the ability to research problems independently. The problem is only exacerbated when a child is given access to a full-fledged chatbot product, such as Google Gemini. Along with the wealth of studies suggesting a reliance on these tools impacts critical thinking , many school districts are wary of thrusting a technology that’s become synonymous with effortless cheating at school assignments into students’ hands.

Mamdani has made AI in education a key part of his agenda. In September, he announced a one-year moratorium on New York City schools using AI in the classroom, a policy he called the “most comprehensive of its kind anywhere in the country.”

For Google, amid all these concerns, to tell schools it’ll now cut off their search access if they restrict AI comes off as an unusually spiteful move. It is by far the dominant search engine and most people’s gateway to the internet. Its bargaining power in this standoff with schools is incalculably outsized — hence Mamdani’s accusation that it’s using “monopoly power to force AI into our public schools.”

A federal judge, on that note, ruled in 2024 that Google held an illegal monopoly over the search engine market and used its dominance to shut out competitors. There’s a compelling argument that it’s now doing something similar with schools, hoping that it can strong-arm them into submission so it can guarantee that this generation of children will be future customers by getting them hooked on its AI ecosystem.

More on education: The Tech Industry’s Aggressive Push to Integrate AI Into Schools Is Turning Into a Disaster

items.title: The hottest new job perk is helping employees buy a house
items.summary: Employers are helping homebuying be within reach with new benefits. panaya chittaratlert/Getty Images As competition in the housing market intensifies, many professionals say homebuying is out of reach. Some employers are offering homebuying assistance perks to entice talent in a tough market. Two CEOs say it will be the next cornerstone of employee benefits, like retirement savings. With competition in the pricey San Francisco housing market reaching new heights, Hilary Petee and her husband had given up on the dream of homeownership. "We brushed it off as something that we couldn't do," Petee, 42, told Business Insider. "We thought, 'We can't afford to do that right now. It doesn't make sense.'" But when Petee and her husband's rent increased by 8.8% in August, they began to seriously consider buying, if they could make it work. Petee, a brand manager, discovered that her employer offered Nestment, a platform that provides homeownership coaching, as an employee benefit, and she decided to try it. She and her husband have since closed on a $1.4 million home. Petee said she wouldn't have been able to do it without her homebuying coach. "It didn't feel like my husband and I were going to be able to compete in the competitive housing market in San Francisco," she said. "I was pretty excited that I would have any support at all to be able to help find a home and to understand that in San Francisco, specifically." Employee benefits, like employer-covered healthcare, retirement plans, and student loan debt relief , are a tried-and-true way to recruit and retain talented employees. As it becomes increasingly difficult to own a home in the current market, some employers are offering housing benefits as a new way to win prospective employees' hearts. The American dream is getting a little help from HR Companies like Nestment are heeding the call from employers. "Our mission at Nestment is to bring homeownership to all who want it," Nestment founder Niles Lichtenstein told Business Insider. "We know that homeownership is part of the American dream. It's part of financial wellness and also physical and mental stability." Lichtenstein founded Nestment in 2021 as a startup focused on educating first-time homebuyers, offering them services like a personal homebuying coach and AI tools that help them plan out the best way to buy a home. When customers began asking for integration into their companies, Lichtenstein obliged, launching the service as an employer benefit in early 2026. "We had a bunch of customers say, 'Can we bring this into our workplace?' We also had a couple of instances where we had organizations who said, 'Hey, we see that you're doing this learning education. Can we send this out to our employees?' Lichtenstein said. "We were like, 'there's something here.'" Your company might give you a 401k. But will they help you buy a home? Constantinis/Getty Images Larry Salazar and his wife, Cheri, came to a similar conclusion in 2025 when they launched NestSteps, an employer-sponsored benefit program that helps employees reduce the financial stress of buying a home. Salazar said his own experience attempting to break into the Southern California housing market in 2000 while working for Boeing made him realize the power of homeownership. At the time, he was overwhelmed, and ultimately bought a home once he moved to a more affordable housing market instead. "We moved for the purpose of owning our home," Salazar told Business Insider. "That was probably, for me, a moment where I started to realize something is there that we need to leverage." Employers around the country are catching on. Streaming company Twitch partnered with Denver-based company Multiply Mortgage to offer employees mortgage rate discounts. Financial services company BNY announced earlier this year that it was offering US employees who make less than $100,000 $6,500 towards a down payment — as well as education and mortgage benefits. Brooks Holtom, a professor of management at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, told Business Insider he could see benefits like these catching on, especially in places where it's tougher to enter the market, like in San Francisco. He cited a 2008 program at Mercy Hospital in Miami, which offered $10,000 toward a down payment to nurses who committed to five years at the hospital, as an example. As more companies begin offering benefits like these, Holtom said, others may consider it, too. "It starts with one firm in an industry offering a benefit, and when competitors see that it gets traction, helps them attract or retain employees, then there's a copycat effect — people will follow that lead," he said. "In some industries, there are arms races, especially when talent is scarce. So you see the most extravagant benefits where talent is worth the most, and where talent makes the biggest difference." Lichtenstein and Salazar both see an immediate need for their programs, which they both hope will one day become standard benefits. "You have your 401(k), I have my 401(k). Sure, we love seeing that it's growing, but how often does it impact us right now?" Lichtenstein said. "What impacts you right now is a home." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly
items.summary: From roundabouts to the stock market, relentless streamlining could be making the world more dangerous We have all been there: packed shoulder to shoulder on the train while the person beside us coughs and sneezes. A protective flu jab offers some reassurance, but so does the thought that there will be a hospital bed for you, should you need it. Yet, in England, about 95% of adult hospital beds were occupied at the height of flu season last year. If hospitals were hotels, that level of occupancy would be good business, and we would commend them for their efficiency. But do we really want a hospital to have so few beds in reserve that it’s just one bad flu week away from having to treat patients in corridors?

items.title: I lost my tech job and couldn't afford my mortgage. Now I live in a 100-square-foot shed in the yard and rent out my house.
items.summary: Lauren Patton moved out of her home and into a tiny home in her backyard. Courtesy of Lauren Patton Lauren Patton was confident that her well-paying job provided enough security to buy a home on her own. After she was laid off from her tech job, she eventually couldn't afford her mortgage. To make ends meet, she built a tiny home in her backyard and is renting out rooms in her main home. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lauren Patton, 36, who built a tiny home in her Texas backyard. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. After a couple of years of living in Chicago, I decided to move back to Texas and get a fresh start. This was in 2022, when the real estate market was booming, and homes in Central Texas were getting bought up quickly. I found a real estate agent on Instagram, and she helped me buy a small bungalow — two bedrooms and about 1,000 square feet — for about $400,000. I was buying alone; it was just me and my dog. I had made a very small down payment on my home and taken out a 30-year mortgage. My monthly payment was about $4,000, which was a lot at first, but I thought it was affordable given my well-paying job. At the time, I was working in tech and doing really well. I had been moving up the data science ladder, and I thought it would be a lucrative field. But I was a bit wrong about that. In early 2023, there were a bunch of tech layoffs . I found out the day after I got back from a trip to South Africa that I had been let go. I was given only two months of severance and sent on my way. I could no longer afford my mortgage For the first couple of months after I was laid off , I was OK. I took time to relax, spent time with my family, and did the things you don't get to do while you're working. Then I started looking for jobs. I wasn't super worried at first. I thought, "Hey, I was a data science manager. I'll be able to find something." But after interviewing at numerous places, nothing was happening. By then, money was tight. I had very little savings and was still paying off a lot of credit card debt. I filed for unemployment, which brought in some money, and started renting out my home on Airbnb to help cover my mortgage. To make this work, I rented a room for myself across town for about six months. But when my unemployment ran out, I had to start crashing on people's couches and driving for Lyft— basically doing whatever I could. In 2024, I reached out to a former boss and asked if I could get my previous accounting job back. I did, and while it paid much less than I was making before, it sustained me for a while. Still, I had no savings, and I had cashed out my 401(k) . I was terrified. My mortgage was just so much; I thought my home was going to go into foreclosure. I was already about 30% underwater on the home, and it had depreciated in value, so I still didn't want to sell. I was 35 and thought, "I can't keep doing this." I knew I needed to do something. That's when I came up with the idea to build a little structure in my backyard to live in. I moved out of my home and into my backyard I wasn't confident enough in my woodworking or carpentry skills, so I decided to buy a cabin-style shed kit I found out about on Instagram. I took out a loan and bought it for about $8,500. While I was building the shed , I moved back into my main house and got a roommate to help cover the mortgage. I charged about $1,200 a month for the room. It wasn't a huge portion of my mortgage payment, but it helped. Looking back, I regret buying a two-bedroom house, because there just aren't enough bedrooms to rent out. The shed is about 100 square feet, and the kit came with stackable wood slats, beams, and big windows, but it didn't include a roof or a floor. I had to build the foundation , too. I also added an outhouse with an outdoor shower and built fences and other things around the property. For the construction, I relied on YouTube and ChatGPT — though ChatGPT definitely led me astray on a few things, especially the roofing. items.summary_html:
Lauren Patton moved out of her home and into a tiny home in her backyard.

Courtesy of Lauren Patton

  • Lauren Patton was confident that her well-paying job provided enough security to buy a home on her own.
  • After she was laid off from her tech job, she eventually couldn't afford her mortgage.
  • To make ends meet, she built a tiny home in her backyard and is renting out rooms in her main home.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lauren Patton, 36, who built a tiny home in her Texas backyard. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

After a couple of years of living in Chicago, I decided to move back to Texas and get a fresh start. This was in 2022, when the real estate market was booming, and homes in Central Texas were getting bought up quickly.

I found a real estate agent on Instagram, and she helped me buy a small bungalow — two bedrooms and about 1,000 square feet — for about $400,000. I was buying alone; it was just me and my dog.

I had made a very small down payment on my home and taken out a 30-year mortgage. My monthly payment was about $4,000, which was a lot at first, but I thought it was affordable given my well-paying job.

At the time, I was working in tech and doing really well. I had been moving up the data science ladder, and I thought it would be a lucrative field. But I was a bit wrong about that.

In early 2023, there were a bunch of tech layoffs. I found out the day after I got back from a trip to South Africa that I had been let go. I was given only two months of severance and sent on my way.

I could no longer afford my mortgage

For the first couple of months after I was laid off, I was OK. I took time to relax, spent time with my family, and did the things you don't get to do while you're working. Then I started looking for jobs.

I wasn't super worried at first. I thought, "Hey, I was a data science manager. I'll be able to find something." But after interviewing at numerous places, nothing was happening.

By then, money was tight. I had very little savings and was still paying off a lot of credit card debt. I filed for unemployment, which brought in some money, and started renting out my home on Airbnb to help cover my mortgage.

To make this work, I rented a room for myself across town for about six months. But when my unemployment ran out, I had to start crashing on people's couches and driving for Lyft— basically doing whatever I could.

In 2024, I reached out to a former boss and asked if I could get my previous accounting job back. I did, and while it paid much less than I was making before, it sustained me for a while.

Still, I had no savings, and I had cashed out my 401(k). I was terrified. My mortgage was just so much; I thought my home was going to go into foreclosure. I was already about 30% underwater on the home, and it had depreciated in value, so I still didn't want to sell.

I was 35 and thought, "I can't keep doing this." I knew I needed to do something. That's when I came up with the idea to build a little structure in my backyard to live in.

I moved out of my home and into my backyard

I wasn't confident enough in my woodworking or carpentry skills, so I decided to buy a cabin-style shed kit I found out about on Instagram. I took out a loan and bought it for about $8,500.

While I was building the shed, I moved back into my main house and got a roommate to help cover the mortgage. I charged about $1,200 a month for the room. It wasn't a huge portion of my mortgage payment, but it helped. Looking back, I regret buying a two-bedroom house, because there just aren't enough bedrooms to rent out.

The shed is about 100 square feet, and the kit came with stackable wood slats, beams, and big windows, but it didn't include a roof or a floor. I had to build the foundation, too. I also added an outhouse with an outdoor shower and built fences and other things around the property.

For the construction, I relied on YouTube and ChatGPT — though ChatGPT definitely led me astray on a few things, especially the roofing.

Patton built her shed-like tiny home on her own without formal training.

Courtesy of Lauren Patton

I officially finished the build in March 2025, though I've been making adjustments ever since — it's never-ending.

Since moving into the shed, I've been renting out my main home full-time on Airbnb and have hosted hundreds of guests.

I let Airbnb handle the pricing. On a typical weekend night, I charge around $200; on a weekday during the school year, it's closer to $125.

October is especially lucrative because of the Austin City Limits music festival. This October, my home had about 96% occupancy, and my gross earnings were about $6,516.70. That's not normal — occupancy and nightly rates were higher — but Airbnb deducted $619 in service fees. I also had the home cleaned seven times for about $100 each time.

I put some of the money I earned toward my mortgage and bills for the shed — my total electric bill, including the shed and the house, is $550, which also includes other utilities.

But overall, Airbnb doesn't cover my full mortgage, which increased by $400 a month this year because of home insurance.

Living in the shed has been difficult

It was tough at first, downsizing to a tiny home. Emotionally, it felt like I was regressing in life, and physically, it felt really claustrophobic. But I don't mind it as much now. I'm doing better mentally.

I have most of what I need in a normal house — a TV, a desk, and a bed. But I have a tiny, itty-bitty fridge, and I don't have ice or running water, so I have to stock up on jugs of water.

I've had to learn a lot about how to live in the space. When I first moved in, I had a portable air conditioner, and the humidity would reach 80%. I'd wake up soaking wet and think, "What's going on?" I'd never had to consider something like that before. Now, I run a dehumidifier 24 hours a day.

The hardest part is remembering to keep everything I need on hand, because there's always one thing missing. I'll go to grill chicken and realize I'm out of salt, or that it's back in the main house. I'm constantly running out to buy little things, and sometimes I wonder whether it's really financially worth it.

Some days, I think, "Man, this is harder than I thought it was going to be."

This has been a hard lesson

At this point, I've tried literally everything I can do to keep my home — I mean everything. If things don't get better in the next couple of years, I'll be comfortable letting it go, because I know I tried my hardest.

Looking back, I wish I had done more research as a first-time homebuyer. Aside from a high mortgage, my house is also like 100 years old, so it often needs repairs. I thought I was handy and could do it all myself, but it really wears on your soul.

I also wish I had thought more about the financial worst-case scenario. You hear advice from your parents: Don't let your mortgage take up too much of your income. I wish I had listened and hadn't gone over that 30% threshold.

The next time I buy a home, I need to stay under it. I also can't be so optimistic. I need to be more realistic, because this has shifted my life so much.

Patton plans to live in the tiny home as long as she can afford to.

Courtesy of Lauren Patton

A couple of weeks ago, I started posting about my layoff and the shed on social media. It's really taken off; I've gained around 12,000 followers on Instagram.

I'm really grateful. Most people have been so great and lovely. And while I haven't earned any money from my reels yet, I'm working on it.

As for a job, I'm currently working on a data analytics project and am still walking dogs. My income from my jobs doesn't cover my mortgage, but I'm just grateful to have a job at all.

I feel sorry for people getting laid off, and I can definitely relate. When I'm back on my feet and in a better place financially, I want to help as many people in similar situations as I can.

One day, I'd like to move back into the main house and rent out the shed for a few hundred dollars to someone who needs an affordable place to live.

items.title: What Mark Zuckerberg, Andy Jassy, Sam Altman, and other tech execs have said about parenting
items.summary: Tech execs like Mark Zuckerberg (left) and Andy Jassy (right) have spoken about their approach to parenting. Chris Unger/Zuffa LLC, David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images Some of the most powerful tech execs have been surprisingly candid about raising their children. Many have shared parenting tidbits — including limits to their own children's screen time. Here's a look at some parenting philosophies of the biggest names in tech. Tech executives are helping build the products, platforms, and companies that will shape life for future generations. So how do the people creating tomorrow's technologies think about raising children for the world those technologies are helping create? We looked through past interviews to find some of the tech leaders' most interesting pointers on parenting and setting kids up for success in today's world. Turns out, even the uber-wealthy leaders have to contend with everyday parenting questions, like whether to limit screen time and how to divvy up chores. Here's what some of the biggest names in tech have said about their approach to raising children. Sam Altman Sam Altman Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images The OpenAI CEO told Jimmy Fallon that ChatGPT has helped him raise his baby. Altman said he "cannot imagine" having figured out how to parent a newborn without the technology . He's asked, for example, why his kid wasn't crawling at a certain age. Altman has also said that his baby "will never be smarter than AI ," but will be "more capable." He told the Senate that he doesn't want his kid to form a best-friend-like bond with an AI bot. And when it comes to cribs, Altman has said he has a clear favorite: Cradlewise . It costs nearly $2,000 and gently bounces the baby to head off any fussing. The crib also includes a built-in baby monitor and music features. Altman also said he's learned the importance of having a lot of burp rags. Mark Zuckerberg Mark Zuckerberg is the richest billionaire in California Chris Unger/Getty Images When asked in 2024 what kids should be studying today, Zuckerberg told Bloomberg that "the most important thing is learning how to think critically and learning values when you're young." "This is somewhat of a hiring philosophy that I have, too," he said. "If people have shown that they can go deep and do one thing really well, then they've probably gained experience in the art of learning something and taking it to an excellent level." He also said in a 2024 interview that, when taking his then-seven-year-old daughter to a Taylor Swift concert, he told her that being like the superstar wasn't "available" to her . A therapist in California who has worked with wealthy parents told Business Insider that encouraging her to instead be herself was the right approach. In a 2019 interview on CBS This Morning, the Meta CEO said he and his wife, Priscilla Chan , "don't give them everything." "They have chores, they have responsibilities," Chan added. "We also take them to work. Mark and I take both of them to the office to see what we do, how we contribute." That same year, he told Fox News that he generally doesn't want his kids parked in front of a television or computer "for a long period of time." At the time, he said he let his daughters use video calls to talk with relatives across the country but is stricter about other forms of screen time. Anne Wojcicki TK Cindy Ord/VF24/Getty Images Wojcicki , the cofounder and former CEO of 23andMe, said she tries to keep her children grounded and protected from the "insanity" of being wealthy. In a 2017 interview with The New York Times , Wojcicki said that while she had professional help cleaning the house a few times a week, she had told them to stop doing the laundry on Fridays so that her children could learn the chore. "It's so easy to be like, 'I don't have to do laundry again. I don't have to cook again.' But then you're not normal," she told the Times. "I have a new rule lately. I just don't go out on weekdays. If I'm raising kids, I need to be focused on helping implement that normalcy." Wojcicki also talked at the time about cutting her children's hair herself. Satya Nadella Microsoft Nadella says his own parents "created an environment where they let me set my own pace and pursue what I wanted," and that influenced his approach to raising his own children. "It's important to focus on what [our kids] need to thrive," he previously told Good Housekeeping . The Microsoft CEO and his wife, Anu, also "both think children should have dogs," she told Good Housekeeping. "There is a different sense of companionship and responsibility that comes with it — that emotional sense that there is a being waiting for you to come back," Anu said. Nadella told Good Housekeeping that he gets reports on what their kids do on their computers. The couple limits how many movies and what kinds of video games and websites their kids can view. Nadella has also said that his experience raising a son with cerebral palsy has taught him the importance of empathy, including at work. Sundar Pichai Google CEO Sundar Pichai. Justin Sullivan/Getty Pichai still helps his kids with their homework — with some assistance from Google Lens . "We use Google Lens for homework. I don't want to get him in trouble, but the class allows you to do that," Pichai previously told Bloomberg. "But sometimes he asks me for help on math. Sometimes I'm lazy and I pretend as if I'm thinking, but I'm also using Google Lens to kind of figure out the answer." The Google CEO told The New York Times in 2018 that his son, then 11 years old, didn't have a phone, and that he limited his son's TV use. Bill Gates Bill Gates at the World Economic Forum in Davos. Fabrice Coffrini/Getty Images The Microsoft cofounder has said he parented his kids following a model developed in the 1970s called the "Love and Logic" approach . The philosophy focuses on exercising control when it comes to emotions, such as by minimizing some reactions as a parent, like shouting or reprimanding. Gates said his dad believed in the same philosophy, and that "he was never panicked." Gates, who for many years was the world's richest man, has also said he tried to keep his kids from being spoiled. "We want to strike a balance where they have the freedom to do anything, but not a lot of money showered on them so they could go out and do nothing," he once said . As far as screen time limits go, Gates forbade his kids from using phones at the dinner table , and didn't give them phones until they were 14 years old. In a 2025 episode of the podcast "Raj Shamani's Figuring it Out," Gates said he was giving his children less than 1% of his total wealth, "because I decided it wouldn't be a favor to them." "I want to give them a chance to have their own earnings and success be significant," Gates added. Melinda French Gates Melinda French Gates. Bloomberg/Getty Images The billionaire philanthropist has said one of her guiding ideas as a parent was learning to be "good enough." French Gates, who has three children with Bill Gates, wrote about "the notion of the good enough parent" in an excerpt from her 2025 autobiography published by Time . She said the idea became especially meaningful when her children were 9, 6, and 2, and Warren Buffett's major donation to the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation required her to spend more time away from home. French Gates wrote that she felt guilty about the time she was missing with her children, but the idea helped her let go of the expectation that good parenting required perfection. "And to any other parent who is reading this, know that this is every bit as true for you," she wrote. "When it comes to taking care of your family — some of the most important work you'll do in this world — I hope you'll refuse to let perfectionism rob family life of precious joy." Jeff Bezos Kevin Winter/Getty At times, Bezos took an unusual approach to raising his four kids. He said in 2017 that he let his kids use "sharp knives" from age 4 and power tools at 7 or 8. The Amazon founder attributed this to his then-wife, MacKenzie Scott , who he said would "much rather have a kid with nine fingers than a resourceless kid." Bezos added that this was "a fantastic attitude about life." Alexis Ohanian Taylor Hill/Getty Images The Reddit cofounder incorporated a fun practice from his upbringing into his approach to parenting. "My favorite parenting tip that I inherited from him was his Sunday tradition of making breakfast for our family," he said in 2020. "I love being able to make pancakes with my family when we're all in the same place on a Sunday, and always do my best to put away outside distractions so we can be together." On a 2025 podcast episode, Ohanian said he "wholeheartedly" wanted his then-seven-year-old daughter to use AI every day . He said he's used the technology to enhance her creativity: he had ChatGPT turn some of his childhood pencil sketches into "full-color illustrations." His daughter, Ohanian said, still draws with old-fashioned markers and paper as well. Ohanian told CNBC in 2018 that he and tennis star Serena Williams want their daughter "to know what it's like to have limits on tech." "My wife and I both want her to be bored," he said. "I do look forward to playing video games with her when she's older, but it's really important that she gets time to just be with her thoughts and be with her blocks and be with her toys, so we'll be regulating it pretty heavily." Evan Spiegel Snap CEO Even Spiegel GONZALO FUENTES/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said in 2018 that he and his wife, supermodel Miranda Kerr, limited their then-seven-year-old's screen time to 1.5 hours a week. The rule, he said, was partly influenced by not being allowed to watch television until he was almost a teenager. He said that parents should lead by example and work to limit their own screen time as well. Spiegel told People in 2025 that he's glad his kids are growing up with digital tools, and Kerr said they don't let their 14-year-old have phones or computers in his bedroom past 9:30 pm. Peter Thiel Peter Thiel's influence in Washington stretches far and wide, from politicians, to tech leaders, to his own companies' government contracts. Nordin Catic/Getty Images for The Cambridge Union At the Aspen Ideas Festival in June 2024, Thiel said his children — who were three and a half and five at the time — were allowed to use screens for only about an hour and a half each week. But Thiel also said it was too simplistic to treat tech and social media companies as the source of all modern problems. "It's too easy to turn tech or the social media companies into the scapegoats of all of our problems," he said. Andy Jassy Andy Jassy. David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images Becoming a dad changed how Amazon CEO Andy Jassy would bring work home. "I realized that I had to change the way I worked, or I was either going to have to leave Amazon or I was going to be a lousy dad," he said in October 2026 during the company's "Bring Your Parents to Work Day." Jassy highlighted three immovable parts of his weekly schedule: a Tuesday date night with his wife, a weekly breakfast with each of his two kids, and dinner with the full family every night. If he had more work to do, it would come after the kids went to bed. "I just think some of those things, you just have to decide they're a priority," he said. His daughter, Ohanian said, still draws with old-fashioned markers and paper as well.

Ohanian told CNBC in 2018 that he and tennis star Serena Williams want their daughter "to know what it's like to have limits on tech."

"My wife and I both want her to be bored," he said. "I do look forward to playing video games with her when she's older, but it's really important that she gets time to just be with her thoughts and be with her blocks and be with her toys, so we'll be regulating it pretty heavily."

Evan Spiegel
Snap CEO Even Spiegel

GONZALO FUENTES/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

Snap CEO Evan Spiegel said in 2018 that he and his wife, supermodel Miranda Kerr, limited their then-seven-year-old's screen time to 1.5 hours a week. The rule, he said, was partly influenced by not being allowed to watch television until he was almost a teenager.

He said that parents should lead by example and work to limit their own screen time as well.

Spiegel told People in 2025 that he's glad his kids are growing up with digital tools, and Kerr said they don't let their 14-year-old have phones or computers in his bedroom past 9:30 pm.

Peter Thiel
Peter Thiel's influence in Washington stretches far and wide, from politicians, to tech leaders, to his own companies' government contracts.

Nordin Catic/Getty Images for The Cambridge Union

At the Aspen Ideas Festival in June 2024, Thiel said his children — who were three and a half and five at the time — were allowed to use screens for only about an hour and a half each week.

But Thiel also said it was too simplistic to treat tech and social media companies as the source of all modern problems.

"It's too easy to turn tech or the social media companies into the scapegoats of all of our problems," he said.

Andy Jassy
Andy Jassy.

David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Becoming a dad changed how Amazon CEO Andy Jassy would bring work home.

"I realized that I had to change the way I worked, or I was either going to have to leave Amazon or I was going to be a lousy dad," he said in October 2026 during the company's "Bring Your Parents to Work Day."

Jassy highlighted three immovable parts of his weekly schedule: a Tuesday date night with his wife, a weekly breakfast with each of his two kids, and dinner with the full family every night. If he had more work to do, it would come after the kids went to bed.

"I just think some of those things, you just have to decide they're a priority," he said.

items.summary_html:
Google has open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin, a design-and-review layer for AI coding agents. The Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin makes an agent write a specification before it writes code. Fresh subagents with no conversation history then attack that spec. Google says thousands of its engineers use it. It is quite simple: catch wrong assumptions in a Markdown file, not in a pull request.

TL;DR
  • Size: 7 skills, 9 reviewer personas, 6 brainstorm lenses, 5 review stages. No model weights; your agent supplies the LLM.
  • Runs on: any harness that can spawn fresh subagents: Antigravity, Claude Code 2.1.271+, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT. Uses your existing model quota.
  • Performance: no accuracy benchmark published. Evidence is adoption and end-to-end harness test runs.
  • Best: Codex 0.163.0 completed 15 native fresh-context reviewers in order. 2 live tests passed in 573.13s.
  • Worst: the Claude Cowork run stopped after stages 5 to 7 on a usage limit. Issue #237 reports AGENTS.md leaking into Codex reviewers.
  • Bottom line: best thing, forced independent review before code. Worst thing, heavy token use and unverified isolation on some hosts.
What is Google’s Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin?

EGM is an Apache 2.0 plugin of skills, reviewer personas and document standards. It is not a new language model. The method comes from Dave Rensin’s essay on elephants and goldfish. The Google Open Source blog frames it as a fix for AI “slop” and session context collapse. The README states it is not an officially supported Google product.

How does the Elephant-Goldfish workflow work?

The Elephant is a long session holding project context and earlier decisions. It drafts the spec and writes no code. Each Goldfish is a stateless subagent. It reads only the draft and the files it references. You resolve trade-offs and approve the design.

The core loop has 3 commands:

  • /egm-brainstorm clarifies the idea, then runs a 6-lens Goldfish swarm. Lenses cover YAGNI, token cost, UX, migration, observability and tech debt. Output: concepts_brief.md.
  • /egm-draft turns the brief into a design doc under docs/designs/, section by section.
  • /egm-review runs the Goldfish review.

/egm-drift-report later compares code with the spec. The docs recommend running it weekly.

What happens in the 5-stage Goldfish review?

The review skill runs 5 sequential stages:

  1. Initial Zoom Out: checks the whole document at a high level.
  2. Comprehension Test: a Goldfish paraphrases the design. A wrong paraphrase means the doc is ambiguous.
  3. Critic Review: design, structural and style reviewers hunt gaps and edge cases.
  4. Intermediate Zoom Out: rechecks architecture after fixes.
  5. Implementation Readiness: checks file paths, data structures and signatures.

Each stage allows at most 1 re-audit. Findings are ranked Blocker, Major or Nit. If a host has no subagent tool, EGM stops. A same-context review is not a Goldfish review.

&&

Which coding agents does EGM support?

Launch coverage described Antigravity-only support, with more coming. The current harness guide covers Antigravity CLI and App, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT, omp and Muse. Antigravity CLI, Claude Code and Codex pass automated end-to-end fixtures.

Claude Code needs version 2.1.271 or later. Reviewers there get only Read, Grep and Glob tools. CLAUDE.md files are excluded from their context.

The test record gives concrete run data:

  • Antigravity CLI 1.4.5: 16 native reviewers ran, stages in order.
  • Codex 0.163.0: 15 native reviewers, 2 live tests in 573.13s.
  • Codex CLI with the v0.1.0 ZIP: full suite passed in 482.30s.
How does EGM compare with Spec Kit, Kiro and Superpowers? FeatureGoogle EGMGitHub Spec KitKiro SpecsSuperpowersTypePlugin (skills + personas)Toolkit + Specify CLIFeature of an agentic IDE/CLI/webSkills pluginLicenseApache 2.0MITCommercial (pricing)MITWorkflowBrainstorm, draft, review, drift reportConstitution, specify, plan, tasks, implement, convergeRequirements, design, tasksBrainstorm, plan, subagent build, TDD, reviewSpec reviewed by fresh-context subagentsYes, 5 stages before codeNot disclosedNot disclosed (Analyze Requirements pass)No; fresh subagents review code per taskHarnessAntigravity, Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, moreCopilot and other agentsKiro only16 harnesses listedSetupPlugin installPython 3.11+, uvKiro accountPlugin installCostFree plugin; host model usageFree toolkit; host model usageSubscriptionFree plugin; host model usage

EGM’s distinct move is reviewing the spec with zero-context agents. Spec Kit and Kiro center on human review between phases. Superpowers isolates subagents mainly at implementation time.

Key Takeaways
  • EGM is a plugin, not a model: Elephant drafts, Goldfish reviews.
  • Specs get 5 zero-context review stages before any code.
  • Works across Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex and ChatGPT.
  • Codex test runs completed 15 fresh-context reviewers end to end.
  • Reviewer isolation still leaks host instruction files on some CLIs.

Check out the GitHub repo, the project site and the Google Open Source blog post. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.

items.title: Gig workers are using AI to fight deactivations on apps like Uber and Instacart
items.summary: Some gig workers are using AI to craft evidence summaries and arguments as they fight companies' decisions to deactivate their accounts. Bloomberg/Getty Images Companies like Uber and Instacart often deactivate gig workers' accounts with little notice. Some workers are turning to AI to access their accounts again. Ride-hailing and delivery workers are asking chatbots to write letters and request arbitration. Gig workers fighting their deactivations on apps like Uber and Instacart say they have a new advocate: AI. The companies often kick ride-hailing and delivery workers off of their apps — sometimes for legitimate safety or fraud reasons, other times without fully explaining why. Workers who want to get back on the apps or reach some other settlement must contact the company and initiate an arbitration process. The procedure can be long and require parsing the contracts that bind the workers. That's led some workers to turn to chatbots to help them negotiate with the companies. They found that AI assistance can help level the playing field with the large companies. One deactivated Instacart worker told Business Insider that he's using ChatGPT to challenge the company's claim that he didn't follow the correct route to deliver an order. The driver said he has used the chatbot to write evidence reports and estimate how much he's lost in wages since Instacart kicked him off the app earlier this year. The driver, who has corresponded with Instacart regarding his case, has also consulted the chatbot on when to send his latest response to Instacart — and whether he might have any luck finding pro bono legal advice. "ChatGPT said to hold off on that for now," he said. "We're gonna see if we can get a lawyer." Since the rise of chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, users have been turning to the tools for advice on legal, medical, and other problems . The responses from these chatbots are often written in an authoritative tone, and they can turn out official-looking documents with a prompt or two. It also carries risks, however. Using AI-generated briefs or arguments in a legal setting can introduce errors and undermine credibility. Robert Bruno, a professor of labor and employment relations at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said AI is still beneficial to gig workers who have few other options. "They're not locked out of being able to defend themselves because they lack the financial means to hire a very good labor attorney," he said. Using AI to generate evidence summaries is just one part of the process, Bruno added. Gig workers fighting deactivations in arbitration also have to make a persuasive argument to be reinstated on the apps — and even tailor that argument to the specific arbitrator hearing their case. "I don't think you could just spit that out of Copilot or Claude," Bruno said. Spokespeople for Uber and Instacart did not comment directly on workers using AI to fight deactivations. An Uber spokesperson said that the company uses "data and facts" to evaluate claims "regardless of how an appeal is submitted." An Instacart spokesperson said that the company does not "take deactivation lightly" and gives workers the chance to appeal those decisions. Uber drivers and Instacart shoppers tend to have few options when they try to take on their employers. As independent contractors, companies usually have wide latitude in terminating them, and lawyers are often hesitant to represent them because of the arbitration requirements in the companies' terms for gig workers. That leaves many on their own — and more amenable to an assist from AI. On Reddit pages for gig workers, some users have posted stories about using ChatGPT to write letters to Uber Eats and DoorDash requesting reinstatement of their accounts. Some wrote that the AI-generated messages worked. One Uber driver in Tennessee told Business Insider that he consulted ChatGPT for advice after the company deactivated his account without a clear explanation. After a back-and-forth with the chatbots, he said he had a letter that cited Uber's driver contract and asked to begin arbitration proceedings. AI also had a strategic suggestion: Email it to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, not just the generic email for arbitration requests, the driver said. About a week later, the driver could access his account again. "I followed AI, and I guess it worked," he said. The companies themselves already use AI when interacting with gig workers. Uber customer service employees, for instance, often use AI to write responses to drivers' messages, Business Insider reported last month. Uber and Instacart have in the past declined to say what role AI plays in the initial decision to deactivate workers. Uber said that appeals of those decisions are reviewed by "a real person." "Final deactivation decisions are always reviewed by a human," the Instacart spokesperson said. Do you have a story idea about the gig economy? items.title: Which Routing Does Each MoE Model Use? DeepSeek, Qwen, Mixtral, Llama 4, gpt-oss Compared
items.summary: Open Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models share one idea but disagree on almost every routing detail. Expert counts range from 8 to 384. Top-k ranges from 1 to 8. Some models keep an always-on shared expert; others drop it. TL;DR Size: 10 models, from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (35B total, 3B active) to DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T total, 49B active). Runs on: gpt-oss-120b fits one 80 GB GPU with MXFP4; DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi K2 need multi-GPU expert parallelism. Performance: Routed sparsity spans 4x in Mixtral (8 experts, top-2) to 128x in Llama 4 Maverick (128, top-1). Best: Kimi K2 found sparsity 48 needed 1.69x fewer FLOPs than sparsity 8 at equal validation loss. Worst: Llama 4 Maverick and gpt-oss do not publish their gating or balancing method in config.json. Bottom line: Best thing: configs make routing fully auditable. Worst thing: names like “17B active” hide very different routers. How do open MoE models route tokens? Every model below uses token-choice routing: each token selects its own experts. They differ on 5 knobs. These are expert count, experts per token, shared experts, the scoring function and the load-balancing method. The table lists each knob per model. MoE routing comparison table (November 2026) Model Total / active params Routed experts Top-k Shared experts Gating Load balancing Mixtral 8x7B 47B / 13B 8 2 0 Softmax over top-k Aux loss, coef 0.02 ( config ) gpt-oss-120b 117B / 5.1B 128 4 0 Softmax over selected Not disclosed Qwen3-235B-A22B 235B / 22B 128 8 0 Softmax, top-k normalized Global-batch aux loss, coef 0.001 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 35B / 3B 256 8 1 Not disclosed Aux loss, coef 0.001 (config) Llama 4 Maverick 400B / 17B 128 1 1 Not disclosed Not disclosed DeepSeek-V3 671B / 37B 256 8 1 Sigmoid Aux-loss-free bias (noaux_tc) DeepSeek-V4-Pro 1.6T / 49B 384 6 1 sqrtsoftplus noaux_tc; hash routing in 3 layers DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B / 13B 256 6 1 sqrtsoftplus noaux_tc; hash routing in 3 layers Kimi K2 1.04T / 32B 384 8 1 Sigmoid noaux_tc + sequence aux, alpha 0.001 GLM-4.5 355B / 32B 160 8 1 Sigmoid Loss-free balance routing Sources: each model’s Hugging Face config.json, model card or technical report, verified November 7, 2026. Configs and cards for Qwen3.6 and Llama 4 omit gating. gpt-oss and Llama 4 omit the balancing method. && How does DeepSeek-V3 routing work? DeepSeek-V3 scores 256 routed experts with a sigmoid, then normalizes the selected scores. A per-expert bias steers the top-8 selection without touching the mixing weights. Experts sit in 8 groups, and the router keeps 4 groups first. Each token reaches at most 4 nodes, according to the technical report . One shared expert runs for every token. What changed in DeepSeek-V4 routing? DeepSeek-V4 raises Pro to 384 routed experts but lowers top-k from 8 to 6. The score function becomes sqrtsoftplus. The first 3 MoE layers use hash routing , a fixed token-to-expert map. Bias-based noaux_tc balancing stays. How many experts does Qwen3 MoE use? Both original Qwen3 MoE models use 128 experts and route each token to 8. Qwen3 dropped the shared experts of Qwen2.5-MoE and adopted a global-batch balancing loss. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B changes course: 256 experts, 8 routed plus 1 shared, per its model card . How does Llama 4 Maverick routing differ? Llama 4 Maverick alternates dense and MoE layers. In each MoE layer, a token goes to 1 shared expert and 1 of 128 routed experts. That top-1 design echoes the Switch Transformer. It keeps 17B active parameters despite 400B in total. How does gpt-oss route tokens? gpt-oss-120b uses a linear router over 128 experts and keeps the top 4. Its config lists no shared expert. Its MoE weights ship in MXFP4, which lets the 117B model fit on a single 80 GB GPU. Why do Kimi K2 and GLM-4.5 look like DeepSeek-V3? Kimi K2 ships with the DeepseekV3ForCausalLM architecture class and the noaux_tc router. It raises routed experts to 384 at the same top-8. The Kimi K2 report found that higher sparsity lowered loss at fixed active compute. GLM-4.5 chose 160 experts and more layers instead, favoring depth over width. What the trend means for serving More experts per layer means more weights resident in memory and more all-to-all traffic. Lower top-k, as in DeepSeek-V4, trims per-token compute and communication. Shared experts add a dense path that every token pays for. Check these fields before sizing GPUs for any MoE deployment. Key Takeaways Expert counts grew from 8 (Mixtral) to 384 (Kimi K2, DeepSeek-V4-Pro). Top-k now spans 1 (Llama 4) to 8 (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5). 7 of 10 models keep 1 shared expert; Mixtral, gpt-oss and Qwen3 do not. Sigmoid or sqrtsoftplus with bias balancing is the DeepSeek-family standard. Llama 4 and gpt-oss leave gating or balancing details unpublished. Model sources: DeepSeek-V4-Pro , DeepSeek-V3 report , Qwen3 report , Kimi K2 report , GLM-4.5 report , Mixtral paper . Also see gpt-oss-120b and the Llama 4 announcement . How do open MoE models route tokens?

Every model below uses token-choice routing: each token selects its own experts. They differ on 5 knobs. These are expert count, experts per token, shared experts, the scoring function and the load-balancing method. The table lists each knob per model.

MoE routing comparison table (November 2026) ModelTotal / active paramsRouted expertsTop-kShared expertsGatingLoad balancingMixtral 8x7B47B / 13B820Softmax over top-kAux loss, coef 0.02 (config)gpt-oss-120b117B / 5.1B12840Softmax over selectedNot disclosedQwen3-235B-A22B235B / 22B12880Softmax, top-k normalizedGlobal-batch aux loss, coef 0.001Qwen3.6-35B-A3B35B / 3B25681Not disclosedAux loss, coef 0.001 (config)Llama 4 Maverick400B / 17B12811Not disclosedNot disclosedDeepSeek-V3671B / 37B25681SigmoidAux-loss-free bias (noaux_tc)DeepSeek-V4-Pro1.6T / 49B38461sqrtsoftplusnoaux_tc; hash routing in 3 layersDeepSeek-V4-Flash284B / 13B25661sqrtsoftplusnoaux_tc; hash routing in 3 layersKimi K21.04T / 32B38481Sigmoidnoaux_tc + sequence aux, alpha 0.001GLM-4.5355B / 32B16081SigmoidLoss-free balance routing

Sources: each model’s Hugging Face config.json, model card or technical report, verified November 7, 2026. Configs and cards for Qwen3.6 and Llama 4 omit gating. gpt-oss and Llama 4 omit the balancing method.

&&

How does DeepSeek-V3 routing work?

DeepSeek-V3 scores 256 routed experts with a sigmoid, then normalizes the selected scores. A per-expert bias steers the top-8 selection without touching the mixing weights. Experts sit in 8 groups, and the router keeps 4 groups first. Each token reaches at most 4 nodes, according to the technical report. One shared expert runs for every token.

What changed in DeepSeek-V4 routing?

DeepSeek-V4 raises Pro to 384 routed experts but lowers top-k from 8 to 6. The score function becomes sqrtsoftplus. The first 3 MoE layers use hash routing, a fixed token-to-expert map. Bias-based noaux_tc balancing stays.

How many experts does Qwen3 MoE use?

Both original Qwen3 MoE models use 128 experts and route each token to 8. Qwen3 dropped the shared experts of Qwen2.5-MoE and adopted a global-batch balancing loss. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B changes course: 256 experts, 8 routed plus 1 shared, per its model card.

How does Llama 4 Maverick routing differ?

Llama 4 Maverick alternates dense and MoE layers. In each MoE layer, a token goes to 1 shared expert and 1 of 128 routed experts. That top-1 design echoes the Switch Transformer. It keeps 17B active parameters despite 400B in total.

How does gpt-oss route tokens?

gpt-oss-120b uses a linear router over 128 experts and keeps the top 4. Its config lists no shared expert. Its MoE weights ship in MXFP4, which lets the 117B model fit on a single 80 GB GPU.

Why do Kimi K2 and GLM-4.5 look like DeepSeek-V3?

Kimi K2 ships with the DeepseekV3ForCausalLM architecture class and the noaux_tc router. It raises routed experts to 384 at the same top-8. The Kimi K2 report found that higher sparsity lowered loss at fixed active compute. GLM-4.5 chose 160 experts and more layers instead, favoring depth over width.

What the trend means for serving

More experts per layer means more weights resident in memory and more all-to-all traffic. Lower top-k, as in DeepSeek-V4, trims per-token compute and communication. Shared experts add a dense path that every token pays for. Check these fields before sizing GPUs for any MoE deployment.

Key Takeaways
  • Expert counts grew from 8 (Mixtral) to 384 (Kimi K2, DeepSeek-V4-Pro).
  • Top-k now spans 1 (Llama 4) to 8 (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5).
  • 7 of 10 models keep 1 shared expert; Mixtral, gpt-oss and Qwen3 do not.
  • Sigmoid or sqrtsoftplus with bias balancing is the DeepSeek-family standard.
  • Llama 4 and gpt-oss leave gating or balancing details unpublished.

Model sources: DeepSeek-V4-Pro, DeepSeek-V3 report, Qwen3 report, Kimi K2 report, GLM-4.5 report, Mixtral paper. Also see gpt-oss-120b and the Llama 4 announcement.

items.title: AWS principal engineer says the best engineers are ‘paranoid and lazy’ when it comes to AI
items.summary: David Yanacek said the best engineers are "paranoid and lazy." AWS David Yanacek, a senior principal engineer at AWS, said the best engineers are "paranoid and lazy." He said paranoia keeps him alert about potential safety risks. Laziness motivates him to find ways to prevent those risks and make things work, he said. Many think that judgment and taste are the traits that set apart the strongest engineers in the AI era. David Yanacek, a senior principal engineer at AWS, thinks the ideal developer has some additional attributes. He told Business Insider that the best engineers nowadays are also "paranoid and lazy." That, he said, makes for a good combination when working with agents . "Paranoid means I'm very sensitive to what could possibly happen if I gave an agent permission to do a thing without supervision," said Yanacek, who works on agentic AI and safety. Laziness, he said, means he doesn't want to perform repetitive tasks manually. The new workflow While AI has taken over most coding tasks, Yanacek said that wasn't the main bottleneck. In addition to writing the actual code, engineers used to spend days waiting for manual tests, code approvals, and design tweaks. Those processes required constant waiting for teammates' reviews. Now, human intervention is reserved for design discussions and complex reviews, while agents handle much of the other work in a loop. These loops involve generating code, running tests, reworking problems, and preparing updates that then get merged and deployed. While one loop can run for hours, Yanacek can shift to other projects or add additional features to a product in the meantime. Setting the right guardrails For agentic workflows to run efficiently and save time, agents need to operate autonomously, Yanacek said. So he spends much of his time deciding which tools agents can use without supervision, which actions need approval, and where those limits should be enforced. To make that work, Yanacek makes sure his "auto-trust" file is sound. That's the set of rules that specifies which tools and commands an agent can use independently, and which ones require a human sign-off. "I always think about what is in the auto-trust file, because that's how you get productivity: by having the agent be able to do things without you having to micromanage every single command that it runs," Yanacek said. His goal is to have a fleet of agents making the right calls without constant review and approval. That requires clear policies for what an agent should and shouldn't do. "Most of what I think about is AI safety," Yanacek said. "And because I'm doing that, I sleep pretty well." Engineers need to have a layer of paranoia and laziness so they can be alert to what could go wrong when an agent acts without supervision, he said. However, they also need to build systems reliable enough that they don't have to supervise every action. The end goal, he said, is to do enough work up front to make the agent trustworthy enough to run unsupervised so it can automate the tedious parts. Read the original article on Business Insider

While AI has taken over most coding tasks, Yanacek said that wasn't the main bottleneck. In addition to writing the actual code, engineers used to spend days waiting for manual tests, code approvals, and design tweaks. Those processes required constant waiting for teammates' reviews.

Setting the right guardrails

For agentic workflows to run efficiently and save time, agents need to operate autonomously, Yanacek said. So he spends much of his time deciding which tools agents can use without supervision, which actions need approval, and where those limits should be enforced.

To make that work, Yanacek makes sure his "auto-trust" file is sound. That's the set of rules that specifies which tools and commands an agent can use independently, and which ones require a human sign-off.

"I always think about what is in the auto-trust file, because that's how you get productivity: by having the agent be able to do things without you having to micromanage every single command that it runs," Yanacek said.

items.title: How We Built an MCP Server on Our Existing APIs
items.summary: We built an MCP server for our product in a few weeks. Most of it was reuse: the same reporting APIs, the same identity provider, the same Kubernetes cluster and pipeline. This is a write up of what we did, what worked and what we plan next. Why Our customers have a lot of operational data in our product: orders, events, exceptions, team and location performance. Today they see it through report screens. When they have a question the screens don't answer, it becomes a feature request or an Excel export. Most of our customers already use an AI assistant. So the ask was: let them connect their own assistant to their data in our product, with the same permissions they have in the web app. No new copy of the data, no new login. flowchart LR subgraph Today Q1[New question] --> F1[Feature request] --> F2[Report built weeks later] --> F3[Answer] Q1 --> E1[Export to Excel] --> F3 end subgraph With MCP Q2[Question in plain language] --> AI[AI assistant] --> T[MCP tools] --> A2[Answer and chart] end What MCP is MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to other systems. A server exposes tools. Each tool has a name, typed inputs and a description. The assistant reads the descriptions, decides which tools to call and uses the results in its answer. Since it is a standard, one server works with Claude, other assistants, IDEs and the customer's own agents. flowchart LR C1[Claude] --> S C2[Other AI assistants] --> S C3[IDE and agent tools] --> S C4[Customer's own agent] --> S S[MCP server] --> P[(Operational data)] We looked at two other options before choosing MCP: Option Why not Build our own chatbot We would own the model, the UI and the cost. Customers already have assistants. Export data to a warehouse for AI New pipelines, stale data, a second permission model and a bigger security review. MCP server Chosen. Works with any assistant and uses our existing security. Where the tools get data There were three choices: A new data API built for AI. A warehouse or lakehouse loaded with reporting data. The reporting APIs our web app already uses. We went with the third. The reporting service already finds the tenant for each request and connects to that tenant's database, checks the user's permissions on every endpoint and reads through stored procedures that are tuned and tested. flowchart TB Q{Where should the tools get data?} Q --> N[New data API] Q --> W[Warehouse or lakehouse] Q --> E[Existing reporting APIs] N --> N1[Duplicate tenancy, auth and queries] W --> W1[New pipelines, new permission model] E --> E1[Tenancy, permissions and queries already exist] E1 --> OK[Chosen for version 1] W1 -. "later, for analytics" .-> LT[See: Next phase] So the MCP server only translates. A tool call comes in, it calls an existing endpoint and returns a compact JSON result. It has no database credentials. If a user can't see something in the web app, the assistant can't see it either. Architecture flowchart LR U[User] --> A[AI assistant any MCP client] A -- "MCP over HTTPS + user's access token" --> G[Ingress / API gateway] G --> M[MCP server stateless container] M -- "same token + tenant header" --> R[Existing reporting API] M -- "same token" --> O[Existing app API e.g. location list] R --> D[(Tenant reporting database)] A -. "OAuth sign in" .-> I[Existing identity provider] M -. "verify token signature" .-> I AI assistant: any MCP client. We used Claude with a custom connector. MCP server: a small TypeScript service on the official MCP SDK. It defines the tools, validates inputs, calls the APIs and trims the results. Identity provider: our existing OpenID Connect provider, same one the web app uses. Reporting API and database: no changes, except two new endpoints (see Performance below). Authentication We expected this to be the hardest part. It was mostly configuration, because MCP uses standard OAuth. sequenceDiagram participant C as AI assistant participant M as MCP server participant I as Identity provider participant R as Reporting API C->>M: Call /mcp (no token) M-->>C: 401 + pointer to resource metadata C->>M: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource M-->>C: "My authorization server is " C->>I: Discover endpoints, start sign in (PKCE) I-->>C: User signs in as usual, gets access token C->>M: Call tool with Bearer token M->>M: Verify signature and issuer M->>R: Same request, same token R-->>M: Data the user is allowed to see M-->>C: Compact result Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728). For a request without a token, the server returns 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header. The header points to a small JSON document that tells the assistant which authorization server to use. Authorization server metadata. Some clients look for discovery documents at specific well known paths, so we serve the identity provider's metadata at those paths too. Authorization code flow with PKCE. The user signs in on the normal login page. PKCE secures the exchange without a client secret, since the assistant is a public client. Token pass through. The server checks the token signature and issuer, then sends the same token to the APIs. The APIs enforce permissions the same way they do for the web app. The model never sees the token. Public client instead of dynamic registration MCP clients can register themselves with the identity provider automatically (dynamic client registration). Many enterprise identity setups don't allow that. Our first try failed with a generic "couldn't register" error. We created one public client for MCP, allowed only the assistant's redirect URL, and entered that client ID in the connector settings. That fixed it. Token claims Our APIs filter data using claims in the token, for example which locations a user can see and which roles they have. A new client doesn't get the same claims as the web app client by default, so we added the same claim mappers. Check this early. A valid token with a missing claim returns empty results, and it takes time to figure out why. Multi tenancy Each customer has its own subdomain and its own identity realm. The MCP server gets everything from the host name of the request: the tenant, sent as a header to the APIs so they connect to the right database, the expected token issuer, so a token from one tenant is rejected on another, the resource metadata URL it advertises. flowchart LR H["Request host customer-a.example.com"] --> P[MCP server parses host] P --> T1[Tenant id customer-a] P --> T2[Expected issuer customer-a realm] P --> T3[Resource metadata URL] T1 --> API[Tenant header on every API call] API --> DB[(customer-a reporting database)] T2 --> V{Token issuer matches?} V -- no --> X[401 rejected] V -- yes --> API One deployment serves all tenants on a cluster, with no per tenant configuration. Signing keys are fetched from each issuer and cached. Tool design Most of the answer quality depends on this. Small set of read only tools. We started with eight, covering a location list, KPI summary, team and location performance, exceptions, slowest events and record lookup. No write actions in version 1. Write descriptions for the model. Each description says what the tool returns, what each input means and when to use it. For example, the location input says to call the location list first if the user gives a city name. With that one line, users can say "Chicago" instead of an internal code. Summarize on the server. API responses built for screens can be hundreds of KB. We aggregate before returning, for example totals per team instead of every event. One response went from over 700 KB to under 50 KB. Smaller results are faster, cost fewer tokens and give more accurate answers. Limit the size. Top 10 by default and row caps on everything. Validate inputs. Zod schemas reject bad dates or missing fields before any API call, with an error message the model can act on. Ask for charts. MCP servers can send instructions to the client. Ours asks for a chart when the result compares items or shows a trend. Example of one question turning into two tool calls. The model decides the order from the descriptions: sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant A as AI assistant participant M as MCP server U->>A: "Where are the biggest delays at our Chicago site this month?" A->>M: list_locations(search: "Chicago") M-->>A: Chicago = location code CHI A->>M: get_slowest_events(location: CHI, from, to) M-->>A: Top 10 items with average delay minutes A-->>U: Bar chart + explanation + suggested actions flowchart LR R[Raw API response every record, every event ~700 KB] --> S[MCP server aggregate, rank, top N] --> O[Tool result per team totals under 50 KB] Performance Two of our questions ("longest delays last month" and "exceptions by location") took several minutes in the first version. The queries were parsing large JSON event records across millions of rows on every call. We fixed it with regular database work: a summary table with one row per event and the duration and exception flags already calculated, a stored procedure that refreshes it for a date range, two small query stored procedures behind two new reporting endpoints. flowchart LR subgraph Before["Before: minutes"] Q1[Tool call] --> J[Parse JSON events across millions of rows] --> A1[Answer] end subgraph After["After: under a second"] S[Scheduled refresh stored procedure] --> T[(Event summary table)] Q2[Tool call] --> P[Small query stored procedure] --> T P --> A2[Answer] end Both now return in under a second. In our tests, the MCP server and APIs take about 0.1 to 2.5 seconds per tool call. Most of the remaining time is the model thinking and writing. A faster model, lower reasoning effort, simple charts and small results help more than tuning the server further. Hosting Nothing new was set up. Container: a small multi stage Docker image. Kubernetes: one more subchart in the existing Helm release, in the same cluster and namespace as the APIs. It calls them by internal service name, so tool traffic stays inside the cluster. Ingress: new routes on the existing gateway for /mcp and the well known discovery paths. The server runs on the tenant's existing host name. Stateless transport: MCP Streamable HTTP in stateless mode. Each request gets a new server and transport, so no sticky sessions and it scales horizontally. CI/CD: the existing pipeline builds, scans and pushes the image with the other services. flowchart TB subgraph CI["CI/CD pipeline (existing)"] B[Build image] --> SC[Security scan] --> PU[Push to registry] end PU --> HL[Helm release new subchart added] subgraph K["Kubernetes cluster (existing)"] IN[Ingress gateway + /mcp and well known routes] --> MS[MCP server pods stateless] MS --> RS[Reporting API service] MS --> AS[App API service] IN --> WEB[Web app] end HL --> MS Internet[AI assistant] --> IN Few things we ran into: Our build installs all workspace packages at once. Adding the MCP server to the main backend workspace pushed a code analysis step over its memory limit. Moving it to its own folder fixed it. After a deploy, the gateway can take a minute or more to pick up new pods. Run at least two replicas for anything you demo live. Our database deployment is incremental and skips new tables, so the summary table needed a release script. Connecting Claude This took a few minutes: An org admin adds a custom connector with the MCP URL. In advanced settings, the admin sets our public client ID (no secret). Each user clicks Connect and signs in on the normal login page. flowchart LR A1[Admin adds custom connector with MCP URL] --> A2[Admin sets public client id, no secret] A2 --> U1[User clicks Connect] U1 --> U2[Normal login page] U2 --> U3[Tools available in chat] After that, a user can ask "How did the Chicago site do last Monday? Show it as a dashboard" and get the answer with charts. What we learned The existing APIs already handled tenancy and permissions. That is why the MCP server is only a few hundred lines. Standard OAuth was enough. Resource metadata, PKCE and a public client worked with our identity provider without custom auth code. Tool descriptions, result size and defaults matter more than the number of tools. If a question is slow in SQL, it is slower through an assistant. Precompute it. Treat a live demo like a release: sign in beforehand, two replicas, and questions that return in seconds. Other next steps Finer scopes, so a customer can give the assistant less access than the full user has. Audience restriction on tokens issued for the MCP client. More tools, based on what customers actually ask. Write actions that only draft a change for a person to approve. Usage telemetry on which tools and questions get used. If you already have secure APIs and an identity provider, you don't need a new platform to get started. A thin MCP server on top of them is enough for version 1. See what people ask, then decide what to build behind it.

We built an MCP server for our product in a few weeks. Most of it was reuse: the same reporting APIs, the same identity provider, the same Kubernetes cluster and pipeline. This is a write up of what we did, what worked and what we plan next.

Why

Our customers have a lot of operational data in our product: orders, events, exceptions, team and location performance. Today they see it through report screens. When they have a question the screens don't answer, it becomes a feature request or an Excel export.

Most of our customers already use an AI assistant. So the ask was: let them connect their own assistant to their data in our product, with the same permissions they have in the web app. No new copy of the data, no new login.

What MCP is

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to other systems. A server exposes tools. Each tool has a name, typed inputs and a description. The assistant reads the descriptions, decides which tools to call and uses the results in its answer. Since it is a standard, one server works with Claude, other assistants, IDEs and the customer's own agents.
