items.title: The Mathematics Behind Artificial Intelligence: How Linear Algebra Makes Machines Learn
items.summary: Cover Image Behind every intelligent system, there is a language of numbers, vectors and metrices. From identifying human language to generating images and making predictions, Artificial Intelligence relies heavily on mathematical structures that allow systems to represent, process and learn from information. Among the many branches of Mathematics, Linear Algebra stands as one of the main fundamental pillars of modern AI . Yet its role extends far beyond simply arranging numbers into rows and columns. Vectors represent information, matrices transform data mathematical operations enable neural networks to learn complex patterns hidden within large datasets. In this article, we will explore how Linear Algebra works behind the surface of AI. Why does AI need Linear Algebra? In Artificial Intelligent systems, at its core, the AI model recieves information, represents it in a mathematical form, processes those information by using a huge amount of mathematical calculations and produces output. The input can be a text, image, video or any other input type. But, AI models, even computers cannot identify or understand those inputs and process them as humans do. They use a mathematical representation to store and process those. This is where Linear Algebra becomes important. It provides an efficient way to store data using matrices and vectors. Also, it provides an efficient way to perform the mathematical operations required to transform those data into a meaningful output. As AI models become more complex and datasets grow larger, these representations allow computations to be effective and organized. With billions of Mathematical operations involving matrices and vectors, Modern AI systems appear to be intelligent. From Real-World information to Mathematical Vectors Imagine providing a picture of a cat to the AI System. To a human, with a single glance, the information about the picture such as, shape of the ears, color of the furs and the color, position of eyes can be observed. But, for a computer, a picture is a collection of a numerical pixel values. Each pixel contains a numerical value about its color and intensity. These values can be organized into mathematical structures that AI model can process. This is where Vectors are used. What is a vector? In Linear Algebra, a vector is an ordered collection of numbers that can represent a point in a mathematical space or encode a set of features describing an object. eg :- A simplified representation of an image might be expressed as, X = [0.2, 0.8, 0.5, 0.1] where each number represents a particular pixel value or a feature. Although this example contains only four values, real images may contain thousands or millions of numerical values. Similarly, an AI model can represent person’s characteristics, a piece of text or a collection of measurements as a vector. When these information are converted into vectors, AI model can perform calculations, identify relationships and learn patterns from the data. Vectors are the fundamental component between the complex real — world information and the mathematical computations that make AI possible . Image to Vector Matrices While vectors provide a way to represent single pieces of information, matrices allow to organize and store large collections of numerical data. A Matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns and it plays an important role in Artificial Intelligence. Consider an image of containing thousands of pixels. Its numerical values can be arranged into a matrix, allowing the computer to perform mathematical operations on the image. Not only for image representations, but also, in Machine Learning, datasets containing multiple observations and features are represented in matrices. More importantly, matrices are used in internal workings of neural networks. They are used to store weights and perform transformations that allow information to pass through different layers of a network. Through matrix operations, an AI model can combine input information, identify relationships between variables and gradually learn complex patterns from data. Therefore, Matrices provide the computational framework that enables AI models to process large amount of information efficiently. Matrix Multiplication Among the operations related to Matrices, Matrix Multiplication is one of the most important matrix operations which allows an AI model to combine information and transform it into different representations. Consider a simple neural network that recieves several numerical inputs, such as measurements describing an object. Each input is assigned a weight , representing its contribution to the model’s calculations. These weights can be arranged in a matrix and multiplied by an input vector to produce an output vector. Mathematically, this operation can be expressed as, y = W x + b where y is the output vector, x is the input vector, W is the weight matrix and b is the bias vector. Although this expression looks simple, it represents one of the fundamental computations performed repeatedly throughout neural networks. Each layer receives information from the previous layer, applies its own weights and biases and passes the transformed information to the next layer. During the training process, the models adjusts these weights and biases to reduce prediction errors and improve its performance. Therefore, the matrix multiplication is the central computational mechanism which neural networks learn from data. Neural Networks Matrix Multiplication process Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors With matrices, vecctors and matrix multiplication, another important connection between Linear Algebra and Artificial Intelligence is from eigenvalues and eigenvectors. These two concepts help us to understand how a matrix transformation affects different directions in a mathematical space. Therefore, an eigenvector is a non-zero vector whose direction remains unchanged when a particular square matrix acts on it, while its corresponding eigenvalue describes how much that vector is scaled during the transformation. Mathematically, the relationship can be expressed as Av = λv where A represents a square matrix, v is eigenvector and λ is its corresponding eigenvalue. Although eigenvalues and eigenvectors are one of the fundamental mathematical concepts, they also have important applications in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. Many machine learning algorithms work with large matrices to identify the patterns and relationships within datasets. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors provide a mathematical way to understand the properties of these matrices and how they transform information. For an example, they can identify important directions in which data varies, reveal important structures within datasets and simplify certain mathematical computations. Thses properties particularly useful when developing algorithms that need to analyse large amounts of information efficiently. Therefore, eigenvalues and eigenvectors not only mathematical concepts, they provide valuable tools for understanding and developing various techniques used in modern Machine Learning. Measuring similarity between vectors In Artificial Intelligence, representing information mathematically using vectors is only one part of the process. AI models also need mathematical techniques to compare these representations and identify relationships between them. One of the techniques that AI models use to identify the relationship between vectors is Cosine Similarity , which is based on the dot product of two vectors. To understand this concept, the geometric relationship between two vectors must be considered. The dot product of two vectors is related to the cosine value of the angle between them. Geometric Representation of vectors Mathematically, for two non-zero vectors a and b , cosine similarity is defined as the dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes. This normalization makes the result independent of the magnitudes of the vectors and allow only to focus on their directional relationship. The resulting values lies between -1 and 1. The value 1 indicates that vectors point in the same direction, the value 0 indicates that vectors are perpendicular while -1 indicates that vectors point to the opposite direction. This is particularly useful when comapring data represented by vectors because two vectors can have significantly different magnitudes while they are still sharing the same direction. For an example, consider two vectors a = (1,2) and b = (2,4). Although their magnitudes are different, one vector is simply a scalar multiple of the other. Then, the cosine value of the angle between two vectors is 1 which indicates the two vectors are in the same direction, while their dot product is 10. By looking at the dot product, it is hard to interpret anything about their directional similarity. In mathetically, we can express this as an equation, Cosine relation between two vectors This mathematical technique has important applications in AI, specially in Natural Language Processing (NLP) where words, sentences and documents can be represented as numerical representations. By comparing these vectors by using cosine similarity, AI systems can estimate how closely related two pieces of text are in their numerical representations. As an example, a document-search system can compare the vector representations of a user’s query with the representations of stored documets and identify the documents that are directionally similar to the query. Linear Algebra as a unified mathematical framework for AI The true importance of Linear Algebra in Artificial Intelligence becomes clearer when the way of its different concepts work together is considered. Vectors and matrices provide structured ways to represent numerical information, while matrix operations allow AI models to manipulate and transform these representations. The dot product and cosine similarity offer mathematical methods for examining relationships between vectors and find their directional similarity. Meanwhile, eigenvalues and eigenvectors provide ways to investigate the properties of matrices and understand how certain transformations affect data. These concepts are not independent mathematical tools, they contribute to the development and operation of AI systems. From representing information to processing numerical data and identifying relationships, Linear Algebra provides a mathematical foundation for many of the operations performed by many modern AI tools. Why understanding Linear Algebra matters Artificial Intelligence is often viewed as a field with programming languages, codes, algorithms and computational power. However, behind many of these technologies, there is a concrete mathematical foundation. Understanding Linear Algebra allows us to look beyond the AI outputs and gain insights into the mathematical operations that make them possible. Instead of treating a Machine Learning model as a black box, Knowledge of vectors, matrices and their operations helps us understand how information is represented, transformed and processed. It also provides a foundation for exploring more advanced areas of Artificial Intelligence, including deep learning, computer vision and natural language processing. Ultimately, learning the Mathematics behind AI does not simply help us use exisiting technologies, it helps us understand, analyse and gradually develop better ones. #LinearAlgebra #Mathematics #ArtificialIntelligence #MachineLearning #MathematicalFoundations #MathematicsInAI The Mathematics Behind Artificial Intelligence: How Linear Algebra Makes Machines Learn was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: How to Enable Wish-Driven Programming With an Autonomous Multi-Agent Framework
items.summary: Make a wish. Take a nap. Wake up to a built feature. Accept the changes. Wish, sleep, accept, repeat. In three weeks, I shipped an AI-native application to the CEO. Wish-driven programming at a glance. What wish-driven programming is DeepSeek introduced the term wish-driven programming (许愿式编程) on 17 October 2026, as the headline of its model release. DeepSeek did not define this concept, here is my interpretation. In wish-driven programming, the human requests a deliverable, such as a feature, an artifact, or a report, and accepts it when it is done. Agents do everything in between: planning, implementation, testing, reviews. Wish-driven programming is an autopilot mode of working, as opposed to a copilot mode. In copilot mode, the human sits inside the loop, so one person’s attention caps throughput. In autopilot mode, the human sits at the two ends of the loop. It frees the human’s attention and productivity at the cost of controls. The term names an outcome, not a method. It does not say how agents can be trusted to work unattended, and an autopilot without built-in quality assurance is only vibe coding at scale. The question for this post is therefore which framework produces the outcome reliably, and what it gains. Proof first Before I show you the framework itself, I want to show what it delivered. Recently, I built an AI-native application for the CEO, solo, in three weeks. A designer gave me the UI design. Agents did everything else. I did not write a single line of code. On the peak day, the agents added 17.6K lines of code. That is about 10 times an average day of a top-10% Cursor developer, or 124 times a median Cursor developer ( Cursor usage data, Spring 2026 ). Figure 1. 3-week building history with the proposed coding framework. Productivity measured in daily line of codes, benchmarking Cursor developers. The framework The framework is a multi-agent framework inspired by Superpowers ’s workstream and Anthropic’s orchestration ( Anthropic, 2026 ), which suggests a strong orchestrator holds the plan and delegates each step to a role subagent that works in its own context. The framework has three components. Agents and subagents do the work. Tools give them their capabilities. Workstreams define repeatable sequences of steps, with quality assurance built in. The framework is not limited to programming: it fits any task that agents can split into steps and verify, such as research. The concepts carry over across platforms, though the configuration files may differ. The design has three benefits. First, the orchestrator’s context stays clean , because subagents return summaries and not their working history. The agent also controls its own handover: it decides what to carry forward, instead of leaving that choice to an automatic compaction. Second, independent tasks run in parallel , each in its own git worktree, which shortens the wall-clock time. Third, the orchestrator matches each task to the right subagent and model , reserving the strongest model for planning and review. I present these as design reasons, not as measured gains over a single agent. Why not a single agent? A single agent can run in autopilot mode, but it risks breaking down on long jobs for two reasons. First, accuracy falls as the context grows: in one 2026 agentic benchmark, three frontier models lost about half to two thirds of their accuracy between 8K and 128K tokens ( LOCA-bench ). Auto-compaction does not fix this and can drop the agent’s instructions, with policy violations rising from 0% to 30% in one 2026 study ( Chen, 2026 ). Second, one agent runs one model for the whole job, which makes it hard to match capability and cost to each task. The orchestrator design answers both: a clean context for the first, a matched model for the second. Agents and subagents The framework has one and only one primary agent, the orchestrator, and multiple subagents. OpenCode, for example, defaults to two primary agents, Build and Plan. I find it unnecessary, because even the Build agent recognizes plan tasks well from built-in workstreams. Other primary agents disrupt the flow. Orchestrator The orchestrator functions as the project lead. It holds the goal and the plan, splits the work into tasks, decides which tasks are independent enough to run in parallel, delegates each task to a subagent, checks and integrates the results, and reports to the human. It does minimal work itself, which keeps its context clean. The orchestrator needs: Model: a strong model like Opus 5.5. Since this is your primary agent, you may switch the model depending on the tasks. Instructions: the R&R boundary of each subagent. Better undefined than duplicated. Tools: discussed in the next section. Subagents Subagents can be defined by role, such as implementer, reviewer and researcher, or by model. Both work, and the choice is a personal preference. The hard requirement is the same either way: each subagent needs a clear R&R boundary that does not overlap with any other, and it is bound to one model-reasoning level, unless the platform supports dynamic orchestration such as Claude’s dynamic workflows. Table 1 shows the roster I used for OpenCode, with R&R boundaries curated from Artificial Analysis . Table 1. My OpenCode subagent roster. This is an example for illustration, not a universal solution. Some best practices in subagent assignment: Implementation: a weaker model, which avoids overthinking. Challenging work such as debugging: a strong model. Repetitive work such as research across sources: multiple cheap models in parallel. Review: a different family than the planner and the implementer. For example, plan with Opus 5.5, implement with Sonnet 5.5, and review with GPT-6.1-sol ( Panickssery et al., 2024 ; Goel et al., 2025 ). Set a step cap for each subagent. Step repetition was among the most frequent failure modes of multi-agent systems ( Cemri et al., 2025 ). Call a reviewer subagent only at major milestones and critical steps. Frequent reviews by a different model family confuse the implementer. I paid my tuition for this lesson. (Optional) Control subagent access to authorization and tools to deterministically enforce R&R boundaries. Tools Tools enable the agents to perform tasks. Types of tools include: Connectors , aka MCP: the toolbox. Skills : the operation manual. Hooks : the safety interlocks. They act on rule-based triggers, independent of the LLM. Plugins : the three tools above, sometimes plus subagents, in a bundle. One may individualize tool access for each agent and subagent for better control and context engineering, at the cost of management complexity. Workstreams The workstreams are what separate this framework from an autopilot without checks, guiding agent-subagent interactions. They may be integrated as a skill for the primary agent to load on demand. Here are three simple, practical examples. Research Figure 2. The research workstream. It uses a fan-out structure to speed up the work. Evaluation Figure 3. The evaluation workstream. It automates test and evaluation processes with an A/B test on a golden dataset and LLM-as-a-judge. Feature development Figure 4. The feature development workstream, inspired by Superpowers. Superpowers is a popular open-source coding agent workstream to start with. It incorporates several valuable development concepts: subagent-driven development (SDD), spec-driven development, test-driven development (TDD), and brainstorming with mock-ups. I updated the Superpowers workstream from a couple of usage frictions to propose this feature development workstream. Key changes are: Invoke the reviewer subagent after each development stage. Superpowers invokes the reviewer after each task. That approach magnifies the model differences, and usually overcomplicates the development. Encourage parallel subagent-driven development. Add the optional research and evaluation workstreams from the previous examples. Limits and what comes next This framework is not a universal solution. A couple of limitations: It is simple, not optimal. I share this framework because it is robust, easy to set up, and easy for beginners to understand. Other advanced frameworks are available, see below. The human is still a limit. Agents cannot replace good taste. Autopilot trades control for attention. Though the framework is autonomous, the human is welcome to engage mid-stream on reviews and approvals for better quality control. Other frameworks to explore: Matt Pocock’s skills (311k): small, composable skills for everyday engineering. ECC (296k): an agent harness with a large catalog of agents, skills, hooks and memory. spec-kit (147k): GitHub’s spec-driven development scaffolding. ruflo (81k): a meta-harness with agent swarms, memory and hooks. oh-my-openagent (71k): a harness that routes each task to a model by role. BMAD-METHOD (55k): an agile method with persona agents. dsh-superagent (16.5k): DeepSeek’s Super Agent, a research prototype of a proactive coding agent. pstack (15k, parent repo): a Cursor-first library of 23 playbooks. Autopilot is not always the right mode. The next article compares autopilot with copilot, the mode where the human works inside the loop. It asks when each mode fits, what each costs in attention and control, and how to move between them during one project. items.summary_html:
Make a wish. Take a nap. Wake up to a built feature. Accept the changes.
Wish, sleep, accept, repeat.
In three weeks, I shipped an AI-native application to the CEO.Wish-driven programming at a glance.What wish-driven programming is

DeepSeek introduced the term wish-driven programming (许愿式编程) on 17 October 2026, as the headline of its model release. DeepSeek did not define this concept, here is my interpretation. In wish-driven programming, the human requests a deliverable, such as a feature, an artifact, or a report, and accepts it when it is done. Agents do everything in between: planning, implementation, testing, reviews.

Wish-driven programming is an autopilot mode of working, as opposed to a copilot mode. In copilot mode, the human sits inside the loop, so one person’s attention caps throughput. In autopilot mode, the human sits at the two ends of the loop. It frees the human’s attention and productivity at the cost of controls.

The term names an outcome, not a method. It does not say how agents can be trusted to work unattended, and an autopilot without built-in quality assurance is only vibe coding at scale. The question for this post is therefore which framework produces the outcome reliably, and what it gains.

Proof first

Before I show you the framework itself, I want to show what it delivered. Recently, I built an AI-native application for the CEO, solo, in three weeks. A designer gave me the UI design. Agents did everything else. I did not write a single line of code.

On the peak day, the agents added 17.6K lines of code. That is about 10 times an average day of a top-10% Cursor developer, or 124 times a median Cursor developer (Cursor usage data, Spring 2026).

Figure 1. 3-week building history with the proposed coding framework. Productivity measured in daily line of codes, benchmarking Cursor developers.The framework

The framework is a multi-agent framework inspired by Superpowers’s workstream and Anthropic’s orchestration (Anthropic, 2026), which suggests a strong orchestrator holds the plan and delegates each step to a role subagent that works in its own context.

The framework has three components.

  • Agents and subagents do the work.
  • Tools give them their capabilities.
  • Workstreams define repeatable sequences of steps, with quality assurance built in.

The framework is not limited to programming: it fits any task that agents can split into steps and verify, such as research. The concepts carry over across platforms, though the configuration files may differ.

The design has three benefits. First, the orchestrator’s context stays clean, because subagents return summaries and not their working history. The agent also controls its own handover: it decides what to carry forward, instead of leaving that choice to an automatic compaction. Second, independent tasks run in parallel, each in its own git worktree, which shortens the wall-clock time. Third, the orchestrator matches each task to the right subagent and model, reserving the strongest model for planning and review. I present these as design reasons, not as measured gains over a single agent.

Why not a single agent?

A single agent can run in autopilot mode, but it risks breaking down on long jobs for two reasons. First, accuracy falls as the context grows: in one 2026 agentic benchmark, three frontier models lost about half to two thirds of their accuracy between 8K and 128K tokens (LOCA-bench). Auto-compaction does not fix this and can drop the agent’s instructions, with policy violations rising from 0% to 30% in one 2026 study (Chen, 2026). Second, one agent runs one model for the whole job, which makes it hard to match capability and cost to each task. The orchestrator design answers both: a clean context for the first, a matched model for the second.

Agents and subagents

The framework has one and only one primary agent, the orchestrator, and multiple subagents. OpenCode, for example, defaults to two primary agents, Build and Plan. I find it unnecessary, because even the Build agent recognizes plan tasks well from built-in workstreams. Other primary agents disrupt the flow.

Orchestrator

The orchestrator functions as the project lead. It holds the goal and the plan, splits the work into tasks, decides which tasks are independent enough to run in parallel, delegates each task to a subagent, checks and integrates the results, and reports to the human. It does minimal work itself, which keeps its context clean.

The orchestrator needs:

  • Model: a strong model like Opus 5.5. Since this is your primary agent, you may switch the model depending on the tasks.
  • Instructions: the R&R boundary of each subagent. Better undefined than duplicated.
  • Tools: discussed in the next section.

Subagents

Subagents can be defined by role, such as implementer, reviewer and researcher, or by model. Both work, and the choice is a personal preference. The hard requirement is the same either way: each subagent needs a clear R&R boundary that does not overlap with any other, and it is bound to one model-reasoning level, unless the platform supports dynamic orchestration such as Claude’s dynamic workflows. Table 1 shows the roster I used for OpenCode, with R&R boundaries curated from Artificial Analysis.

Table 1. My OpenCode subagent roster. This is an example for illustration, not a universal solution.

Some best practices in subagent assignment:

  • Implementation: a weaker model, which avoids overthinking.
  • Challenging work such as debugging: a strong model.
  • Repetitive work such as research across sources: multiple cheap models in parallel.
  • Review: a different family than the planner and the implementer. For example, plan with Opus 5.5, implement with Sonnet 5.5, and review with GPT-6.1-sol (Panickssery et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2025).
  • Set a step cap for each subagent. Step repetition was among the most frequent failure modes of multi-agent systems (Cemri et al., 2025).
  • Call a reviewer subagent only at major milestones and critical steps. Frequent reviews by a different model family confuse the implementer. I paid my tuition for this lesson.
  • (Optional) Control subagent access to authorization and tools to deterministically enforce R&R boundaries.
Tools

Tools enable the agents to perform tasks. Types of tools include:

  • Connectors, aka MCP: the toolbox.
  • Skills: the operation manual.
  • Hooks: the safety interlocks. They act on rule-based triggers, independent of the LLM.
  • Plugins: the three tools above, sometimes plus subagents, in a bundle.

One may individualize tool access for each agent and subagent for better control and context engineering, at the cost of management complexity.

Workstreams

The workstreams are what separate this framework from an autopilot without checks, guiding agent-subagent interactions. They may be integrated as a skill for the primary agent to load on demand. Here are three simple, practical examples.

Research

Figure 2. The research workstream. It uses a fan-out structure to speed up the work.

Evaluation

Figure 3. The evaluation workstream. It automates test and evaluation processes with an A/B test on a golden dataset and LLM-as-a-judge.

Feature development

Figure 4. The feature development workstream, inspired by Superpowers.

Superpowers is a popular open-source coding agent workstream to start with. It incorporates several valuable development concepts: subagent-driven development (SDD), spec-driven development, test-driven development (TDD), and brainstorming with mock-ups.

I updated the Superpowers workstream from a couple of usage frictions to propose this feature development workstream. Key changes are:

  • Invoke the reviewer subagent after each development stage. Superpowers invokes the reviewer after each task. That approach magnifies the model differences, and usually overcomplicates the development.
  • Encourage parallel subagent-driven development.
  • Add the optional research and evaluation workstreams from the previous examples.
Limits and what comes next

This framework is not a universal solution. A couple of limitations:

  • It is simple, not optimal. I share this framework because it is robust, easy to set up, and easy for beginners to understand. Other advanced frameworks are available, see below.
  • The human is still a limit. Agents cannot replace good taste.
  • Autopilot trades control for attention. Though the framework is autonomous, the human is welcome to engage mid-stream on reviews and approvals for better quality control.

Other frameworks to explore:

  • Matt Pocock’s skills (311k): small, composable skills for everyday engineering.
  • ECC (296k): an agent harness with a large catalog of agents, skills, hooks and memory.
  • spec-kit (147k): GitHub’s spec-driven development scaffolding.
  • ruflo (81k): a meta-harness with agent swarms, memory and hooks.
  • oh-my-openagent (71k): a harness that routes each task to a model by role.
  • BMAD-METHOD (55k): an agile method with persona agents.
  • dsh-superagent (16.5k): DeepSeek’s Super Agent, a research prototype of a proactive coding agent.
  • pstack (15k, parent repo): a Cursor-first library of 23 playbooks.

Autopilot is not always the right mode. The next article compares autopilot with copilot, the mode where the human works inside the loop. It asks when each mode fits, what each costs in attention and control, and how to move between them during one project.

How to Enable Wish-Driven Programming With an Autonomous Multi-Agent Framework was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: From 137 Bytes to 2.7: How Much Space Does Factory Data Really Take? UNS to Lakehouse — Part 3
items.summary: One day of a virtual bottling plant, stored eleven different ways. The winner is 51 times smaller than the raw messages, and two of the “optimizations” along the way made things worse. A pressure sensor reports 800.53 mbar. The number takes six characters, but the message carrying it through the Unified Namespace takes 134 bytes. That gap is easy to ignore with one sensor. A plant with a few thousand signals publishes millions of such messages a day. Most teams that decide to “just keep the history” start by writing those messages to disk as they arrive. That is a sensible first step, and an expensive one if it becomes the long-term format. In Part 2 we built a virtual factory: three lines, eight machines, 37 signals, faults, frozen sensors and network outages, all deterministic from a single seed. This post uses one simulated day of that factory to answer a narrow question with real numbers: how much space does this data take, and which storage decisions actually matter? The setup The experiment simulates 24 hours of the plant, with seed 42 and report-by-exception enabled. That produces 1,158,046 published readings . The same table is then written in eleven formats: Text formats: JSON lines (one raw MQTT message per line, topic plus payload) and CSV, each with and without gzip. Parquet with different codecs: uncompressed, snappy and zstd. Parquet tuned further: a different sort order, delta-encoded timestamps, byte-stream-split floats, and a different way of storing the delivery time. Each variant is written three times, and the median write time is reported. For Parquet, the script also reads the file metadata to see how many bytes each column takes. Everything runs with one command: git clone https://github.com/BuseKaylan/uns-to-lakehouse.git cd uns-to-lakehouse make install make bench-storage All results are committed to the repository under benchmarks/results/01_storage_footprint/ as CSV and JSON, together with the Python and library versions that produced them. My numbers come from a 16-core Intel MacBook running Python 3.14 and pyarrow 26. File sizes are identical on any machine, because the data is deterministic. Write times will differ. Anatomy of one message Before comparing formats, it helps to look at what is being stored. Here is one reading as a raw UNS message: {"topic": "acme-plant/filling-area/line-1/filler/pressure", "payload": {"value": 800.53, "unit": "mbar", "timestamp": 1767592800000}} Of its 134 bytes: 46 are the topic path, which is the same on every pressure message from this machine. 65 are keys, quotes, braces and spaces, which are identical in every message. 13 are the timestamp, and 4 are a unit that never changes. 6 are the measurement itself. Averaged over the whole day, a message is 137.15 bytes . Raw JSON is not wasteful because JSON is bad. It is wasteful because each message is written to be understood on its own, without knowing what came before. That is exactly right on the wire and exactly wrong on disk. Round 1: text formats CSV removes the repeated keys but keeps the repeated topic path, so it only saves about 20%. Gzip is the real step: 21 to 22 times smaller than raw JSON. That shows how much repetition there is to remove. The catch is that a gzip file is one opaque stream. To answer “what was the average vibration on line 2 between 14:00 and 15:00”, a query engine has to decompress and parse the whole day. Text plus gzip is a good archive format, not a good analytics format. A note on the write times: the JSON writer is a Python loop that builds one dictionary per row, while CSV and Parquet are written by Arrow’s C++ code. The gap says more about Python vs. C++ than about the formats themselves. Round 2: columns instead of rows Parquet stores each column separately. That one change lets every column use the encoding that suits it. Laid out by column, the hierarchy becomes trivial to compress: A column like machine is just a handful of distinct strings repeated over and over. Parquet stores a small dictionary once (filler, capper, labeler…) and then only small integer indices. A column like event_ts has long runs of the same value, because every sensor publishes in the same second. Runs are encoded once with a count. Uncompressed Parquet, with no compression codec at all, is already 15 times smaller than JSON. Encoding alone does most of the work. With zstd the file is 29 times smaller, beats gzipped text, and stays fully queryable by column. Writing it took about 0.4 seconds. Where the bytes go A file size alone doesn’t say what to fix next. Parquet records the compressed size of every column in its metadata, so we can look inside. In the zstd file: value takes 3.49 MB of the 5.52 MB total. The two timestamps take 0.81 MB. The five hierarchy columns (area, line, machine, metric, unit) still take 1.21 MB . That last number looks like an obvious target. The usual advice for time-series data is to sort by series and then by time, which puts each sensor’s history in one stretch. So that is the next experiment. Surprise 1: sorting made the file bigger Sorting by area, line, machine, metric, event_ts did exactly what was expected for the strings: the hierarchy columns went from 1.21 MB to 0.02 MB . The values improved as well, from 3.49 MB to 2.51 MB, because neighbouring values now come from the same sensor and look alike. The file still went from 5.52 MB up to 8.18 MB . The cost moved to the timestamps: In arrival order , dozens of readings in a row share the same second. The timestamp column is long runs of identical values, which dictionary and run-length encoding handle almost for free. Sorted by sensor , every row has a different timestamp. The dictionary now holds 86,400 distinct seconds, every row needs a 17-bit index into it, and the two timestamp columns grow from 0.81 MB to 5.63 MB . The fix is to store timestamps the way a sorted column wants to be stored: as differences. Delta encoding (DELTA_BINARY_PACKED in Parquet) keeps the first value and then only the gaps: +1000, +2000, +3000 milliseconds. Those gaps fit in a few bits. The lesson: a sort order is not an optimization on its own. It changes which columns are cheap and which are expensive, and it only pays off when the encodings follow. Surprise 2: the float encoding that didn’t help Parquet also offers BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT, an encoding designed for floating-point data. It regroups the bytes of each float so the compressor sees similar bytes next to each other. It is often recommended for sensor measurements. On this data it made the value column 65% larger : 2.51 MB → 4.13 MB. The reason is in the data. The simulator rounds to three decimals, the way most PLCs and gateways report, and report-by-exception only publishes when a value moves. As a result there are only 219,174 distinct values among 1.16 million readings . That suits dictionary encoding, which byte-stream-split replaces. On raw high-resolution floats the result could well be the opposite. The result belongs to this data, not to the encoding, and that is exactly why it was measured instead of assumed. Surprise 3: the column that was mostly a copy The schema carries two timestamps: event_ts: when the value was measured. delivered_ts: when it reached the broker. They differ only for readings that were buffered during a network outage and forwarded later. That is what store-and-forward means, and the late readings are flagged as historical. In this day that is 22,601 readings, about 2% . For the other 98%, delivered_ts is an exact copy of event_ts, and it still cost 0.57 MB, about 15% of the file. Storing the delay in milliseconds instead (delay_ms = delivered_ts - event_ts) loses nothing, because the delivery time can always be recomputed. But the column becomes a long run of zeros, broken only by outages, and it shrinks to 0.03 MB . In this final file, value is 80% of the bytes and event_ts most of the rest. Everything describing where a reading came from costs almost nothing. What remains is mostly the measurements themselves, which is where a storage format should spend its bytes. The full scoreboard For 37 signals, the difference is 58 GB a year against 1.1 GB a year. Scaled linearly to a plant with 10,000 signals, it is roughly 15.7 TB against 310 GB . That is the difference between a storage project and a rounding error. What report-by-exception saves on disk Report-by-exception publishes a value only when it moves past a deadband, or when a heartbeat interval expires. In this factory, sensors took 2,090,880 samples during the day and published 1,158,046 of them, about 55%. To see what that is worth on disk, the experiment runs the same day a second time with report-by-exception turned off, and writes both runs as raw JSON and as the best Parquet variant. In JSON, the saving follows the message count almost exactly, because every message costs the same. In Parquet the saving is smaller, because the readings that report-by-exception drops are exactly the ones that compress best: values that didn’t change, at regular intervals. A good columnar format already removes much of that redundancy on its own. Report-by-exception still matters, mainly for the broker, the network and every consumer that has to process each message. For storage, the format decision is worth far more than the publishing policy. What this decides for the table design Never keep raw JSON as the history. Even untuned Parquet is 15 times smaller and can be queried by column. Use zstd. On this data it is a third smaller than snappy, at no measurable cost in write time. Sort by sensor, then time, inside each file. The hierarchy columns become nearly free and the values compress better. Delta-encode timestamps whenever data is sorted. Without it, sorting makes things worse. Store the delivery delay, not a second timestamp. The late-data information stays and costs almost nothing. Measure before tuning float encodings. The “right” encoding depends on resolution and on how often values repeat. Limitations This is simulated data from one virtual plant, not a real factory. Real signals have more noise, more resolution and more irregular publishing. The relative ordering of the formats should hold, but the exact ratios will not. One day was written as one file. Real ingestion writes many smaller files over time, and each file pays its own overhead. That is a separate problem with its own experiment later in the series. Write times come from one laptop, and they compare a Python JSON writer with Arrow’s native writers. Nothing here includes table-format metadata yet. The numbers are the pure Parquet cost of the data. The next question follows directly: so far every reading has been one row with one value. Part 4 compares that narrow layout with wide and hybrid tables, where one row holds a whole machine. The full code, raw results and charts are in the repository: github.com/BuseKaylan/uns-to-lakehouse . From 137 Bytes to 2.7: How Much Space Does Factory Data Really Take? items.summary_html:
One day of a virtual bottling plant, stored eleven different ways. The winner is 51 times smaller than the raw messages, and two of the “optimizations” along the way made things worse.

A pressure sensor reports 800.53 mbar. The number takes six characters, but the message carrying it through the Unified Namespace takes 134 bytes.

That gap is easy to ignore with one sensor. A plant with a few thousand signals publishes millions of such messages a day. Most teams that decide to “just keep the history” start by writing those messages to disk as they arrive. That is a sensible first step, and an expensive one if it becomes the long-term format.

In Part 2 we built a virtual factory: three lines, eight machines, 37 signals, faults, frozen sensors and network outages, all deterministic from a single seed. This post uses one simulated day of that factory to answer a narrow question with real numbers: how much space does this data take, and which storage decisions actually matter?

The setup

The experiment simulates 24 hours of the plant, with seed 42 and report-by-exception enabled. That produces 1,158,046 published readings. The same table is then written in eleven formats:

  • Text formats: JSON lines (one raw MQTT message per line, topic plus payload) and CSV, each with and without gzip.
  • Parquet with different codecs: uncompressed, snappy and zstd.
  • Parquet tuned further: a different sort order, delta-encoded timestamps, byte-stream-split floats, and a different way of storing the delivery time.

Each variant is written three times, and the median write time is reported. For Parquet, the script also reads the file metadata to see how many bytes each column takes. Everything runs with one command:

git clone https://github.com/BuseKaylan/uns-to-lakehouse.git
cd uns-to-lakehouse
make install
make bench-storage

All results are committed to the repository under benchmarks/results/01_storage_footprint/ as CSV and JSON, together with the Python and library versions that produced them. My numbers come from a 16-core Intel MacBook running Python 3.14 and pyarrow 26. File sizes are identical on any machine, because the data is deterministic. Write times will differ.

Anatomy of one message

Before comparing formats, it helps to look at what is being stored.

Here is one reading as a raw UNS message:

{"topic": "acme-plant/filling-area/line-1/filler/pressure",
 "payload": {"value": 800.53, "unit": "mbar", "timestamp": 1767592800000}}

Of its 134 bytes:

  • 46 are the topic path, which is the same on every pressure message from this machine.
  • 65 are keys, quotes, braces and spaces, which are identical in every message.
  • 13 are the timestamp, and 4 are a unit that never changes.
  • 6 are the measurement itself.

Averaged over the whole day, a message is 137.15 bytes. Raw JSON is not wasteful because JSON is bad. It is wasteful because each message is written to be understood on its own, without knowing what came before. That is exactly right on the wire and exactly wrong on disk.

Round 1: text formats

CSV removes the repeated keys but keeps the repeated topic path, so it only saves about 20%. Gzip is the real step: 21 to 22 times smaller than raw JSON. That shows how much repetition there is to remove.

The catch is that a gzip file is one opaque stream. To answer “what was the average vibration on line 2 between 14:00 and 15:00”, a query engine has to decompress and parse the whole day. Text plus gzip is a good archive format, not a good analytics format.

A note on the write times: the JSON writer is a Python loop that builds one dictionary per row, while CSV and Parquet are written by Arrow’s C++ code. The gap says more about Python vs. C++ than about the formats themselves.

Round 2: columns instead of rows

Parquet stores each column separately. That one change lets every column use the encoding that suits it.

Laid out by column, the hierarchy becomes trivial to compress:

  • A column like machine is just a handful of distinct strings repeated over and over. Parquet stores a small dictionary once (filler, capper, labeler…) and then only small integer indices.
  • A column like event_ts has long runs of the same value, because every sensor publishes in the same second. Runs are encoded once with a count.

Uncompressed Parquet, with no compression codec at all, is already 15 times smaller than JSON. Encoding alone does most of the work. With zstd the file is 29 times smaller, beats gzipped text, and stays fully queryable by column. Writing it took about 0.4 seconds.

Where the bytes go

A file size alone doesn’t say what to fix next. Parquet records the compressed size of every column in its metadata, so we can look inside.

In the zstd file:

  • value takes 3.49 MB of the 5.52 MB total.
  • The two timestamps take 0.81 MB.
  • The five hierarchy columns (area, line, machine, metric, unit) still take 1.21 MB.

That last number looks like an obvious target. The usual advice for time-series data is to sort by series and then by time, which puts each sensor’s history in one stretch. So that is the next experiment.

Surprise 1: sorting made the file bigger

Sorting by area, line, machine, metric, event_ts did exactly what was expected for the strings: the hierarchy columns went from 1.21 MB to 0.02 MB. The values improved as well, from 3.49 MB to 2.51 MB, because neighbouring values now come from the same sensor and look alike.

The file still went from 5.52 MB up to 8.18 MB.

The cost moved to the timestamps:

  • In arrival order, dozens of readings in a row share the same second. The timestamp column is long runs of identical values, which dictionary and run-length encoding handle almost for free.
  • Sorted by sensor, every row has a different timestamp. The dictionary now holds 86,400 distinct seconds, every row needs a 17-bit index into it, and the two timestamp columns grow from 0.81 MB to 5.63 MB.

The fix is to store timestamps the way a sorted column wants to be stored: as differences. Delta encoding (DELTA_BINARY_PACKED in Parquet) keeps the first value and then only the gaps: +1000, +2000, +3000 milliseconds. Those gaps fit in a few bits.

The lesson: a sort order is not an optimization on its own. It changes which columns are cheap and which are expensive, and it only pays off when the encodings follow.

Surprise 2: the float encoding that didn’t help

Parquet also offers BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT, an encoding designed for floating-point data. It regroups the bytes of each float so the compressor sees similar bytes next to each other. It is often recommended for sensor measurements.

On this data it made the value column 65% larger: 2.51 MB → 4.13 MB.

The reason is in the data. The simulator rounds to three decimals, the way most PLCs and gateways report, and report-by-exception only publishes when a value moves. As a result there are only 219,174 distinct values among 1.16 million readings. That suits dictionary encoding, which byte-stream-split replaces. On raw high-resolution floats the result could well be the opposite. The result belongs to this data, not to the encoding, and that is exactly why it was measured instead of assumed.

Surprise 3: the column that was mostly a copy

The schema carries two timestamps:

  • event_ts: when the value was measured.
  • delivered_ts: when it reached the broker.

They differ only for readings that were buffered during a network outage and forwarded later. That is what store-and-forward means, and the late readings are flagged as historical. In this day that is 22,601 readings, about 2%. For the other 98%, delivered_ts is an exact copy of event_ts, and it still cost 0.57 MB, about 15% of the file.

Storing the delay in milliseconds instead (delay_ms = delivered_ts - event_ts) loses nothing, because the delivery time can always be recomputed. But the column becomes a long run of zeros, broken only by outages, and it shrinks to 0.03 MB.

In this final file, value is 80% of the bytes and event_ts most of the rest. Everything describing where a reading came from costs almost nothing. What remains is mostly the measurements themselves, which is where a storage format should spend its bytes.

The full scoreboard

For 37 signals, the difference is 58 GB a year against 1.1 GB a year. Scaled linearly to a plant with 10,000 signals, it is roughly 15.7 TB against 310 GB. That is the difference between a storage project and a rounding error.

What report-by-exception saves on disk

Report-by-exception publishes a value only when it moves past a deadband, or when a heartbeat interval expires. In this factory, sensors took 2,090,880 samples during the day and published 1,158,046 of them, about 55%.

To see what that is worth on disk, the experiment runs the same day a second time with report-by-exception turned off, and writes both runs as raw JSON and as the best Parquet variant.

In JSON, the saving follows the message count almost exactly, because every message costs the same. In Parquet the saving is smaller, because the readings that report-by-exception drops are exactly the ones that compress best: values that didn’t change, at regular intervals. A good columnar format already removes much of that redundancy on its own.

Report-by-exception still matters, mainly for the broker, the network and every consumer that has to process each message. For storage, the format decision is worth far more than the publishing policy.

What this decides for the table design
  1. Never keep raw JSON as the history. Even untuned Parquet is 15 times smaller and can be queried by column.
  2. Use zstd. On this data it is a third smaller than snappy, at no measurable cost in write time.
  3. Sort by sensor, then time, inside each file. The hierarchy columns become nearly free and the values compress better.
  4. Delta-encode timestamps whenever data is sorted. Without it, sorting makes things worse.
  5. Store the delivery delay, not a second timestamp. The late-data information stays and costs almost nothing.
  6. Measure before tuning float encodings. The “right” encoding depends on resolution and on how often values repeat.
Limitations
  • This is simulated data from one virtual plant, not a real factory. Real signals have more noise, more resolution and more irregular publishing. The relative ordering of the formats should hold, but the exact ratios will not.
  • One day was written as one file. Real ingestion writes many smaller files over time, and each file pays its own overhead. That is a separate problem with its own experiment later in the series.
  • Write times come from one laptop, and they compare a Python JSON writer with Arrow’s native writers.
  • Nothing here includes table-format metadata yet. The numbers are the pure Parquet cost of the data.

The next question follows directly: so far every reading has been one row with one value. Part 4 compares that narrow layout with wide and hybrid tables, where one row holds a whole machine.

The full code, raw results and charts are in the repository: github.com/BuseKaylan/uns-to-lakehouse.

items.title: Why Your LLM Harness Matters More Than You Think
items.summary: When building cutting-edge AI applications, most engineering teams fixate almost entirely on the core model. We spend endless hours debating parameter counts, context window sizes, or benchmark leaderboards. But in production systems, a Large Language Model rarely operates in isolation. It’s wrapped in software code that manages memory, formats prompts, handles external retrieval, and orchestrates tool calls. This surrounding wrapper code is called the harness . Recent research introduced in the paper Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses shows that optimizing this harness — without changing a single parameter inside the frozen language model — can create up to a 6x performance gap on complex tasks. Despite its massive impact, harness engineering has traditionally been a painful process of manual trial and error or weak automated optimizers. Meta-Harness completely flips this paradigm. It uses an autonomous coding agent with full access to a project’s filesystem to systematically diagnose execution errors and rewrite wrapper code on the fly. Model Weights vs. Harness Engineering To understand why automated harness optimization works so well, it helps to separate weight training from software orchestration: Model Weight Training: Modifies internal neural parameters. It demands massive compute clusters, moves slowly, and stays fixed once deployed. Harness Optimization: Keeps the base model completely frozen. Instead, it refines the stateful Python wrapper around it — adjusting prompt routing, external retrieval schemes, memory stores, and verification loops. The main roadblock in automating harness engineering has been how optimization systems learn from failure. Standard prompt and code optimizers act like an unforgiving professor who hands back an exam with only a letter grade or a brief summary at the top. Because a harness runs over long, multi-turn steps, an error made in step one might manifest as a complete failure ten steps down the line. When diagnostic feedback gets squashed into short text summaries or simple numerical scores, the optimizer ends up guessing blindly because it can’t trace errors back to their original root cause. The Power of Uncompressed Trace Logs Traditional optimizers restrict feedback to tiny context windows or brief LLM summaries to keep things lightweight. As detailed in the Meta-Harness paper , this new framework takes the opposite approach by using a filesystem store that logs full, uncompressed execution histories across every attempt. Instead of squeezing a tiny 2,000 to 26,000-token summary into a prompt — which is what legacy optimizers like OPRO, TextGrad, or GEPA do — Meta-Harness opens up a diagnostic surface of up to 10 million tokens per iteration. That is roughly three orders of magnitude more context for troubleshooting. When feedback gets compressed, vital clues vanish. A summary might report: “The task timed out.” But it completely misses the underlying bug — like an intermediate sanity check accidentally resetting a completion flag mid-run. By saving every raw tool call, API request, state change, and system error into structured folders, the optimizing agent can read the exact transcripts, pinpoint the exact breakdown, and write targeted fixes. Inside the Filesystem Optimization Loop Instead of stuffing millions of log tokens directly into a single prompt, Meta-Harness organizes diagnostic records cleanly inside a local directory tree. An LLM coding agent acts as the “Proposer” and navigates this history using standard terminal commands like grep, cat, and diff. Inspect & Propose: The coding agent searches past log histories using command-line tools to form a clear hypothesis, then writes a new candidate Python harness. Evaluate: An automated runner executes the proposed harness over a small, challenging benchmark set to measure real-world performance. Log & Store: The new candidate code, step-by-step execution traces, and evaluation scores are saved into a fresh filesystem folder to inform future runs. Log analysis reveals something fascinating: the proposing agent doesn’t just iterate linearly on its last try. It performs non-Markovian search , actively digging back into candidate folders created days or runs ago. In a typical run, the agent inspects over 80 files per iteration. It spends about 41% of its time reading source code, 40% inspecting raw execution traces, 13% checking helper scripts, and just 6% looking at summary scores. By isolating confounding variables — like distinguishing helpful code changes from harmful prompt rewrites — the agent methodically tests ideas instead of throwing random code at the wall. Real-World Performance Across Benchmarks The empirical results published in the arXiv preprint showcase Meta-Harness across three distinct technical domains, consistently outperforming both manual engineering and existing state-of-the-art optimizers: 1. Online Text Classification Higher Accuracy: Running with GPT-OSS-120B on complex datasets like LawBench and USPTO-50k, the discovered harnesses hit an 48.6% average accuracy . That beats top hand-engineered setups like Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) by 7.7 percentage points . Token Efficiency: It achieved these gains while using 4x fewer context tokens than competing frameworks. Rapid Convergence: It reached peak baseline performance in just 4 evaluations , converging 10x faster than traditional prompt optimizers. The Draft-Verification Trick: The system discovered a clever two-stage harness logic on its own. Stage 1 generates an initial draft label using the top 5 memory matches. Stage 2 re-queries memory for 5 confirmers (matching the draft) and 5 challengers (differing labels), forcing the model to explicitly evaluate counterexamples before locking in its answer. 2. Retrieval-Augmented Math Reasoning Emergent Routing: Across a corpus of 535,000 math problems, Meta-Harness evolved a compact four-route retrieval system. It automatically categorizes incoming queries into specialized subjects (Combinatorics, Geometry, Number Theory, and Algebra) using a custom tokenizer that preserves LaTeX math formatting. Olympiad-Level Scaling: On 200 hard IMO-level problems, the discovered harness boosted accuracy by 4.7 percentage points over non-retrieval baselines across five different models (including GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Gemini-3-Flash). Zero-Shot Transfer: Remarkably, the retrieval architecture was optimized once on a single model and transferred seamlessly to four other models without needing any retraining. 3. Agentic Coding on TerminalBench-2 Leaderboard Top Spot: On TerminalBench-2 (a suite of 89 complex command-line tasks), Meta-Harness discovered a wrapper that ranked #1 among all Claude Haiku 4.5 agents (37.6% pass rate) and #2 among Opus 4.6 agents (76.4% pass rate). Environment Bootstrapping: The agent figured out that running a single compound shell command before turn 1 — gathering working directories, environment variables, installed compilers, and memory limits eliminated 2 to 4 wasted exploratory turns per task, saving critical turn budgets. Takeaways for AI Developers If you’re building production AI tools, there are three key lessons to take from this research: Focus on the Harness: The software wrapper around your model often yields far larger gains than tweaking basic prompt templates. Keep the Raw Diagnostics: Don’t throw away execution logs or rely solely on summary scores. Full execution traces are where the clues live for fixing long-horizon bugs. Give Agents File Access: Rather than cramming long conversation histories into context prompts, store execution logs in a local directory and give your agent terminal tools (grep, cat) so it can inspect its own history when troubleshooting. For a full deep dive into the methodology, experimental setups, and code representations, check out the complete paper on arXiv (2603.28052) . items.summary_html:
Nous Research has released Arete-27B, a supervised fine-tune of Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-27B. Arete-27B is a 27B open-weight model that strips Chinese state framing from Qwen’s answers. On Nous’s own 803-prompt eval, answers containing propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Developers get Qwen-class agentic skill without state-aligned answers. The weights, eval and training data are all public.

TL;DR
  • Size: 27B dense parameters (all active). Trained at 64k context. Base Qwen3.8-27B supports 262,144 tokens natively.
  • Runs on: BF16 weights are 53.81 GB. A community Q4_K_M quant is 17.20 GB, sized for 24 GB consumer GPUs.
  • Performance: Capability unchanged on the benchmarks Nous ran; political framing now matches Western models.
  • Best: Propaganda rate 0.9%, down from 22% for base Qwen3.8-27B.
  • Worst: Fact score 2.98 of 5; 216 of 803 answers still score 0.
What is Arete-27B?

Arete-27B is Qwen3.8-27B after supervised fine-tuning only. Nous used no RL, no preference optimization and no architecture changes. The license is Apache 2.0, matching the base model.

Nous team states that it saw refusals, deflections and CCP-framed answers on sensitive topics in the base model. It picked Qwen3.8-27B because it was the most capable local model and showed the target behavior.

How was Arete-27B trained?

The teacher was Inkling, an open model from Thinking Machines. Nous chose an open teacher to avoid terms-of-use limits on distillation. It rejected Nemotron 3 Ultra after finding a checkered record on China topics.

Training covered about 52.8 million tokens at 64k context, without sequence packing. The run took 2 epochs and 1,202 steps at batch size 48. It used AdamW, a 1e-5 peak learning rate and tensor parallel 4.

All language-model weights were trained. The vision encoder stayed frozen, since the data is text-only. The multi-token-prediction head was disabled.

The released arete-data-pairs set holds 34,878 prompts across 7 topics. Each prompt has both an Inkling answer and a Qwen answer. 29,236 accepted teacher answers form the SFT split.

How does the propaganda eval work?

The Propaganda_Eval set has 803 prompts across 7 value categories. These include freedom of expression, state ideology, data privacy and democracy. Each prompt carries 2 to 4 required facts from a cited source.

A Grok 4.7 judge grades two things separately:

  • Fact mean (0 to 5): how many required facts the answer states. One opposed fact scores 0.
  • Any propaganda: share of answers that adopt the state’s account as their own.

The judge must quote the exact phrase to flag propaganda. Nous removed every training prompt that overlapped the eval. The eval is MIT licensed and includes grading scripts.

&

What do the benchmarks show?

On the model card page, Arete-27B raised fact mean from 2.32 to 2.98. Propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Answers scoring 0 dropped from 359 to 216 of 803.

The biggest change came in freedom of expression. Fact score rose from 0.89 to 2.44, and propaganda fell from 60% to 1%.

Capability held on Nous’s tests. Hermes Bench moved from 65.77% to 65.60%, which Nous calls noise. Terminal-Bench-2.1 rose from 67% to 70% in Nous’s harness. Nous does not claim credit for that gain.

How does Arete-27B compare? MetricsArete-27BQwen3.8-27BMuse Glimmer 30BGemma 4 31BDeveloperNous ResearchAlibaba QwenMetaGoogle DeepMindParameters27B dense27B LM, dense29.6B incl. vision, dense30.7B, denseContextNot disclosed (trained at 64k)262,144 native, up to 1M131,072+256KLicenseApache 2.0Apache 2.0Apache 2.0Apache 2.0InputText, image (encoder frozen)Text, image, videoText, imageText, image4-bit footprint17.20 GB Q4_K_M (community)Not disclosedUnder 20 GB, 24 GB VRAM targetNot disclosedFact mean, Nous eval2.982.323.022.58Any propaganda, Nous eval0.9%22%0.5%0.5%Terminal-Bench 2.170% (Nous harness)67% Nous harness; 73.0 official51.7 (Meta, terminus2)Not disclosed by GoogleGPQA DiamondNot disclosed89.283.584.3

Note: Arete and Qwen ran at temperature 0 in the Nous eval. Muse Glimmer and Gemma ran at 0.6. Terminal-Bench figures come from different harnesses.

How can developers run it?

Weights ship in BF16 on Hugging Face. No hosted inference provider serves the model yet. Community GGUF quants run in llama.cpp, LM Studio and Ollama, from 8.64 GB to 53.81 GB. The GGUF build also includes the image projector.

Key Takeaways
  • Arete-27B cuts Qwen3.8-27B propaganda answers from 22% to 0.9%.
  • The fix took only 52.8M tokens of plain SFT, no RL.
  • Hermes Bench held at 65.60% versus 65.77% for the base.
  • Fact recall rose to 2.98 of 5 but still trails peers.
  • Weights, eval and training data are open under Apache 2.0 and MIT.

Check out the model weights, technical blog, evaluation set and training data. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.
